subject: ALED
title: Personal Leadership Education
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Development, application and reflection of personal leadership capabilities through self-assessments and experiential learning activities; development of leadership identity through personal leadership inventories including strengths, personality type, values, vision and emotional intelligence. Prerequisite: ALED or USAL-LED major; junior, or senior classification; grade of C or better in ALED 202 .
prereq_text: ALED or USAL-LED major; junior, or senior classification; grade of C or better in ALED 202 .

subject: ALED
title: Cultural Leadership and Exploration for Society
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Social theories in terms of class, gender, race, ethnicity, and nationality; multidisciplinary approach to the study of leadership with a special emphasis on culture.

subject: ALED
title: Leadership for a Multicultural World
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles of multicultural leadership; how to be an effective leader while understanding the self in terms of class, gender, race, ethnicity, and nationality; special emphasis on culture through experiential learning.

subject: ALED
title: Leadership and Identity Development
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Identity development and leadership; dialogue about the implications of their multiple identities in the classroom organizations and in their careers; self-reflections concerning leadership development and active community-based service learning. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Agricultural Extension Philosophy and the Land-Grant Mission
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy of Cooperative Extension and roles within the land-grant system; history, organization, program areas and guiding principles; relationship with the teaching and research branches of the land-grant system. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ALED
title: Survey of Leadership Theory
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of leadership as a scholarly discipline; critical analysis of and evolution of multiple leadership models and theories; synthesis of leadership theory through experiential learning; integration of course content with personal experiences. Prerequisites: ALED or USAL-LED major, junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: ALED or USAL-LED major, junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Team Learning
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Team development theory; emphasizes research on team member behaviors, team decision making models and positive conflict in team environments. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ALED 340 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ALED 340 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Leadership of Volunteers
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles, theories, concepts, techniques and applications for leading volunteers in agriculture and life sciences nonprofit, governmental and community organizations. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ALED 340 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ALED 340 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Public Leadership Development
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Major issues in the study of public leadership, development of leadership skills, and a field investigation done in conjunction with local public leaders. Prerequisites: Junior classification and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior classification and approval of instructor.

subject: ALED
title: Advanced Professional Leadership Development
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Investigation of the best practices of successful leaders representing various organizational contexts; merging of scholarly mastery of theory with practice. Prerequisites: Selection for ALED Leadership Fellows Program; grade of C or better in ALED 340 or ALED 301 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Selection for ALED Leadership Fellows Program; grade of C or better in ALED 340 or ALED 301 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Followers and Followership
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of the role of followers and followership; identification of follower motivations, followership styles, leader and follower dynamics, and characteristics of courageous followers. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ALED 340 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ALED 340 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Cultural Pluralism in Agriculture
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Selected topics on the diversity of human resources in agriculture; emphasis on working in a multicultural society and developing a sensitivity toward different cultures; explores the interrelationships between the contributions of diverse individuals and the state, nation and global success of agriculture. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Applied Ethics in Leadership
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of ethical and moral theories and the application to multiple leadership contexts and situations. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Leading and Training Adult Learners
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Planning educational training programs, including leadership programs, to implement with an adult audience; includes needs assessment, instructional design, lesson plan development, evaluation and other items related to leading adults. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ALED 340 , junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ALED 340 , junior or senior classification.

subject: ALED
title: Leading Change
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Analysis of change models and theories and the leadership application on individual, organizational and societal changes. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; grade of C or better in ALED 202 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; grade of C or better in ALED 202 .

title: Agricultural Extension Organization and Methods
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Cooperative extension in agriculture and home economics; development, objectives, organization, program building and methods of teaching. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

title: Seminar
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Individual and team approaches to the review of leadership concepts and their application; observation and discussion of current leadership trends and issues. subject: ANSC
title: Introductory Seminar for Animal Science
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Orientation to programs and opportunities in the Department of Animal Science, to create an awareness of campus resources for financial aid and tutoring, to develop goals for college career and to initiate planning for internship and job opportunities.

subject: ANSC
title: General Animal Science
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (AGRI 1319, 1419*) General Animal Science. General understanding of all aspects of the livestock industry; basic agriculture nomenclature of breeds, species and types of livestock; reproduction, nutrition, genetics, food safety, growth and development of beef cattle, sheep, horses, swine, dairy cattle and poultry; brief description of the companion animal industry.

subject: ANSC
title: General Animal Science Laboratory
description: Credit 1. 2 Lab Hours. (AGRI 1119, AGRI 1419*) General Animal Science Laboratory. General overview of the beef cattle, dairy cattle, horse, sheep, swine and poultry industries; information on major breeds, anatomy, phenotypic and genotypic selection criteria and production practices for each species; major disciplines of the animal industry including breeding and genetics, nutrition, reproductive physiology and products; utilization of live animals, models and feedstuffs/equipment to enhance experiential learning approach. Prerequisite: Concurrent enrollment in ANSC 107 .
prereq_text: Concurrent enrollment in ANSC 107 .

subject: ANSC
title: Animal Production Systems
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Transformative experiences related to beef cattle, dairy cattle, equine, sheep, swine, goats, companion animals, meats, food products and food safety; exposure to available animal science careers and potential areas of future/additional study. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 101 or AGLS 101 , ANSC 107 , and ANSC 108 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 101 or AGLS 101 , ANSC 107 , and ANSC 108 .

subject: ANSC
title: Farm Animal Biosystems
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Information regarding the processes by which networks of cells are controlled and coordinated within the farm animal. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 107 and ANSC 108 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 107 and ANSC 108 .

subject: ANSC
title: Texas Barbecue
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Survey, demonstration and participation in preparation techniques of Texas barbecue; comparison of regional and international barbecue methods. Prerequisite: First year students.
prereq_text: First year students.

subject: ANSC
title: Introductory Equine Care and Use
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Survey of basic equine care and use; breeds of horses and their use; care and maintenance of equines including feeding, health care, housing and equipment.

subject: ANSC
title: Livestock Breeds
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Comprehensive overview of major livestock breeds used in animal agriculture; includes history of breed development, breed characteristics, production traits, roles of breeds in different production systems; consideration of distinction between purebred and standardbred livestock; examination of how breed registries, selection and performance standards influence classification, breeding decisions and commercial production practices. Prerequisites: BIOL 111 or BIOL 107 .
prereq_text: BIOL 111 or BIOL 107 .

subject: ANSC
title: Animal Science Laboratory Preparation Methods
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 2 Lab Hours. . Study of basic animal production systems knowledge and effective pedagogical techniques to prepare animal science laboratories and animal handling methods; includes high-impact learning opportunity to allow the practice of pedagogical techniques learned in a controlled and supported environment. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ANSC 107 , ANSC 108 , and ANSC 111 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 107 , ANSC 108 , and ANSC 111 .

subject: ANSC
title: Art and Heritage of Livestock
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Using art as a venue to understand the legacy and heritage of livestock production and livestock's contribution to civilization and society; from man as hunter, agriculturalist, and finally, as industrialist; from cave paintings to Russell and Remington; history of the effects of painting, poetry, architecture and sculpture on agriculture.

subject: ANSC
title: Heritage and Impact of Western Livestock Sports
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Overview of western livestock sports and events; emphasis on history of rodeo specific events and their history and connection to today’s sport of rodeo; topics include impact of western livestock sports and rodeo events at the local community, state and national level; appreciation for development in Europe and South America; insight into cultural and economic impact.

subject: ANSC
title: Companion Animal Science
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Types, care, physiology, common diseases and common treatments of companion animals (dogs, cats, exotic pets); careers including biomedical research; solutions for problems such as behavior and overpopulation.

subject: ANSC
title: Equine Industry and Career Preparation
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Identify opportunities and skill sets required to pursue a career in the equine industry; development of resume, communication, professional etiquette and interview skills.

subject: ANSC
title: Introduction to Livestock Evaluation
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. (AGRI 2321) Introduction to Livestock Evaluation. Live market animal appraisal in relation to carcass and composition; criteria for selection of breeding livestock; techniques for preparation and delivery of oral reason.

subject: ANSC
title: Equine Handling and Safety
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Working around horses safely and effectively; includes equine behavior, proper handling techniques, controlling movement of horses, health assessment and basic management. Prerequisite: ANSC 201 or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: ANSC 201 or concurrent enrollment.

subject: ANSC
title: Animal Welfare Judging
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. . Preparation for competition in Intercollegiate Animal Welfare Judging/Assessment competition; use of primary literature to strengthen knowledge of welfare issue present in the species chosen for competition scenario; required for participation on the Animal Welfare Judging Team. Prerequisites: ANSC 107 .
prereq_text: ANSC 107 .

title: Research

subject: ANSC
title: Basic Beef Cattle Production
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Fundamental concepts of beef management and production principles; service course recommended for non-animal science majors. Prerequisites: ANSC 107 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: ANSC 107 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: /NUTR 303 Principles of Animal Nutrition
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Scientific approach to nutritional roles of water, carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, minerals, vitamins, and other dietary components; emphasis on the comparative aspects of gastrointestinal tracts and on digestion, absorption, and metabolism of nutrients. Prerequisites: CHEM 119 and a grade of C or better in ANSC 113 , or CHEM 222 , CHEM 227 or CHEM 257 ; junior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: NUTR 303/ANSC 303 .
prereq_text: CHEM 119 and a grade of C or better in ANSC 113 , or CHEM 222 , CHEM 227 or CHEM 257 ; junior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Animal Breeding
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. A systems approach to selection and mating of livestock; gene frequency, heritability, relationship, inbreeding, linebreeding, heterosis, crossbreeding, direct and correlated response to selection, and use of pedigree, family, progeny testing and indices for selection. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 111 and ANSC 113 ; GENE 301 ; STAT 301, STAT 302 , STAT 303 , or ANSC 309 ; junior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 111 and ANSC 113 ; GENE 301 ; STAT 301, STAT 302 , STAT 303 , or ANSC 309 ; junior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Meats
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Integrated studies of the meat animal processing sequence regarding the production of meat-type animals and the science and technology of their conversion to human food. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 113 ; junior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 113 ; junior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Applied Animal Record Keeping
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Keeping, analyzing and interpreting records to make fully-informed decisions on a day-to-day basis for production and management scenarios; practical application unique to animal science and meat processing. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: Equine Behavior and Training
description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 5 Lab Hours. Equine behavior and application of principles of psychology to training horses; systematic approaches to horse training emphasizing principles of learning; equipment and its use; stable management and preparation of horses for future riding. Prerequisites: ANSC 201 and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: ANSC 201 and approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Intermediate Horse Training and Sales
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. Advanced scientific methods and techniques for execution of equine performances in hunter, dressage and stock horse events; anatomical, physiological and psychological implications; preparation of horses and riders. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: Wool Evaluation and Grading
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. Evaluation of U.S.D.A. grades for wool and mohair; steps involved in processing raw wool into finished fabric; genetic and environmental factors affecting quality characteristics of wool and mohair; grading, evaluation and selection of fleeces for economic value; oral and written defense of judgments.

subject: ANSC
title: Livestock Judging
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. Selection and evaluation of beef cattle, swine, sheep and horses. Ability to present accurate, clear and concise oral and written reasons stressed. Prerequisites: ANSC 107 and ANSC 108 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: ANSC 107 and ANSC 108 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: Equine Selection and Judging
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. Detailed evaluation and comparison of horses; selection and critique of athleticism and performance in horses; industry trends addressed; oral and written defense of judgments also explained and expected; required for participation on the Horse Judging Team. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Meat Selection, Evaluation and Grading
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. Selection and grading of carcasses and wholesale cuts of beef, pork and lamb; principles of evaluation included in carcass contests and progeny testing. Prerequisites: ANSC 107 and ANSC 108 .
prereq_text: ANSC 107 and ANSC 108 .

subject: ANSC
title: Animal Feeds and Feeding
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Scientific approaches associated with precision feeding and diet formulation to match nutrient availabilities of feedstuffs with requirements of various classes of livestock species; emphasis on cost-effective feeding strategies to optimize animal productivity, and end-product quality and safety, while mitigating environmental impacts and enhancing animal health and welfare. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ANSC 111 , ANSC 113 and ANSC 303/NUTR 303 ; junior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 111 , ANSC 113 and ANSC 303/NUTR 303 ; junior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Animal Nutrition and Feeding
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Nutritional functions of water, protein, carbohydrates, fats, minerals and vitamins and their digestion, absorption, use and excretion; energy, protein and forage feedstuff characteristics and processing; nutritional requirements, ration formulation and feeding methods for farm animals; general course for non-animal science majors. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; restricted to students in the college of agriculture and life sciences.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; restricted to students in the college of agriculture and life sciences.

subject: ANSC
title: Advanced Livestock and Product Evaluation
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. Advanced evaluation of cattle, swine, sheep and equine; products produced or associated with each species; advanced oral or written defense of judgments associated with changing trends in these industries. May be repeated three times for credit. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: /FSTC 326 Food Bacteriology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Microbiology of human foods and accessory substances; raw and processed foods; physical, chemical and biological phases of spoilage; standard industry techniques of inspection and control. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: FSTC 326/ANSC 326 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Reproduction in Farm Animals
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Physiological principles of reproductive processes in cattle, sheep, swine, and horses including sperm and ova production, estrus, fertilization, gestation and parturition. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 113 or ANSC 303/NUTR 303 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 113 or ANSC 303/NUTR 303 .

subject: ANSC
title: Reproduction in Farm Animals Laboratory
description: Credit 1. 0 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. . Laboratory techniques relevant to reproductive processes in cattle, sheep, swine, and horses including sperm and ova production, estrus, fertilization, gestation, and parturition. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ANSC 333 or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 333 or concurrent enrollment.

subject: ANSC
title: Meat Merchandising
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. Steps of meat processing and merchandising of retail and foodservice; merchandising practices such as selection, identification, fabrication, pricing, packaging and distribution. Prerequisites: ANSC 307 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: ANSC 307 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: System Dynamics for Animal Sciences
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. . System dynamics modeling for the analysis of business policy and strategy; study of visualization of a business organization in terms of structures and policies that create dynamics and regulate performance; emphasis on animal production. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ANSC 303/NUTR 303 or ANSC 320 , or approval of the instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 303/NUTR 303 or ANSC 320 , or approval of the instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Animal Science for Agricultural Science
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. . Preparation to become agriculture, food and natural resources (AFNR) teachers with an opportunity for the expansion of knowledge of the primary livestock species; information relating to breeding and genetics, reproduction, physiology, nutrition, management systems, products and disease; a brief exploration of companion animals. Prerequisite: ANSC 107 and Agricultural Science major.
prereq_text: ANSC 107 and Agricultural Science major.

subject: ANSC
title: Animal Science Experience
description: Credits 0. 0 Lecture Hours. Participation in an approved high-impact learning practice; reflection on professional outcomes from animal science body of knowledge; documentation and self-assessment of learning experience at mid and final curriculum points. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: Behavior and Management of Domestic Animals
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Application of behavior of cattle, horses, sheep, goats and swine to their management; basic principles, physiology of behavior, perception, training, predators, use of dogs in livestock production, stress and animal welfare. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 318 and ANSC 333 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 318 and ANSC 333 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: Beef Cattle Production and Management
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Principles involved for profitable and sustainable, integrated beef cattle production as considered from the perspective of the U.S. cow-calf sector and from an overall systems-based approach. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 305 , ANSC 307 , ANSC 318 , and ANSC 333 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 305 , ANSC 307 , ANSC 318 , and ANSC 333 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
title: Management of Stocker and Feedlot Cattle
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Basic principles involved in feeding, management, marketing and disease control of stocker and feeder cattle from weaning through slaughter for economical production of beef. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 305 , ANSC 307 , ANSC 318 , and ANSC 333 ; STAT 301, STAT 302 , STAT 303 , or ANSC 309 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 305 , ANSC 307 , ANSC 318 , and ANSC 333 ; STAT 301, STAT 302 , STAT 303 , or ANSC 309 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: Equine Nutrition and Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Designed to provide knowledge of nutrition and health in the horse; gastrointestinal anatomy, nutrient utilization, feeding management and nutritional requirements; metabolic diseases, infectious diseases, internal and external parasites, and herd health management. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANSC
title: Swine Production and Management
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Basic principles and their practical application in efficient, economical pork production; all areas of production--breeding and selection, nutrition, housing and equipment, marketing, herd health and economic management. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANSC 333 ; grade of C or better in ANSC 305 and ANSC 318 , or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Introduction to Anthropology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (ANTH 2346, HUMA 2323) Introduction to Anthropology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates anthropology as the holistic and relativistic study of humankind, exploring human life across diverse cultures, time periods and geographical locations. Examines the discipline through its four major subfields: archaeology (the study of material culture and the past), biological anthropology (the study of human evolution and variation), sociocultural anthropology (the study of cultural systems and social organization) and linguistic anthropology (the study of language construction and symbolism). Applies fundamental concepts, including the scientific method and evolutionary theory, to complex human experiences. Develops abilities in critical thinking, analysis of empirical data and effective communication, engaging with culturally diverse and sometimes controversial subjects. Analyzes the discipline’s relationship with society and its impact on global communities over time. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores human evolutionary history, including primate behavior and hominin development; analyzes the history of human biological variation and the lack of a scientific basis for "race"; examines material culture, ancient civilizations and archaeological methods; studies language construction, symbolism and communication patterns; investigates social organization, including kinship, family, marriage and gender; explores economic systems, political structures, religion and belief systems; and applies anthropological thinking to contemporary issues such as, but not limited to, health, medicine, forensics, violence and global challenges. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world; also taught at Qatar campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Introduction to Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (ANTH 2302) Introduction to Archaeology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the basic principles of studying past human cultures through material remains. Surveys the fundamentals of archaeological practice and frameworks, applying interdisciplinary methods to reconstruct and interpret the archaeological record. Engages with written, oral and visual communication of archaeological data. Develops an understanding of how cultures adapt and change through time and across space. Engages critical thinking skills in evaluation of evidence and synthesis of different types of information. Introduces careers in anthropology and archaeology and the skills needed for them. TOPICS AND THEMES. Interdisciplinary nature of archaeological research. Site formation, survival and identification. Field and laboratory methods including survey, excavation, recording, curation and various types of analysis including dating methods. Relationships between humans and environments. Human evolution and behavior including past movement, subsistence strategies, foraging strategies, trade, tool production and development, sedentism, symbolic and ritual behaviors, domestication, city and state formation and reconstruction of past social and individual identities. Archaeological ethics, the role of archaeology in contemporary society and heritage management. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: The Human Past
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the development of human societies and world prehistory from the earliest humans to the emergence of complex civilizations. Applies archaeological and historical methods and theories used to reconstruct past lifeways including culture, identity, migration and social development. Engages with written, oral and visual communication of archaeological and historical data. Develops an understanding of how cultures adapt and change through time and across space. Engages critical thinking skills in evaluation of evidence and synthesis of different types of information. Introduces ideas of personal and social responsibility and the skills needed for careers in anthropology and archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Human evolution and migration. Human relationships with the environment including climate change, subsistence strategies, extinction events, domestication and agriculture. Production, evolution and spread of material culture. Symbolic and ritual behavior. Development of sedentism, complex societies, urbanism, collective labor, written language, monument building, early states and empires. Discussion of individual and social identity, individual agency, archaeological ethics and the role of archaeology in contemporary society. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology.

subject: ANTH
title: Peoples and Cultures of the World
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys human cultures around the world using case studies of customs and cultural organization. Explores how anthropology is a holistic discipline focused on all of humanity, which integrates knowledge from diverse fields like history, economics, psychology, sociology and traditional sciences. Explores global interconnectedness alongside cultural diversity, addressing questions of "us and them". Develops a greater understanding of the breadth of variation in the human condition and the power of culture to shape individual experience. Recognizes the trade-offs between cultural relativist and universalist perspectives. Gains cultural awareness to inform future evaluations of domestic and global issues. Practices communicating opinions in a culturally respectful manner. Relates outcomes of cultural study to one’s understanding of one’s own culture. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analyzes key anthropological concepts, including fieldwork, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, holism and ethnography. Considers human universals and cultural uniqueness. Studies cultural expressions related to basic perceptions (color, space, distance) and the body (beauty standards, adornment, modification). Explores systems of social organization, including gender, sports, games, communication, gestures and greetings. Investigates cultural practices concerning food, eating, reciprocity, trade, etiquette, folklore and magic. Examines cultural approaches to death, dying, medicine, illness and health.

subject: ANTH
title: Social and Cultural Anthropology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (ANTH 2351) Social and Cultural Anthropology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides overview of the field of social and cultural anthropology, exploring the diverse ways that human cultures shape experience across the globe, and the anthropological theory and research that attempt to understand this process. Through an exploration of different cultures, examines the major dimensions of cultural variation, including subsistence, family structure, political systems, language, religion and more. Fosters critical evaluation of cultural theories and different perspectives while promoting respectful discussion of complex and provocative topics. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Key themes include culture, ethnographic methodology and the tension between relativist and universalist perspectives. Additional topics include kinship, family structure, gender, religion, language, subsistence, political systems, race, colonialism and applied anthropology; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Foundations of Museum Studies
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. An introduction to the interdisciplinary field of museum studies, exploring how museums collect, preserve, interpret and exhibit material culture to convey cultural, historical and scientific knowledge. Emphasizes museums as dynamic institutions shaped by ethical, educational and civic responsibilities and fosters critical inquiry into questions such as: Who do museums serve? How do objects acquire meaning? What responsibilities do museums have to communities and history? Provides a foundation for further study in museum work while developing skills in civic engagement, applied learning, collaboration, inclusion and leadership. Engages museums as spaces for dialogue and lifelong learning, encouraging reflection on how they shape public understanding and express broader social values. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in museum studies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include: history and development of museums; collecting practices from antiquity to the present; analysis of museum organization, leadership structures and varying types of institutions; consideration of professional standards, collections stewardship; evaluation of interpretation, educational programming and strategies for access and inclusion; ethical, educational and civic responsibilities of museums. Cross Listing: ARCH 221 and MUST 221 .

subject: ANTH
title: Cross Cultural Competency
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops skills vital for effective engagement in an increasingly diverse and interconnected world. Fosters personal awareness of biases, attitudes, values, beliefs and ways of knowing (epistemology). Explores the profound impact of culture on the ability to think critically and communicate effectively. Trains students to critically appraise how their worldview and life experiences shape the decisions they make. Synthesizes core concepts like culture, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, stereotypes, worldview and holism, applying them to the student's chosen discipline or subject of interest. Promotes enhanced self-knowledge and cross-cultural awareness through active, reflexive inquiry. Encourages challenging one's own thinking, especially when subject matter elicits an emotional reaction, to ensure critical engagement with evidence. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analyzes fundamental concepts in anthropology, including culture, diversity, race and ethnicity. Consideration of holism and reductionism in understanding systems and thought processes. Explores personal learning styles, personality strengths and systems of knowledge (epistemology). Examines communication dynamics, ethnocentrism, stereotypes, myths, fallacies and assumptions. Discusses ethical frameworks, including critical cultural relativism. Studies critical thinking skills applicable across varied professional, cultural and scientific contexts.

subject: ANTH
title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (ANTH 2301, 2401*) Introduction to Biological Anthropology. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates human biology and evolution by exploring the origins of humanity through evolutionary processes and the Primate fossil record. Analyzes the mechanisms of evolutionary change, such as human genetics and heredity, that shape human populations and non-human primate diversity. Trains students to ask how shared evolutionary history influences modern human adaptation and variation, gaining a deeper awareness of how humans fit into the natural world. Discussion addresses the genetic and environmental basis of human biological variation, our relationship to other primates and the fossil record associated with our extinct hominin relatives/ancestors. Writing-intensive assignments are designed to develop students' critical thinking, analytical skills and ability to communicate effectively. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers evolutionary processes acting on modern and ancient human populations; analyzes human genetics, heredity and molecular biology; studies non-human Primate anatomy, fossil record, classification, behavior and ecology; methods used to study the fossil record including comparative anatomy, taphonomy, basic fieldwork protocols and age estimation techniques; examines the human fossil record, including our earliest possible relatives, the Australopithecines, and species in the genus Homo; explores contemporary human biological variation, anatomy, adaptation, health and forensic anthropology; develops skills in critical thinking, inquiry and analysis of relevant sources. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: Concurrent registration in ANTH 226 recommended; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Concurrent registration in ANTH 226 recommended; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology Laboratory
description: Credit 1. 3 Lab Hours. (ANTH 2101, 2401*) Introduction to Biological Anthropology Laboratory. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores fundamental evolutionary principles and the concepts of population genetics. Applies the scientific method to investigate evolutionary trends relevant to humans through hands-on exposure to fossils of non-human primates, human relatives and ancestors, and modern human evolution. Evaluates and synthesizes information regarding human ancestry and contemporary variation. Analyzes key trends related to human evolution, such as encephalization and bipedalism, by measuring and comparing real and modeled skeletal specimens. Lab exercises are designed to complement and reinforce topics covered in the lecture course ANTH 225 . TOPICS AND THEMES. Discussions of basic genetic principles, evolutionary mechanisms and population genetics. Analyzes human and non-human primate anatomy, focusing on skeletal morphology. Applies qualitative and quantitative methods for bone identification, skeletal growth, dental variation and locomotor function. Studies extant and extinct primate specimens, including their taxonomy, behavior and fossil record. Examinations of the hominin fossil record including casts of specimens from the following taxa: Australopithecus, Paranthropus and the genus Homo, including H. habilis, H. erectus, Middle Pleistocene Homo, Neanderthals and H. sapiens. Prerequisites: Concurrent registration in ANTH 225 is recommended; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Introduction to Forensic Anthropology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examine the foundational role of forensic anthropology within the broader forensic sciences which involves analyzing human skeletal remains for medico-legal applications, covering the history of the field and its development. Build theoretical knowledge of the discipline including the history of how the discipline developed and its role in the broader forensic sciences and international, federal and state levels. Apply proper anatomical terminology, taphonomy and comparative morphological methods to discuss and describe skeletal trauma, pathologies and anomalies. Apply and practice methods used to create a "biological profile" for an individual by estimating sex, age, stature and ancestry. Explore scene recovery methods and how skeletal analysis is applied in a variety of contexts, including routine casework, large-scale natural disasters, war casualties and human rights investigations. Critically discuss and analyze forensic methods by addressing the practical and ethical issues facing practicing forensic anthropologists today. TOPICS AND THEMES. Consider the history and foundations of forensic anthropology; study the broader medicolegal system, professional ethics and error assessment; apply osteological methods and anatomical terminology to describing human skeletal material; describe scene recovery methods such as location, recovery and taphonomic processes; apply and critically examine methods for estimating sex, age, stature and ancestry; identify and classify infectious disease, congenital conditions and nutritional deficiencies on the skeleton and teeth; explore individual identification techniques such as facial reconstruction and genetic genealogy; critically assess how forensic anthropology is portrayed in popular culture and the media. Discuss current topics considered relevant to the field by the American Academy of Forensic Science including, but not limited to, research ethics, reassessment of biological profile estimation methods and demographic underrepresentation in comparative collections.

subject: ANTH
title: Cultural Change and Development
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates the broad spectrum of cultural dynamics, providing an overview of how societies transform and adapt through cultural change. Examines diverse methodologies and theoretical approaches used to document and interpret these shifts. Draws on case studies and source materials from all areas of anthropology, integrating knowledge from allied fields. Develops a strong understanding of the complexities inherent in cultural change. Enhances the ability to employ theoretical concepts in novel and innovative ways. Clarifies the practical need to apply anthropological knowledge in programs of directed change. Encourages respectful critique and defense of diverse points of view regarding current social issues. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies the fundamental concept of culture; analyzes definitions, overviews and data sources related to cultural change; investigates dynamic processes such as innovation, diffusion and acculturation; considers theoretical approaches including functionalism, cultural materialism and cultural evolution; examines maladaptive traits and Darwinian evolutionary principles applied to culture; explores the intersection of cultural change and health; and analyzes colonial legacies and the dynamics of directed change.

subject: ANTH
title: North American Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the archaeology of North America from the first arrival of humans on the continent through recent historical archaeology. Emphasis will be upon the geographic area of the continental United States and Canada, with a focus on past Indigenous lifeways and their variation in time and in space. Discusses individual sites and places them into their regional context. Develops critical analysis skills of the lines of evidence most common to North American archaeology, including archaeological site reports, academic papers, historical records and other primary sources. Compares sites across space and time to form ideas of changing lifeways, technologies and social and individual identities of past people of North America. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include the concept of culture areas and its evolution over time, environmental archaeology, migration; adaption and environment; domestication and agriculture; technological innovation and development; trade; social complexity, warfare, culture contact, archaeological laws, ethics and politics, including the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act and Indigenous archaeology in North America. The course will include historical archaeology but focuses upon pre-European archaeology. Special attention is given to the diverse lines of evidence archaeologists use to explore these themes—including paleoenvironmental proxies, material culture analysis, iconography, colonial-era documents and ethnographic accounts. This multidisciplinary approach fosters a more holistic understanding of North American societies and their rich, complex histories. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to North American archaeology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisite: ANTH 201 , ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 , ANTH 205 , or ANTH 210 .
