subject: ANTH
title: Mesoamerican Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the peoples and civilizations of Mesoamerica—a cultural region encompassing the southern two-thirds of Mexico and the northern half of Central America, including present-day Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador and northwestern Honduras. Traces the full arc of human occupation in the region, from the earliest settlements over 14,000 years ago to the arrival of Europeans in the 15th century. Critically evaluates archaeological data and interpretations and situates Mesoamerican case studies within broader anthropological and theoretical frameworks. TOPICS AND THEMES. Emphasizing critical engagement with key debates in Mesoamerican archaeology, the course examines topics such as the origins of agriculture and urbanism, household and state economies, social stratification, ritual and religion, warfare, mobility and migration, and processes of collapse and resilience. Special attention is given to the diverse lines of evidence archaeologists use to explore these themes—including ancient DNA, material culture analysis, iconography, writing systems, linguistics, colonial-era documents and ethnographic accounts. This multidisciplinary approach fosters a more holistic understanding of Mesoamerican societies and their rich, complex histories. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 , or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 , or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Fossil Evidence of Human Evolution
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines human evolution from the time of divergence from the other African apes through the appearance of anatomically modern humans. Delves into the detailed study of the fossil antecedents of humans. Applies fundamental principles from evolutionary biology, geology, primatology and paleontology to interpret the human lineage. Integrates evidence from the human fossil record, archaeological material, ancient DNA and living human populations. Studies comparative osteology and paleoecology to interpret the evolutionary relationships, diet and behavior of extinct and living human and non-human Primate species. Analyzes the evolutionary mechanisms that have patterned life on Earth and the forces that have acted upon these processes. Develops a deeper awareness of how humans fit into the natural world. Develops a comprehensive understanding of the evolutionary mechanisms that position humans within the larger Primate clade and the genetic and environmental underpinnings of modern human variability and dispersal. Hands-on, discussion and writing-intensive assignments are designed to develop students’ critical reading/thinking skills and apply paleoanthropological methods to real and modeled skeletal materials. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers human evolutionary biology, including evolutionary processes, natural selection and macroevolutionary principles. Analyses geological and paleontological contexts, focusing on fossils, taphonomy and dating techniques. Examines living and extinct primate diversity and evolution, covering early primates and apes. Studies specific hominin species, including the earliest possible hominins, Australopithecus, Paranthropus, Homo species (such as H. erectus, H. naledi and H. neanderthalensis) and Homo sapiens. Investigates comparative morphology, osteology and diagnostic skeletal features of the human skeleton. Explores and describes paleoecology, anatomy, diet, human evolutionary trends and the genetic and environmental underpinnings that have shaped our species. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisite: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Historical Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the material and documentary evidence of European colonization in North America and its impact on Indigenous populations, African enslaved peoples and the environment. Integrates historical records with archaeological findings to understand how European imperial powers such as the Spanish, the Basques, the French, the Dutch and the English shaped the Americas through settlement, trade and social structures. Includes case studies from contact-era settlements, plantations, forts, battlefields and maritime contexts, highlighting how artifacts, architecture and written documents complement and sometimes challenge one another. Emphasizes methods of historical archaeology, including document transcription, genealogical research, artifact analysis and field methods that provide students with tools to critically interpret North American history through a material lens. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in historical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. European exploration and colonial expansion led by European nations including Spain, Portugal, France, the Netherlands and England; Indigenous populations; forced migration and enslavement of Africans; trade, exchange and economic structures; archaeology of gender, identity, racialization, plantations, forts, battlefields, settlements, graves and shipwrecks; historical archaeological theory and methods including survey and excavation methods, absolute and relative dating methods and artifact analysis; archival and research skills including genealogical research, transcription and historical document analysis; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Nautical Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines shipwrecks, sunken harbors and other submerged evidence of human activity from the Stone Age through early modern times. Explores the archaeology, technology and cultural significance of maritime societies, emphasizing the methods used to survey, map, excavate, conserve and interpret submerged sites. Reviews case examples from the Mediterranean and northern Europe, including Bronze Age, Classical, Byzantine, medieval and Viking vessels, while considering the relationship of seafaring to cultural geography and the broader human past. Ship construction, diving technology, site preservation and surveying techniques are addressed and explored through various case studies. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in nautical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Shipwrecks; submerged harbors; inundated archaeological sites; Bronze Age Mediterranean vessels; Egyptian Nile boats; Classical Greek and Phoenician ships; Greek warships (triremes, polyremes); Roman merchantmen; Byzantine ships; late medieval Mediterranean ships; late medieval warships; carracks; Scandinavian and Northern European ships; Viking ships; cogs; hulks; ship construction; rigging; armament; nautical technology; maritime trade; naval warfare; cultural geography; survey and mapping techniques; excavation and conservation methods; diving technology; artifact analysis; heritage management; iconography; relevance to modern maritime research. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: /RELS 317 Introduction to Biblical Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces students to the archaeology and material culture of the Land of the Bible from the Epi-Paleolithic period through the first century A.D. The course examines the peoples, cities and societies of biblical times through material remains, integrating artifacts, iconography and texts to develop a holistic understanding of the ancient Near East. Students explore archaeological discoveries in relation to biblical narratives, including early agricultural communities, Canaanite city-states, Egyptian influence and Iron Age polities. The course also emphasizes the interpretation of archaeological evidence, historical context and the relationship of seafaring and trade to cultural development in the ancient biblical world. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in biblical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Epi-Paleolithic period; Neolithic period; first agriculturists; Chalcolithic period; Early Bronze Age; Early Bronze IV; Middle Bronze Age I-II; Late Bronze Age; Egyptian influence in Canaan; maritime trade and seafaring; Iron Age I; Sea Peoples; Philistines; United Monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon); Divided Monarchy; Persian period; archaeology of biblical texts; material culture; urbanism; Canaanite city-states; fortifications; religious architecture; iconography; ceramics; metallurgy; inscriptions; settlement patterns; excavation techniques; interpretation of artifacts; relationship between archaeology and biblical narrative; cultural geography and human-environment interaction. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: RELS 317/ANTH 317 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Ships and Shipwrecks of the Americas
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how ships and seafaring shaped the history and culture of the Western Hemisphere from 1492 through the American Civil War. Draws on archaeological discoveries and historical records to examine exploration, colonization, trade, naval conflict and technological innovation through the lens of maritime material culture. Reviews case studies of shipwrecks and other maritime sites, revealing the vessels, technologies and practices that connected cultures, facilitated economic systems and transformed warfare. From Indigenous watercraft to colonial gunboats, steamboats and Civil War submarines, engages with the archaeological evidence that illuminates change and continuity in the maritime world of the Americas. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in nautical archaeology of the Americas. TOPICS AND THEMES. Ship construction; ship rigging; seafaring technologies; European and American shipwreck archaeological case studies; Iberian voyages of exploration; Basque whaling; Spain’s maritime empire; Northern European maritime exploration; colonization; technological developments; economics and history of the Western Hemisphere; European-Indigenous relationships; Indigenous watercraft; Anglo-French wars; piracy and privateering; Revolutionary War; War of 1812; Shipping in the Commercial Age; canal transport; horse-powered boats; steamboats; packet ships; clipper ships; whaling fleets; Arctic exploration; Civil War naval warfare. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Nautical Archaeology of the Ancient Mediterranean
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys seafaring and maritime culture in the Mediterranean from the Stone Age through the Roman Republic, with an excursus on fluvial galleys of Imperial Rome. Examines the archaeological and historical evidence for ancient navigation, shipbuilding and maritime trade, with a focus on both land-based and underwater sites. Students explore Egyptian seafaring on the Nile and in the Red Sea, Bronze Age shipwrecks such as Uluburun and Cape Gelidonya, Phoenician and Greek colonization, Etruscan maritime activity and Roman naval and merchant vessels. The course integrates material culture, iconography and archaeological discoveries to illuminate the technological, economic and cultural aspects of ancient Mediterranean seafaring. TOPICS AND THEMES. Stone Age seafaring; earliest evidence for boats; Egyptian Nile boats; Funerary Barge of Khufu; Tomb of Ti; Middle Kingdom Egyptian ships; New Kingdom Egypt; Queen Hatshepsut; Punt expedition; obelisk barge; Ramses III naval battles; Syro-Canaanite ships; Cape Gelidonya shipwreck; Late Bronze Age ships; Uluburun shipwreck; cosmopolitan trade; Phoenicians; Greeks; Etruscans; Greek shipwrecks; Western and Eastern Mediterranean; Bronze Age warships; penteconter; Archaic warships; Classical warships; Athenian trireme; Hellenistic giant warships; galley rams; Roman trade and economy; Roman merchantmen; Battle of Actium; Roman Imperial warships and shipwrecks; ship construction; rigging; armament; nautical technology; maritime trade; naval warfare; artifact analysis; cultural geography; surveying; excavation; conservation; interpretation of seafaring evidence; integration of material culture and texts; economic and social history of the Mediterranean. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: /MUSC 324 Music in World Cultures
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of music from an ethnomusicological perspective focusing on musical performance and the complex interrelationship of music to culture, society and daily life; examination of music from a variety of cultures through a series of case studies. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: MUSC 324/ANTH 324 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Field Research in Anthropology
description: Credits 1 to 9. 1 to 9 Other Hours. Training for students in formulating and solving anthropological problems through field research; problem oriented field research under supervision. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANTH 201 , ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 , ANTH 205 , ANTH 210 , or ANTH 225 ; approval by instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANTH 201 , ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 , ANTH 205 , ANTH 210 , or ANTH 225 ; approval by instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Cultures of Central Asia
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Study of anthropological research in Central Asia: ecological adaptations; colonialism and post-colonialism; ethnic politics and ethnic conflict; religion and identity; gender and family; globalization and modernization. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: South American Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Archaeological study of South America from initial human settlement through European colonial encounters, with emphasis on the Central Andes. This region encompasses striking environmental diversity where societies developed technological innovations, monumental architecture and complex political systems. The course examines how archaeologists reconstruct past lifeways through material evidence, considering interactions between environment, technology, social organization and cultural expression. Students explore long-term processes of change, including agricultural development, urbanization, political centralization and cultural transformation. Study includes major pre-Inca societies, the rise of the Inca Empire and Spanish colonization. Contemporary Andean communities and their maintenance of ancestral practices provide context for understanding long-term cultural continuity. TOPICS AND THEMES. Course topics may include: environmental diversity and human adaptation across ecological zones; early settlement patterns and cultural change; agricultural systems, technological innovations and monumental architecture; artistic traditions and material culture as expressions of identity and belief; pre-Inca political systems and the development of complex societies; Inca imperial strategies, administrative technologies and infrastructure; Spanish colonial encounters and Indigenous responses; ethical dimensions in archaeological practice, including repatriation and collaboration with descendant communities; connections between archaeological evidence and contemporary Andean societies. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: European Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of human prehistory and history on the European continent and surrounding islands through the remains of material culture such as artifacts, human and animal remains, structures, landscapes and environments. Investigates the wide time span from the earliest Paleolithic hunter-gatherer hominids (up to two million years ago), through the Neolithic agricultural “revolution”, the metal ages, the classical civilizations of Greece and Rome, the medieval period and up to the modern era. Develops critical analysis skills using different types of information including archaeological site reports, academic papers, historical records and other primary sources to understand individual sites. Compares sites across space and time to form ideas of changing lifeways, technologies, and social and individual identities of past Europeans. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include human origins and migration; adaption and environment; domestication and agriculture; technological innovation and development; trade; social complexity, urbanization and state formation including hunter-gatherers, small scale societies, cities and empires; conflict and warfare; religion and ritual; art, music and culture; social, cultural and individual identity. Methodologies discussed include archaeological excavations, surveys, GIS, spatial analysis, analysis of landscapes and buildings, dating methods, artifact analysis, examination of human and animal remains, environmental and geoarchaeology, lab methods including ancient DNA, proteins, lipids, and stable isotopes, ethnographies and experimental archaeology. Class discussions may be thought-provoking and introduce new perspectives and material that students may not have encountered before. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Classical Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Origins and spread of Western civilization through the material remains of Minoan, Mycenaen, Etruscan, and early Greek and Roman cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: /CLAS 353 Archaeology of Ancient Greece
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Greece from the Stone Age through the Hellenistic Period, concluding with the rise of Rome. Explores the material culture, art, architecture and social history of the Greek world across its major cultural phases, from the Bronze Age civilizations of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece to the flourishing of Classical Athens and the cosmopolitan Hellenistic kingdoms. Emphasizes the integration of archaeological evidence, ancient texts and artistic traditions to illuminate Greek religion, civic life, domestic space and cultural interactions across the Mediterranean. By examining key sites, monuments, artifacts and artistic achievements, students gain a comprehensive understanding of Greek society and its enduring legacy in Western civilization. TOPICS AND THEMES. Stone Age and Neolithic Greece; Bronze Age civilizations; Minoan Crete; Mycenaean palaces and the Trojan War; the Greek Dark Ages; Geometric period art and society; Archaic architecture, sculpture and vase painting; Classical Athens and the Acropolis; sanctuaries such as Delphi; fourth-century Greece and the rise of Macedon; Hellenistic art, architecture and urbanism; Greek houses and domestic mosaics; shipwreck archaeology; coinage and economic history; Greek religion and votive practices; interactions with Magna Graecia and the wider Mediterranean; Greek artistic and cultural legacy in Rome and later neoclassicism. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: CLAS 353/ANTH 353 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: /CLAS 354 Archaeology of Ancient Italy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Italy from the Stone Age through the collapse of the Roman Empire in the fourth century CE. Students examine the material culture, art and architecture of the Etruscans and Romans, as well as the prehistoric and early Italic foundations that shaped them. Explores how Italy’s peoples expressed identity, religion and power through sculpture, painting, mosaics, inscriptions, temples, homes and civic monuments. Special emphasis is placed on the development of Rome from a small city-state into a vast imperial capital, the role of urbanism and daily life, and the ways in which material remains reveal both continuity and transformation across centuries of Italian history. TOPICS AND THEMES. Prehistoric Italy and the Stone Age; Villanovans and the emergence of the Etruscans; Etruscan cities and art; early Rome and urban foundations; Romanization and the Republic; Augustan classicism; imperial art and architecture under the Julio-Claudians, Flavians and Antonines; wall painting, mosaics and domestic life; Pompeii and Herculaneum; the lure of the games and public spectacles; baths, theaters and civic monuments; coinage and inscriptions as evidence of social and political life; Ostia and imperial urbanism; ships and shipwrecks of Roman Italy; Severan and Late Roman art; Constantine and the transformation of Roman identity; collapse of the Roman Empire in the fourth century CE. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: CLAS 354/ANTH 354 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Ancient Civilizations of the World
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores archaeological studies that have contributed to our understanding of the emergence and decline of states and civilizations between 3500 BCE and 1500 CE. Examines the complex origins of anthropology and archaeology within the discourses on "civilization" and comparative models of human development. Explores the political organization, social structures, cultural practices and technological advancements of complex societies in regions such as the Near East, Africa, Europe, India, China, Mesoamerica and North America. Explores theoretical frameworks, methodological approaches and the interpretation of archaeological and related data to comprehend the nature of these complex societies in various parts of the world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Theories of civilization and socio-political organization of ancient societies, neo-evolutionary models of social complexity, agricultural societies and the rise of states, archaeological evidence of hierarchy, heterarchy, urbanism, and state formation in ancient societies, environmental factors in the rise and fall of complex societies; trade, warfare and cooperation in ancient societies; comparative studies of complex societies, states and empires in various regions of the world; the collapse of ancient states and lessons for modern states. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Cultural Diversity and Ethics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of the cultural construction of ethical values and how cultural diversity, including beliefs, values and ways of doing business, impacts human technological innovation; focuses on developing a holistic, social-science mindset and application of critical thinking skills.

subject: ANTH
title: /HIST 382 Conflict Archaeology and Military History
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Military history; conflict archaeology; human conflict; diplomacy, ethics, and leadership in conflicts; warfare; modern global issues; public service. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: HIST 382/ANTH 382 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Ice Age Humans in the Americas
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines archaeological, environmental, geological and genetic evidence related to the timing of human entry into the Americas and megafaunal extinctions at the end of the Pleistocene. Engages students in the most recent findings from archaeological sites across the Americas. In this class students learn to evaluate evidence critically and synthesize the most up to date information on human dispersals in the western hemisphere at the end of the last Ice Age. TOPICS AND THEMES. Chronology and migration routes of early settlement; environmental and landscape change, important archeological sites in North, Central and South America, controversial claims and standards of evidence, theories of forager mobility and landscape learning and current methods accelerating the pace of discoveries. Prerequisite: ANTH 202 or equivalent.
prereq_text: ANTH 202 or equivalent.

subject: ANTH
title: Archaeological Artifact Conservation
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides an in-depth introduction to the theory and practice of conserving archaeological artifacts, emphasizing the stabilization and long-term preservation of materials recovered from terrestrial and underwater sites. Examines both theoretical grounding and extensive hands-on experience in the laboratory, learning to assess artifact condition, select appropriate treatment strategies and apply conservation techniques to a wide range of materials including organics, ceramics, glass and metals. Through lectures, readings and laboratory exercises, students explore the chemical and physical principles underlying conservation, the ethical considerations surrounding intervention and preservation and the role of conservation within archaeological research and curation. TOPICS AND THEMES. Principles of archaeological conservation and preservation; conservation ethics and documentation; health and safety in the conservation laboratory; adhesives and consolidants; conservation of organic materials including bone, ivory, wood, leather, textiles and rope; stabilization of siliceous materials such as ceramics, glass and stone; corrosion processes and treatment of archaeological metals including iron, copper alloys, lead, tin and precious metals; electrolytic and chemical cleaning methods; desalinization and drying processes; material identification and condition assessment; factors of decay in burial environments; field conservation practices; reconstruction techniques and aesthetic reintegration; and integration of conservation data into archaeological interpretation and collections management. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: /RELS 403 Anthropology of Religion
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Develops skills to critically assess research findings, analyze differing viewpoints and perspectives and formulate hypothetical research agendas. Engages potentially charged topics in diverse settings, challenging students to explore their own assumptions and biases regarding their personal worldview. Fosters greater understanding of self-awareness and personal responsibility in society through exploration of the diversity of religious behaviors. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers theoretical approaches to the study of religion; analyzes religious features including symbolism, myth and ritual; studies religious specialists, magic, divination and witchcraft; explores altered states of consciousness; evaluates beliefs regarding gods, spirits, souls, ghosts and death; assesses religious change and searches for new meaning; examines religious violence and fundamentalism; and investigates vernacular religion, secularism, atheism and irreligion. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: RELS 403/ANTH 403 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Applied Archaeology - Methods and Practices
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Provides practical experience in both terrestrial and maritime archaeological field methods. Emphasizes the applied aspect of archaeology by introducing tools, techniques, software and hardware, and prepares participants to design, implement and lead field projects across diverse environments. Includes engagement with the full spectrum of field operations, from initial planning to data collection and team coordination to final report writing. Explores the foundational principles of applied archaeology, with a particular focus on its role in cultural resource management (CRM). Examines how consultant archaeologists conduct investigations in advance of land development or resource extraction, offering insight into the professional, ethical and regulatory frameworks that guide CRM practice. Students develop technical proficiency, problem-solving and leadership skills. Major themes include project design; terrestrial and underwater surveying and mapping techniques; the use of GPS, compasses and maps; GIS applications and Google Earth; introduction to remote sensing and geophysical tools including side-scan sonar, magnetometers, echo sounders, LiDAR and sub-bottom profilers; terrestrial and underwater excavation methods; stratigraphy, spatial control and in-situ recording; data management and post-excavation analysis; use of software for 2D/3D modeling and hydrostatics; documentation and reporting standards; regulations governing fieldwork; ethical principles and professional standards; current trends and employment opportunities in archaeology; and effective methods for presenting archaeological data. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Science, Pseudoscience and Critical Thinking in Anthropology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examination of extraordinary claims made across a wide spectrum of media in the fields of anthropology, biological anthropology and archaeology. Emphasis on distinguishing science from pseudoscience through application of the scientific method, logical reasoning and critical evaluation of empirical evidence. Writing-intensive assignments develop students’ critical thinking, analytical skills and ability to communicate effectively about complex and sometimes controversial issues in anthropology and in broader scientific inquiry. Attention to recognizing and refuting poor scientific reasoning, evaluation of media portrayal of science and clear dissemination of ideas within and beyond academic contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of science, pseudoscience, pathological science, junk science and anti-science; scientific hoaxes, frauds and exaggeration of evidence; the scientific method and the use and misuse of statistics and illustrations; distortions of anthropological and scientific knowledge across a variety of media platforms, including social media and ‘fake news’; history of the discipline of anthropology; IQ testing, race, and racism; creation science, natural selection, and evolution; cryptozoology, bigfoot and aquatic apes; the use, misuse and abuse of the archaeological record in both scientific and popular discourse; the supernatural realm; and conspiracy theories, climate science and vaccine efficacy. Course discussions may also engage diverse and sometimes unfamiliar perspectives, reflecting a variety of contexts – scientific, professional, political, cultural – in which group communication occurs. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Anthropological Theory
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the history and foundations of anthropological theory, connecting these historical concepts to contemporary professional concerns. Critiques the core assumptions, preferred questions and specific methods associated with major theoretical schools. Engages diverse points of view to examine current social issues and applied problems, fostering respect for cultural and human biological diversity. Develops comprehensive expertise in articulating theoretical explanations for research questions, identifying the major theorist(s) credited for theory development and detailing how theory is currently used by anthropologists. Practices critical synthesis of theoretical knowledge within existing disciplinary frameworks. Evaluates arguments by questioning the type and sufficiency of evidence presented. Assesses the cultural position, background and historical context of authors conveying messages, including whether the argument is shaped by a particular historical moment or if the author has an agenda. Requires active application of theoretical models against individual student areas of interest. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores foundational classics; analyzes epistemology, axiology and related conceptual frameworks; considers the Nature/Nurture Debate; investigation of functional thinking, processes, structures and pragmatics; transformation and evolution; symbols and coherence; cultural materialism and economies; and critical advocacy, feminisms, Post Modernism, post-structuralism and the ontological turn. Prerequisite: ANTH 210 or ANTH 205 .
prereq_text: ANTH 210 or ANTH 205 .

subject: ANTH
title: Archaeological Theory
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. An advanced undergraduate course reviewing the history of scientific archaeological thought, major theoretical paradigms and current trends in archaeology, provides firm grounding in the development and current application of archaeological theory, a fundamental component of all students’ training in archaeology, no matter their specialty. Covers the major theoretical “movements” in the development of anthropological archaeology, as well as important intellectual developments in other disciplines which have influenced explanation in archaeology (e.g., cultural anthropology, geology, evolutionary biology and other social sciences). Historically oriented, reviews how archaeological theory has evolved in the past century and how contemporary archaeologists use theory to explain variability in the material-culture record of past humans. TOPICS AND THEMES. History of scientific archaeological exploration; major theoretical paradigms and movements in archaeological theory; current trends in archaeology; intellectual developments from other disciplines that influenced archaeological thought. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Geoarchaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. An applied course on the contribution of earth sciences to the interpretation of archaeological contexts, this course consists of field, lab and lecture components. Reviews Quaternary geomorphology. Investigates site formation processes in different depositional environments and impacts on archaeological sites. Provides training in stratigraphic description and interpretation and archaeological dating methods and interpretations. Applies earth science fields and methodologies to archaeological problems. Field trips will be a required component of the course in order to complete field descriptions and sampling. TOPICS AND THEMES. The development of geoarchaeology; sediments and soils and their relevance to archaeological sites; stratigraphy; dating methods and archaeological applications; landscape reconstruction and geoarchaeological interpretations; depositional environments and site formation processes; remote sensing; geophysics. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to geoarchaeology. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Anthropological Writing
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Practices critical reading and writing skills through the study and discussion of anthropologically relevant literature. Examines various styles and formats of anthropological writing, treating the discipline as an ongoing conversation and discourse community. Develops writing proficiency necessary for professional participation in anthropology and related career paths, including the interpretation, critique and evaluation of scientific papers. Emphasizes effective peer review and the capacity to accept constructive criticism. Cultivates clear communication strategies for discussing complex anthropological topics with both academic and broader audiences. Organizes written work using careful and critical thought. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers common citation styles, including the appropriate inclusion of primary sources. Analyzes the scientific publication process and Reference Management Software (RMS) usage. Studies professional writing, including personal statements, cover letters, CVs and resumes, prepared as part of an application packet for jobs, internships or graduate school. Explores writing clearly and concisely for diverse audiences, including rewriting scholarly work for non-academic audiences and developing an original research paper on a topic of the student’s choosing. Examines various styles of scientific papers, including research articles, review articles, programmatic essays, ethnographies and popular media. Practices peer review techniques and critical analysis of complex texts. Verbal communication and synthesis of anthropological research in small group settings and an individual oral presentation. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: /CLAS 417 Naval Warfare and Warships in Ancient Greece and Rome
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys topics such as Greek and Roman warships, naval warfare, naval strategy and tactics, drawing upon archaeological evidence, literary documentation and iconographic material. Covers the development of Mediterranean naval power from the Bronze Age (including Ancient Egypt and the mythical Trojan War) to the Imperial Roman Navy. Examines Greek naval dominance during the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars, the evolution of warships such as triremes, Roman naval organization and imperial fleets, and the technological, strategic and political dimensions of naval warfare. Students analyze ship construction, rigging, armament and naval technology within their historical and cultural context. TOPICS AND THEMES. Bronze Age Mediterranean warships; Egyptian naval warfare; Bronze Age naval battles; Athenian Navy; trireme; Greco-Persian Wars (499-449 B.C.); Peloponnesian Wars (431-404 B.C.); naval campaigns of Alexander the Great; Age of Titans; Greek war machines and weapons; Greek naval monuments; Phoenician Navy; Punic Navy; Roman naval organization; Roman Imperial Navy; Roman warships and tactics; Mare Nostrum; Punic Wars (264-146 B.C.); Roman Navy in the Eastern Mediterranean; naval campaigns of Julius Caesar; naval campaigns of Octavian; Roman fluvial warships; Roman naval shipwrecks; Roman war machines and tactics; ship construction; rigging; armament; naval technology; maritime strategy; naval logistics; naval archaeology; iconography; material culture; maritime military history; technological arms race at sea. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: CLAS 417/ANTH 417 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Romans, Arabs, and Vikings--Seafaring in the Mediterranean during the early Christian Era
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of seafaring, maritime commerce, naval affairs, and shipbuilding in the Mediterranean from the late Roman Period until the fall of Constantinople in 1453. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Pirates, Privateers and Sea Raiders
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides an in-depth survey of the history and archaeology of piracy, privateering and sea raiding from ancient times in the eastern Mediterranean through the Viking Era in the Northern Atlantic and the rise of piracy in the New World and Caribbean during the 16th–18th centuries. Examines archaeological evidence of pirate ventures, the social organization of pirate and privateering communities and the economic, political and cultural effects of piracy on empires, trade networks and maritime law. Explores the sensationalism of pirate legend in literature, film and music, and introduces contemporary piracy in Africa, the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia. Through lectures, readings, presentations and research assignments, students develop critical skills to evaluate primary and secondary sources, analyze cause-and-effect relationships and assess the broader impact of piracy across time and regions. TOPICS. May include: origins, causes and major periods of piracy, privateering and sea raiding; archaeological evidence of pirate activity in the Mediterranean, Northern Atlantic, Caribbean and Americas; Viking, European and New World piracy; raids, privateering and colonial interactions; social structure, codes of conduct and daily life of pirate communities; economic and political effects of piracy on trade, colonialism, slavery and national sovereignty; sensationalism of pirate legend in literature, film and music; cultural responses to piracy; female pirates and gender dynamics in seafaring communities; contemporary piracy in Africa, the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia; case studies of shipwrecks, pirate lairs and maritime settlements; research methods and critical evaluation of primary and secondary sources. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: /MUST 421 Advanced Museum Studies
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. 0 Lab Hours. Advanced exploration of historical, political and cultural forces shaping contemporary museum practices and exhibition design, with emphasis on ethical and professional responsibilities in modern institutions. Focuses on the collaborative and interdisciplinary processes behind exhibition planning and production, with attention to visitor experience, inclusive design and object-based interpretation. Critically engages with contemporary challenges in the museum field, including representation, decolonization, repatriation, activism, censorship and institutional accountability. Highlights the museum’s role in public service, education, knowledge advancement and civic discourse. Includes field trips to campus and local museums, archives and historical or cultural institutions to support experiential learning and engagement with professional practices and careers. Fulfills core requirement for the Museum Studies Minor. Topics and themes may include: Historical and contemporary models of museum programming; research methodologies and scholarly use of collections; educational theory and practice in museum contexts; public outreach and community engagement; ethics of representation, access and inclusion; museums and democratic ideals, civic responsibility and public trust; professional standards and leadership in museum operations; critical evaluation of exhibitions and interpretive strategies; responsive programming tied to current events and emerging issues. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MUST 221 , ANTH 221 , ARCH 221 or MAST 220 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: MUST 421/ANTH 421 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MUST 221 , ANTH 221 , ARCH 221 or MAST 220 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Bioarchaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Role of human skeletal studies in reconstructing the biological and cultural past of humans; evidence gleaned from human skeletal remains recovered from archaeological sites such as data regarding diet, health, genetics and migration. Prerequisites: ANTH 225 ; junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: ANTH 225 ; junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
title: Human Osteology
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores human osteological analysis, which provides fundamental skills for fields such as bioarchaeology, paleontology, biomechanics, human anatomy and forensic anthropology. Investigates the concepts and methods anthropologists employ to identify, describe and analyze skeletal remains from archaeological and forensic contexts. Trains students in the proper use of anatomical terminology and the respectful handling of human remains. Intensive hands-on activities develop and apply essential skills in identifying and siding core skeletal elements and teeth. Focuses on how the human skeleton functions, grows and changes throughout the lifespan. Addresses the possibilities and limitations of anthropological skeletal analysis and the ethical concerns inherent in modern osteological study. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies skeletal and dental biology, including gross and microscopic bone and tooth structure. Analyses effects of ontogeny, development and age on the skeletal system. Estimates parameters such as sex, age, ancestry, stature, anomalies and pathologies of human skeletal remains using standardized anthropological methods. Considers pathological analysis, dietary reconstruction and comparison with faunal remains. Examines cultural, occupational and postmortem modifications, including taphonomy. Reviews methods used in initial assessment, inventory and recovery of remains. Prerequisites: ANTH 225 and ANTH 226 , or VIBS 305 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: ANTH 225 and ANTH 226 , or VIBS 305 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Dental Anthropology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the methods used to study teeth, a subdiscipline central to biological anthropology (the study of human evolution and variation), bioarchaeology (the study of human remains in archaeological contexts), anatomy, dentistry and palaeontology (the study of fossil life). Explores the essential questions regarding dental analysis: How are teeth studied, and what insights can dental research provide? Gains in-depth experience with the core concepts of dental anatomy, dental development, dental ecology and dental evolution. Develops confidence in identifying teeth in both human and non-human primates and their closest living relatives. Analyzes current literature concerning dental form, function and evolutionary patterns. Cultivates critical thinking abilities necessary for evaluating cutting-edge dental research and effectively presenting and writing about these findings. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers dental anatomy and introduces the tribosphenic molar as a key evolutionary feature. Analyzes the evolution of mammalian mastication and its implications for dietary adaptation. Explores evolutionary developmental biology as it relates to tooth formation and variation. Studies dental eruption patterns, life history traits and dentition patterns in primates. Investigates dental ecology and applies methods for reconstructing ancient diets. Examines dietary reconstruction techniques including macro- and microwear analysis, enamel thickness and dental topography. Reviews the dental-pulp complex, dental pathology and the role of dental form in understanding phylogenetic relationships among human and non-human primates. Prerequisites: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Anthropology of Human Reproduction
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines human courtship, marriage, reproduction, family structure and parenting through the lens of evolutionary ecology. Explores how human reproductive and parenting patterns compare with those of other primates and how they vary across cultures. Evaluates different viewpoints on and approaches to the application of evolutionary logic to the study of these topics. Critically examines hypotheses explaining human behavior through biological, cultural and ecological lenses. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include evolutionary approaches to the study of human behavior, life histories, reproductive strategies, sexual selection, marriage, parental care, infidelity, divorce, as well as explorations of cross-cultural and cross-species variation in these areas. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Medical Anthropology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces medical anthropology, the subfield exploring the biological and cultural dimensions of health, illness and healing across diverse societies. Defines and discusses key concepts, such as health, illness and disease, in relation to various social, environmental, political and evolutionary contexts. Analyzes the interconnections among micro- and macrobiological, cultural, social and political determinants to construct a holistic view of human health. Engages with contemporary and emerging issues in health and healthcare, emphasizing the comparative analysis of global medical systems. Compares and contrasts biomedicine with other ethnomedical systems to evaluate its role within diverse cultural contexts. Develops critical thinking, reading, writing and collaboration skills for engaging with multiple perspectives on health. Note that course content may include complex or sensitive topics designed to foster critical engagement. TOPICS AND THEMES. Surveys foundational theories and methodologies. Analyzes cultural beliefs and environmental influences on health, including ecological and evolutionary disease patterning. Explores health-related behaviors, mental health, medical systems and explanatory models across diverse cultural contexts. Examines environmental health challenges, globalization and infectious disease. Considers gender, race/racism, social inequality and health disparities. Discusses professional applications and emerging issues in the subdiscipline. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: /RELS 436 Ancient Egypt I - The Rise of Egypt
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from earliest times to the end of the New Kingdom period. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: RELS 436/ANTH 436 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Ethnobotany
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the dynamic relationships between people and plants through the interdisciplinary lens of ethnobotany. Introduces the field by examining how disciplines such as botany, anthropology, ethnopharmacology, ethnoecology and ethnomedicine contribute to understanding plant use across cultures. Engages critically with foundational concepts, including plant adaptations for defense, human strategies for utilizing those adaptations, diverse ways of knowing and the development of knowledge systems that codify plant use. Emphasizes analytical and methodological inquiry into how plant ecosystems and knowledge systems shape human-plant interactions. TOPICS AND THEMES. Studies plant structures, functions and identification using botanical methods; analyzes traditional ecological knowledge and cognitive ethnobotany through ethnographic and comparative approaches; considers ethnopharmacological practices including tinctures, infusions and salves with attention to preparation and efficacy; explores sensory and perceptual ecology using qualitative and observational techniques; examines ethnoecology and conservation strategies through field-based and participatory methods; investigates ethnomedicine, medical models and health conditions using cross-cultural and clinical perspectives; and evaluates ethical issues in research and practice through case studies and applied frameworks. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: /RELS 438 Ancient Egypt II - Egypt in Decline
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from the end of the New Kingdom through the Graeco-Roman period, focusing on the years 1185–30 BCE. Examines the decline of pharaonic power, the rise of foreign influences and the resilience of Egyptian society under Libyan, Nubian, Persian and Ptolemaic rule. Reviews the interplay between political, social and cultural dynamics, exploring Egyptian adaptations to Hellenistic dominance, while tracing continuity and change in art, religion, literature and urban development. Through lectures, readings and analyses of primary and secondary sources, students gain a humanistic understanding of Egyptian civilization during its final dynastic phases and develop skills in interpreting archaeological, textual and iconographic evidence. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues pertaining to ancient Egypt. TOPICS AND THEMES. Decline of pharaonic authority; fragmentation of the Egyptian state; Libyan, Nubian and Persian interventions; internal political strife and social change; resilience of Egyptian cultural identity; Ptolemaic dynasty and Hellenistic influence; Cleopatra VII and the last Ptolemies; Alexandria as a cultural and economic center; Greco-Egyptian art, religion and literature; continuity and transformation of Egyptian traditions; interactions between foreign rulers and Egyptian elites; archaeological and textual methods for reconstructing late Egyptian history; humanistic approaches to interpreting material culture; synthesis of historical, artistic and archaeological evidence. Prerequisites: Completion of ANTH 436/RELS 436 or RELS 436/ANTH 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: RELS 438/ANTH 438 .
prereq_text: Completion of ANTH 436/RELS 436 or RELS 436/ANTH 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Lithic Artifact Analysis
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Laboratory-based course reviewing methods archaeologists use to analyze stone tools and debitage, including identification of tool-stone sources, reconstruction of technology, explanation of assemblage variability, and microscopic use-wear analysis. subject: ANTH
title: Quantitative Methods in Anthropology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Presents practical training in statistics applicable to anthropological and archaeological data. Provides anthropology students with the sophisticated statistical skills needed for an increasingly quantitative field. Discusses reasons why anthropological and archaeological data does not always meet the criteria set by many formal statistical models. Teaches the methods to analyze the chronological, geographic, morphometric, demographic, phylogenetic, genetic, linguistic, network/interaction and observational datasets (among others) that pose unique challenges for both analysis and interpretation. Conducts scientific statistical analyses of these datasets. Applies statistical concepts and techniques to real and hypothetical anthropological or archaeological problems during weekly lab sections. TOPICS AND THEMES. Quantitative analytical methods employed by anthropologists; includes statistical analyses, statistical software and sampling theory commonly used in anthropological research. Graphical techniques and statistics specific to anthropological datasets and research questions, including exploratory data analysis (e.g. principal components, canonical variates, factor analysis), and other multivariate methods (e.g. MANOVA). This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; STAT 302 or STAT 303 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; STAT 302 or STAT 303 .

subject: ANTH
title: The Archaeology and Anthropology of Foraging Societies
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the archaeology and anthropology of foraging (hunting and gathering) societies in time and space. Includes an overview of archaeology focused on foraging societies and current methodological and theoretical issues, especially the use of ethnographic and environmental data. Investigates ecologically oriented case studies of late Pleistocene and Holocene hunter-gatherers paired with the ethnographic record used to interpret these sites. Archaeological case studies will have an emphasis on land-use, site-structure and site formation analyses. Ethnographic case studies will focus on the diversity of hunting and gathering societies, change in these societies through time and discussion of forager economies, with specific attention to critiquing ethnohistoric accounts and the applicability of these case studies to the archaeological record. TOPICS AND THEMES. Forager (hunter-gatherer) variation in different environments; forager variation through time; forager social structures; forager mobility; forager subsistence; socio-political complexity in foraging societies; ethnographic critiques; archaeology of foraging societies; resource management; foragers in the modern world and change in forager societies in the recent past; archaeological site structure; lithic analysis; site formation processes; archaeological site survey; archaeological theory of foragers; site modeling and resource modeling. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Quantitative Ethnographic Methods
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces quantitative ethnographic field methods commonly used in anthropological research to formally test hypotheses. Explores the benefits and challenges of applying structured, quantitative techniques to the study of complex cultural phenomena within a field largely dominated by qualitative methods. Covers best practices for managing and analyzing anthropological datasets. Surveys common ethnographic methods designed to enhance comparability and analytical rigor of ethnographic research, including structured interviews, text analysis and network analysis. Through hands-on assignments, provides practical experience in developing and executing small-scale research projects. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include ethical considerations in field research, research design, data management, statistical analysis, structured interviews, online survey tools, standardized observation, network analysis, text analysis and cultural consensus analysis. Also includes student participation in all stages of the research process, including research design, data collection, data management and analysis, and write-up. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Environmental Archaeology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. 0 Lab Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the paleoecological context in which past humans interacted with the natural environment encompassing plants, animals and landscape. Introduces students to theories and methods relevant to studying past human-environment interactions. Outlines types of environmental data that survive in the archaeological record (geological, botanical, faunal, chemical), recovery and analytical methods, absolute chronology and inferences made based on these data. Develops long-term, global perspective on human-environment interactions provided by the fields of archaeology and earth science. TOPICS AND THEMES. The use of archaeological sites as paleoenvironmental archives, human impacts on ancient environments, Quaternary extinctions, long-term landscape evolution, plant and animal domestication, the Anthropocene and cultural collapse and resilience. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Method and Theory in the Peopling of the Americas
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Reviews current evidence from the fields of archaeology, genetics, biological anthropology and paleoecology for the dispersal of modern humans to the New World during the Pleistocene. Examines terminal Pleistocene cultures in Asia and the earliest sites in the Americas. Discusses various models proposed for this migration. Critically examines major archaeological sites and cultures. Stresses an interdisciplinary approach. Applies theory and method used to explain prehistoric human migration and colonization of empty lands. TOPICS AND THEMES. Pleistocene Americas; ancient DNA; paleoenvironments; radiocarbon dating; archaeological modeling; lithic analysis; ethnographic analogy; zooarchaeology and extinctions; archaeological site formation processes; critical analysis of fragmentary data; statistical analysis. This course will incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to the peopling of the Americas. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
title: Cultural Heritage and Resource Management
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Evaluation of modern ideas about how and why archaeological, architectural, ethnographic, and natural resources should be preserved and presented to current and future societies; critical examination of the theories, methods, regulations, and ethics that guide efforts to preserve and protect cultural heritage within a context of past endeavors and future directions. subject: ANTH
title: Ancient Biomolecules
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how biomolecules — DNA, proteins, lipids and metabolites — persist in plant and animal remains, artifacts and sediments for thousands to millions of years, preserving key insights into long-term ecological and human history. Determines how these molecules are preserved, identified and analyzed within archaeological contexts to address interdisciplinary questions about evolution, migration, diet, disease, culture, tool production, health and environmental change. Interpretation of biomolecular evidence will draw from archaeological, historical and scientific sources to reconstruct past lifeways within their own cultural and environmental settings. Develops the ability through lectures, discussions and data analysis to assess the suitability for different biomolecular methods for addressing specific research questions and critically evaluate current scientific literature in the field. Skills learned are directly applicable to making informed, evidence-based decisions, empowering students to navigate information-rich environments with discernment and confidence. Prior knowledge in either biology/biochemistry or archaeology is required, but not both. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analysis of the hereditary biomolecules DNA, proteins, lipids and metabolites; large-scale ‘omics’ approaches, including genomics, metagenomics, proteomics, metaproteomics, lipiomics and metabolomics used to investigate complex systems; instrumentation including PCR, Sanger sequencing, whole genome sequencing (NGS and WGS), chromatography and mass spectrometry; specialized applications such as environmental DNA, microbiomes and dental calculus genetics and proteomics; biomolecule preservation and degradation; ways biomolecular techniques are adapted for archaeological considerations; integration with other lines of archaeological, textual, historic and scientific evidence. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to archaeological biomolecules. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANTH 202 or BIOL 111 , or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ANTH 202 or BIOL 111 , or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
title: Anthropology of Body Image
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Evaluates core psychological, medical, evolutionary and anthropological theories of body image, eating disorders, fat and cosmetic surgery. Surveys and critiques theories of body image from the lens of medical anthropology and global mental health. Develops expertise in articulating the major theoretical questions, strengths and limitations of different frameworks, particularly in relation to cross-cultural variation. Critically analyzes global case studies of body image-related illnesses. Applies anthropological theories to identifying biases in the body image literature and public health consequences. Formulates anthropological solutions to conversations and concerns in the body image literature surrounding emerging trends, cross-cultural value- and knowledge-systems, and the challenges of treatment. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analysis of anthropological theories of the body; critique of current theories of body image and eating disorders; assessment of psychological and anthropological approaches to fat talk; critique and synthesis of biomedical and social justice approaches to weight and weight stigma; evaluation of limitations of eating disorders research from a cross-cultural perspective; formulation of anthropological solutions to emerging discussions in body image among men, racial minorities and sexual minorities; evaluating the cross-cultural motivations and ethics of cosmetic surgery; critiquing current treatments for eating disorders and obesity from an anthropological lens. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: ARCH
title: Architecture Design I
description: Credits 5. 2 Lecture Hours. 10 Lab Hours. Issues and methods in designing environments for human habitation and well-being; projects addressing site, functional planning, spatial ordering, form generation through a recognition of the synthesis of space, structure, use and context; reinforcement of appropriate graphic and model building techniques. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ARCH 105 and ARCH 106 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ARCH 105 and ARCH 106 .

subject: ARCH
title: Architecture Design II
description: Credits 5. 2 Lecture Hours. 10 Lab Hours. Fundamental issues of innovative design processes and creation explored through the creative use of past, present and future materials, tools, and technologies; with an emphasis upon the research of materials, methods, scale, craft and technique as instruments of design, fabrication, and production. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ARCH 205 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ARCH 205 .

subject: ARCH
title: Social and Behavioral Factors in Design
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Social and behavioral factors in the built and natural environment; environmental perception and spatial cognition; social-environmental processes such as privacy and crowding; setting-oriented discussion on residences, education, and the workplace; the psychology of nature and natural resource management; social design and social science contribution to architectural design.

subject: ARCH
title: Sustainable Architecture
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. A comprehensive introduction to sustainability concepts, techniques and applications at all levels of the built environment, history of contemporary development of sustainable architecture from 1960 to the present; design strategies, environmental technologies and social factors for reducing building energy needs and carbon foot prints; global applications of sustainable approaches.

subject: ARCH
title: Computational Methods in Architecture
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Software and processes for computation design in architecture; image editing and creation, vector drawing, 3D modeling, parametric modeling, rendering techniques and simulation.

subject: ARCH
title: Foundations of Museum Studies
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. An introduction to the interdisciplinary field of museum studies, exploring how museums collect, preserve, interpret and exhibit material culture to convey cultural, historical and scientific knowledge. Emphasizes museums as dynamic institutions shaped by ethical, educational and civic responsibilities and fosters critical inquiry into questions such as: Who do museums serve? How do objects acquire meaning? What responsibilities do museums have to communities and history? Provides a foundation for further study in museum work while developing skills in civic engagement, applied learning, collaboration, inclusion and leadership. Engages museums as spaces for dialogue and lifelong learning, encouraging reflection on how they shape public understanding and express broader social values. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in museum studies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include: history and development of museums; collecting practices from antiquity to the present; analysis of museum organization, leadership structures and varying types of institutions; consideration of professional standards, collections stewardship; evaluation of interpretation, educational programming and strategies for access and inclusion; ethical, educational and civic responsibilities of museums. Cross Listing: ANTH 221 and MUST 221 .

subject: ARCH
title: Foundations of Historic Preservation
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration and evaluation of the cross-disciplinary work of historic preservation; emphasis on the significance of historic places to societal well-being and conservation alternatives for historic and cultural environments; review of preservation projects and treatments; guest presentations and case studies from practicing professionals and researchers in a variety of fields.

subject: ARCH
title: Survey of World Architecture History I
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (ARCH 1301) Survey of World Architecture History I. A survey of world architecture and the human-designed and built environment from prehistory to the 13th century.

subject: ARCH
title: Survey of World Architecture History II
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (ARCH 1302) Survey of World Architecture History II. A survey of world architecture and the human-designed and built environment from the 13th to the 19th century.

subject: ARCH
title: Comparative Theory in the Built and Virtual Environments
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction of cultural theory and the environment; theories, special concepts and ideas relevant to the built and virtual environments with primary focus on the last fifty years; theory, theory building, and application to buildings and urban design; formation of ideas and critical ways of assessing the environment.

subject: ARCH
title: Seminar in Contemporary Architecture
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Presentations by and discussions with professionals representing specialty areas related to environmental design through the Department of Architecture Lecture Series. May be taken four times for credit. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis.
