subject: COMM
title: Communication, Organizations and Society
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how organizations communicate with — and are shaped by — the societies in which they operate. Considers communication as a means of building organizational identity, reputation and/or legitimacy among stakeholders such as employees, customers, communities, governments and advocacy groups. Addresses how organizational messaging is used to maintain trust, manage expectations and respond to public concerns or criticism. Course content and discussion may draw on real-world cases involving corporate responsibility, crisis communication, ethics or public controversy for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops workforce-relevant understanding of how organizations maintain credibility, manage public expectations and communicate across diverse stakeholders, including clients, employees, communities and regulators. Builds practical insight into how communication strategies influence trust, cooperation and decision-making in professional settings. Supports the ability to interpret, evaluate and respond to organizational messaging in ways that inform decision-making in both professional and civic settings. Supports academic advancement in communication studies, organizational leadership and related fields. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how organizations can relate to broader publics rather than act as isolated entities. Explores how communication choices can shape public perception, accountability and long-term viability. Considers the role of transparency/honesty, responsibility, empathy and ethical reasoning in navigating public expectations and competing interests. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of organizational identity and image; stakeholder communication and engagement; reputation management; ethics and corporate responsibility; crisis response and public accountability; communication across internal and external audiences; globalization and cultural expectations; digital communication and public scrutiny. Course material may involve discussion of reputational disputes, social or environmental issues or critiques of corporate behavior, examined for purposes of understanding organizational communication processes. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: COMM
title: Communication, Group Processes and Collaboration
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of communication processes that enable or hinder collaboration in dyads, teams and group settings. Considers on how dialogue, facilitation, leadership and group dynamics shape collective decision-making and problem-solving. Course activities may include applied or project-based facilitation scenarios where communication strategies are tested in practice. Course content and discussions may address issues of disagreement or public concern for purposes of understanding communication dynamics. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce-ready skills in teamwork, listening, meeting facilitation, conflict navigation and collaborative problem-solving; competencies relevant in organizational, nonprofit, community and civic environments. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in organizational communication, leadership or deliberative democracy. Reinforces civic readiness by modeling constructive engagement across differing viewpoints and interests. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how group collaboration is not merely a matter of goodwill but a communicative process that can involve power, emotion, structure and shared responsibility. Explores ways that conflict and disagreement, when managed effectively, can generate innovation, trust and shared ownership rather than division. Considers leadership as a distributed and communicative practice rather than a top-down role. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of collaboration and facilitation methods; dialogue and deliberation frameworks; leadership and followership in groups; conflict management and negotiation; roles, norms and group climate; ethics of neutrality and mediator responsibility; decision-making models; communication in diverse or high-stakes teams; online versus face-to-face collaboration. Course material may draw on real-world cases or simulations involving disagreement or public issues, analyzed for communicative strategy. Prerequisites: COMM 210 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: COMM 210 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: Media Campaigns
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of the principles and processes behind designing media campaigns across domains such as health, politics, human rights, advertising and/or the environment. Considers theory-driven planning, persuasive strategy, message execution and evaluation in mass and digital media contexts. Includes critical analysis of real-world campaign cases past and present alongside applied exercises in campaign design. Course content may feature campaign messages involving sensitive or controversial topics, examined to understand communication strategy. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds professional competencies relevant to advertising, strategic communication, public relations, health promotion, political advocacy and nonprofit outreach. Develops skills in message targeting, audience analysis, media planning and persuasive evaluation necessary for roles involving campaign development or consultancy. Supports preparation for advanced coursework in communication strategy and reinforces civic literacy by enhancing the ability to interpret and assess persuasive messaging encountered in public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how effective campaign messaging requires more than creativity, demanding ethical reasoning, audience insight, emotional appeal and theoretical grounding. Expands understanding of how persuasive appeals can operate differently across issues and identities, encouraging reflection on both intended and unintended effects. Frames media campaigns not only as tools for influence but also as cultural artifacts that reveal public priorities, fears and beliefs. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of campaign theory and history; message design and persuasive appeals; audience segmentation and targeting; media channel strategy across television, radio, print and digital platforms; evaluation of campaign effectiveness; social marketing and public health initiatives; political and issue advocacy; environmental and safety campaigns; crisis communication and public service announcements. Examples may draw from domestic and international cases and include campaign content that is emotional, graphic and/or politically charged, used for promoting informed, critical analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: COMM
title: Cultural Studies of Communication Technology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication technologies shape and are shaped by culture, power and everyday life. Examines theories of technological change, media history and/or digital culture, including how new and emerging technologies are often met with complex social dilemmas. Draws on historical and contemporary examples to show how technologies such as telegraphy, television, social media and surveillance platforms carry assumptions about progress, identity, work and/or control. Course content may include cases involving political conflict, privacy concerns or online controversy, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports professional preparation in fields concerned with media policy, strategic communication, digital storytelling, user experience, ethics or advocacy. Strengthens civic literacy by analyzing how technological narratives influence public trust, participation and responsibility. Builds awareness of how institutions, governments and communities negotiate access, autonomy and accountability in digital environments. Clarifies how contemporary debates over technology shape journalism, marketing, policy development, design practice and workplace communication. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals ways technology is not always neutral but can be embedded within cultural expectations, economic systems and political values. Differentiates between everyday assumptions about innovation and scholarly approaches that analyze who benefits, who is excluded and how technological systems reinforce or redistribute power. Informs reflection on how personal devices, platforms and infrastructures can shape interaction, memory, identity and/or agency. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of technological determinism and cultural shaping of technology; utopian and dystopian narratives in media; infrastructures of communication throughout history; surveillance, data tracking and privacy; identity formation in digital communities; automation, labor and human-machine relations; digital inequality and access; governance of communication technologies in democratic and non-democratic contexts. Course materials may include historical case studies or contemporary examples involving censorship, exploitation and/or graphic or profane content as relevant to understanding communication and technology. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: Communication and Video Games
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores video games as a field of communication study, examining their development as media industries, cultural practices and technological environments. Surveys scholarship on game studies history, video game production models, audience experiences and/or game design strategies. Investigates how gameplay involves storytelling, emotion, identity and interaction across different genres and mediums. Course material may include video games or related media that contain violence, mature content or controversial themes, examined for purposes of critical analysis and informed perspectives. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages skills applicable to media strategy, entertainment industries, marketing, game design, journalism and audience analysis. Builds familiarity with economic models, platform ecosystems and/or emerging markets surrounding digital entertainment. Supports academic preparation in communication, media studies, cultural studies and technology research. Enhances civic and cultural awareness by examining how interactive media shape norms, values and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how video games function not only as entertainment but also as sites of persuasion, identity performance, experimentation and cultural meaning. Examines distinctions between technological innovation and social consequences. Informs reflection on assumptions about players, genres, violence and/or interactivity by contrasting public debates with empirical and critical research. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of game history and platform evolution; analysis of development pipelines, publishing models and global industry structures; exploration of narrative design and emotional engagement; consideration of online communities, fandoms and participatory cultures; examination of regulation, monetization, labor, access and ethics. Course material may draw from games or case studies involving conflict, gender representation or political controversy as relevant to communication analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: /JOUR 458 Global Media
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how globalization and media are intertwined across national, transnational and diasporic circuits. Explores frameworks for understanding globalization through media ownership, migration, representation, content flow, technology, everyday life and/or political influence. Considers how news, entertainment, advertising and/or digital platforms travel across regions and are reshaped by local and transnational values, communities and regulations. Highlights both integration and inequality in global media landscapes. Course content may reference political or cultural controversies, including propaganda, censorship, immigration or conflict reporting, for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of how media industries function in global markets, supporting preparation for careers in journalism, strategic communication, public affairs, media production, policy analysis and international business. Supports adaptability within multicultural and internationally connected workplaces. Develops abilities to assess media influence across national and cultural boundaries, relevant skills in organizations operating in global or multicultural environments. Strengthens academic grounding for advanced study in communication, media studies, international relations or cultural analysis. Supports civic literacy by clarifying how global media shape public opinion, diplomacy and perception between nations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals that media are not neutral carriers of information but products of political, economic, ideological and cultural systems. Highlights how similar content can carry different meanings depending on context, history, ideology and/or regulation. Encourages reflection on how local and/or personal media environments are shaped by assumptions and practices that may differ substantially across national and cultural boundaries, fostering greater awareness of perspective and context. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of transnational media ownership and conglomerates; global circulation of news, entertainment and advertising; audiences and consumers; comparative media systems in democratic, authoritarian and transitional societies; localization and cultural adaptation; media policy, censorship and regulatory control; streaming platforms, social media and telecommunications infrastructure; migration, diaspora, citizenship and identity across borders. Course material may reference real-world cases involving political or cultural controversy, such as extremism, disinformation or state propaganda, for purposes of analysis and critique within an environment of respectful dialogue. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: JOUR 458/COMM 458 .

subject: COMM
title: Communication and Contemporary Issues
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of how communication practices construct, contest, circulate and/or suppress contemporary issues. Focus may draw on rhetorical, critical, interpretive and/or empirical approaches to message design, media representation, public discourse and/or everyday interaction. Emphasizes analytical reading and case analysis grounded in scholarship. Course focus varies by instructor and term. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Uses the study of individual contemporary issues as a laboratory for understanding how communication shapes public problems across domains. Builds recognition of how messages influence perception, policy and action in government, health, technology, culture and/or everyday life. Develops skills relevant to professional roles involving analysis, advocacy, media interpretation, strategic messaging or organizational decision-making. Strengthens academic preparation by deepening proficiency in applying theory to real-world cases. Supports civic readiness by refining the ability to interpret competing claims, identify persuasive strategies and critically engage issues with clarity. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of how communication shapes issues related to health, environment, technology, labor, education, identity or public policy. May examine political rhetoric, media representation, scientific controversy, organizational messaging, global and transnational issues, colonialism and decoloniality and/or grassroots advocacy. Cases may draw from news, social media, institutional reports, cultural texts and/or lived experiences. Course material may include perspectives that conflict or critique one another, addressed for the purpose of understanding how issues are framed, debated and acted upon. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: Communication in Health Care Contexts
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how communication functions across health care settings, including interpersonal interactions, organizational systems and/or public messaging. Explores approaches to patient-provider dialogue, teamwork and/or institutional communication, alongside principles used in health campaigns and information dissemination. Addresses how communication practices influence access, understanding, decision-making and/or coordination. Course material may involve discussion of sensitive health topics, addressed for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices applicable to professional effectiveness in clinical, nonprofit, corporate and public-facing health roles. Develops analytical tools for evaluating message strategies, assessing interactional dynamics and interpreting communication within institutional structures. Supports preparation for advanced study in fields related to health, communication or organizational practice, as well as for participation in public discourse surrounding health issues. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how communication in health care involves more than information delivery, incorporating factors such as context, perception, institutional procedures and interpersonal dynamics. Informs understanding of how misunderstandings emerge and ways different approaches to communication may facilitate or impede clarity, coordination and trust. Considers communication as a process with measurable effects. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of physician-patient interaction; health literacy and information accessibility; teamwork and coordination in clinical settings; communication breakdowns and system-level challenges; message design and campaign strategy; risk communication; digital health platforms and telemedicine; confidentiality, regulation and public messaging. Course material may reference real-world health controversies or policy debates as useful for understanding communication processes. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: Media, Health and Medicine
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how health, illness and medical practice are represented across media environments, including news, social media, entertainment, advertising and/or public information campaigns. Analyzes how messages about bodies, risk, care, expertise and/or responsibility are constructed and circulated. Considers how media shape public expectations of patients, professionals and/or institutions. Course content may include real-world examples involving sensitive topics such as illness, disability, gender, sexuality, social class and/or race, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to workforce settings in which effective communication about health is essential, including healthcare industries, public relations, nonprofit outreach, journalism and strategic communication. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in health communication, media studies and public health or policy. Strengthens civic media literacy by examining how health information and misinformation spread through media systems, institutional messaging and cultural narratives. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how portrayals of health are shaped not only by medical knowledge but also by narrative conventions, commercial pressures and/or cultural assumptions. Builds understanding of how media depictions of illness, caregiving and wellness can inform, inspire, mislead and/or stigmatize, depending on framing. Facilitates comparison between professional expertise and popular narratives to better understand how public perceptions of health are formed and challenged. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of medical dramas and documentaries; news coverage of disease outbreaks or medical innovation; health marketing and pharmaceutical advertising; public health campaigns and crisis communication; social media communities around wellness, disability or chronic illness; narratives of caregiving and recovery; depictions of healthcare providers and institutions. May include feminist and/or critical approaches to the intersections of health with topics like gender, race and sexuality. Course material may reference real-world historical and contemporary health controversies when useful for understanding communication processes. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
title: Advanced Social Media
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the strategic use of social media in professional, organizational and/or public communication contexts. Analyzes how platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and/or X structure their visibility, engagement and audience expectations. Explores how organizations and individuals craft identity, manage interaction and respond to feedback across different platform cultures. Includes both critical evaluation of existing accounts and hands-on creation of posts, visuals and/or campaigns for specific purposes. Course material may reference real-world social media campaigns related to political, cultural and/or commercial controversy, examined for purposes of communication analysis. Builds fluency in platform conventions, analytics, message design and audience targeting; skills applicable in both corporate and nonprofit communication roles. Supports academic growth in media analysis and prepares students for civic participation in increasingly networked communication environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how social media operates not only as a tool for promotion but as a space of negotiation between creators, institutions and publics. Highlights differences between personal posting, strategic messaging and algorithmic influence. Informs reflection on the challenges of authenticity, persuasion and accountability when communication is continuous, participatory and highly public. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of platform affordances and algorithmic logics; branding and identity construction; audience engagement strategies; visual and multimedia storytelling; analytics and performance metrics; influencer models and creator economies; platform policy, moderation and crisis response. Course examples may draw from corporate, political, entertainment, activist and/or nonprofit accounts. Content creation components may involve drafting posts, graphics, videos and/or campaign plans in response to simulated or real-world communication goals. subject: COMM
title: /RELS 480 Religious Communication
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: RELS 480/COMM 480 .

prereq_text: Grade C or better in CSCE 120 or CSCE 121 ; grade of C or better in CSCE 222 or ECEN 222, or concurrent enrollment.

subject: CSCE
title: Discrete Structures for Computing
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Mathematical foundations from discrete mathematics for analyzing computer algorithms, for both correctness and performance; introduction to models of computation, including finite state machines and Turing machines. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MATH 142 , MATH 147 , MATH 151 , or MATH 171 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 142 , MATH 147 , MATH 151 , or MATH 171 .

subject: CSCE
title: Computing Ethics
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Introduction to legal, social and ethical issues in computing and software development; emphasizes ethical decision-making, professional responsibility and communication, with coverage of professional codes, organizational ethics, law and policy, intellectual property, open-source software and variety of contemporary topics. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 ; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 ; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CSCE
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 0 to 4. 0 to 4 Lecture Hours. Special project in computer science; project must be approved by the department. Prerequisite: Approval of department head; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Approval of department head; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CSCE
title: Special Topics in...
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Lecture Hours. Selected topics in an identified area of computer science. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Research
description: Credits 0 to 4. 0 to 4 Other Hours. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in computer science. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Computational Data Science
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Computational practice of data science through a sequence of interactive modules that provides an integrated hands-on approach to its methods, tools, applications and supporting technologies including high performance and cloud computing platforms. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102 , CSCE 110 , CSCE 111 , or CSCE 206 ; grade of C or better in MATH 251 , MATH 253, or STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: ECEN 360 and STAT 315 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102 , CSCE 110 , CSCE 111 , or CSCE 206 ; grade of C or better in MATH 251 , MATH 253, or STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: CSCE
title: Database Systems
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. File structures and access methods; database modeling, design and user interface; components of database management systems; information storage and retrieval, query languages, high-level language interface with database systems. Prerequisites: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; junior or senior classification.

subject: CSCE
title: Computer Organization
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Computer systems from programmer's perspective including simple logic design, data representation and processor architecture, programming of processors, memory, control flow, input/output, and performance measurements; hands-on lab assignments. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 , or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: CSCE
title: Introduction to Computer Systems
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Introduction to system support for application programs, both on single node and over network including OS application interface, inter-process communication, introduction to system and network programming, and simple computer security concepts; hands-on lab assignments. Prerequisite: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; grade of C or better in CSCE 312 or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 350/ECEN 350 or ECEN 350/CSCE 350 .
prereq_text: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; grade of C or better in CSCE 312 or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 350/ECEN 350 or ECEN 350/CSCE 350 .

subject: CSCE
title: Programming Languages
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of the design space of programming languages via an in-depth study of functional and object-oriented programming concepts, using concrete programming languages as examples. Focuses on idiomatic uses of programming language constructs and on features characteristic for each language. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 , or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: CSCE
title: Programming Studio
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Intensive programming experience that integrates core concepts in Computer Science and familiarizes with a variety of programming/development tools and techniques; students work on 2 or 3 month-long projects each emphasizing a different specialization within Computer Science; focuses on programming techniques to ease code integration, reusability, and clarity. Prerequisite: CSCE 312 and CSCE 314 , or CSCE 350/ECEN 350 or ECEN 350/CSCE 350 ; concurrent enrollment in CSCE 313 .
prereq_text: CSCE 312 and CSCE 314 , or CSCE 350/ECEN 350 or ECEN 350/CSCE 350 ; concurrent enrollment in CSCE 313 .

subject: CSCE
title: /STAT 335 Principles of Data Science
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Theoretical foundations, algorithms and methods of deriving valuable insights from data; includes foundations in managing and analyzing data at scale, e.g. big data; data mining techniques and algorithms; exploratory data analysis; statistical methods and models; data visualization. Prerequisites: STAT 211 or ECEN 303 ; STAT 212 or CSCE 222 ; MATH 304 . Cross Listing: STAT 335/CSCE 320 .
prereq_text: STAT 211 or ECEN 303 ; STAT 212 or CSCE 222 ; MATH 304 .

subject: CSCE
title: Foundations of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Foundations of artificial intelligence and machine learning; search, reasoning and knowledge representation; planning, decision making and problem solving; supervised and unsupervised learning; deep learning methods and generative AI; applications across domains such as language, vision and robotics; evaluation of systems; ethical and societal implications. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 and CSCE 222 ; grade of C or better in STAT 211 or ECEN 303 ; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 and CSCE 222 ; grade of C or better in STAT 211 or ECEN 303 ; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CSCE
title: Foundations of Software Engineering
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Intensive programming experience and provision of the fundamentals needed for larger-scale software development; integration of concepts in computer science and familiarization with a variety of programming and development tools and techniques; team projects each with an emphasis on a different specialization within computer science; emphasis on programming techniques to ease code integration and clarity; practical exposure to software-engineering processes through large-scale projects and specification and documentation. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 314 , CSCE 350/ECEN 350 , or ECEN 350/CSCE 350 ; grade of C or better or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 313 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 314 , CSCE 350/ECEN 350 , or ECEN 350/CSCE 350 ; grade of C or better or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 313 .

subject: CSCE
title: /ECEN 350 Computer Architecture and Design
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Computer architecture and design; use of register transfer languages and simulation tools to describe and simulate computer operation; central processing unit organization, input/output and memory system architectures. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 248 and CSCE 120 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: ECEN 350/CSCE 350 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 248 and CSCE 120 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: CSCE
title: High-Impact Experience
description: Credits 0. 0 Other Hours. Participation in an approved high-impact learning practice; documentation and self-assessment of learning experience. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CSCE
title: Law and Policy in Cybersecurity
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of law and policy issues related to cybersecurity for the spectrum of cybersecurity jobs; includes procurement, operations and maintenance, governance and oversight, protection and defense, analysis, intelligence collection and operation and investigation cybersecurity jobs. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; MARA-403 taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: MARA 403 and CYBR 402 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; MARA-403 taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CSCE
title: Operating Systems
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Hardware/software evolution leading to contemporary operating systems; basic operating systems concepts; methods of operating systems design and construction including algorithms for CPU scheduling, memory and general resource allocation, process coordination and management; case studies of several operating systems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 313 ; grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 313 ; grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 .

subject: CSCE
title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Study of computer algorithms for numeric and non-numeric problems; design paradigms; analysis of time and space requirements of algorithms; correctness of algorithms; NP-completeness and undecidability of problems. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 and CSCE 222 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 and CSCE 222 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Cloud Computing
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Operating system and distributed systems fields that form the basis of cloud computing such as virtualization, key-value storage solutions, group membership, failure detection, peer to peer systems, datacenter networking, resource management and scalability; popular frameworks such as MapReduce and HDFS and case studies on failure determination. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 .

subject: CSCE
title: Software Security
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Basic principles of design and implementation of defect-free software, code reviews including tool-assisted review by static and dynamic analysis, risk analysis and management and methods for software security testing. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: /ECEN 416 Hardware Design Verification
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Hardware functional verification; case studies on verification in integrated circuit design; introduction to industry best practices; introduction to logic functional verification. Prerequisites: CSCE 312 , CSCE 350/ECEN 350 , or ECEN 350/CSCE 350 , or equivalent in computer architecture; familiarity with C/C++/Verilog/VHDL programming. Cross Listing: ECEN 416/CSCE 416 .
prereq_text: CSCE 312 , CSCE 350/ECEN 350 , or ECEN 350/CSCE 350 , or equivalent in computer architecture; familiarity with C/C++/Verilog/VHDL programming.

subject: CSCE
title: Artificial Intelligence
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Fundamental concepts and techniques of intelligent systems; representation and interpretation of knowledge on a computer; search strategies and control; active research areas and applications such as notational systems, natural language understanding, vision systems, planning algorithms, intelligent agents and expert systems. Prerequisite: CSCE 411 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 411 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Machine Learning
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Theoretical foundations of machine learning, pattern recognition and generating predictive models and classifiers from data; includes methods for supervised and unsupervised learning (decision trees, linear discriminants, neural networks, Gaussian models, non-parametric models, clustering, dimensionality reduction, deep learning), optimization procedures and statistical inference. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MATH 304 , MATH 311 , or MATH 323 ; Grade of C or better in STAT 211 , and STAT 404 or CSCE 221 , or ECEN 303 , and CSCE 121 or CSCE 120 . Cross Listing: ECEN 427 and STAT 421 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 304 , MATH 311 , or MATH 323 ; Grade of C or better in STAT 211 , and STAT 404 or CSCE 221 , or ECEN 303 , and CSCE 121 or CSCE 120 .

subject: CSCE
title: Software Development, Globalization and Culture Abroad
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Software development cycle; software outsourcing model, execution and practices; software industries on products, services and consultancy; software globalization; and offshore development culture; travel abroad required. Prerequisite: CSCE 315 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 315 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Problem Solving Programming Strategies
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Methods for analyzing fundamental programming problems from a variety of domains and implementing solutions quickly and efficiently; problems based on competitive programming contests to develop skills in problem analysis, coding and testing; solving problems will involve identifying and applying a range of algorithmic solutions; includes dealing with combinatorics, dynamic programming, graphs, numerical calculations, string processing and geometry, along with other specialized algorithms. Prerequisites: CSCE 411 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 411 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Software Engineering
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Application of engineering approach to computer software design and development; life cycle models, software requirements and specification; conceptual model design; detailed design; validation and verification; design quality assurance; software design/development environments and project management. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Accessible Computing
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of the characteristics of traditionally disenfranchised user populations due to disability including discrimination; universal design concepts; exploration of ethical and legal motivations for creating accessible technology; development, evaluation, design, and implementation of equitable and inclusive software and computer based solutions; study of multiple existing accessibility standards. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 .

subject: CSCE
title: Formal Languages and Automata
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Basic types of abstract languages and their acceptors; the Chomsky hierarchy; solvability and recursive function theory; application of theoretical results to practical problems. Prerequisite: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Compiler Design
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Programming language translation; functions and general organization of compiler design and interpreters; theoretical and implementation aspects of lexical scanners; parsing of context free languages; code generation and optimization; error recovery. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 .

subject: CSCE
title: Parallel Computing
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Overview of parallel computing technology and programming methods; includes multiprocessor architectures, programming tools, parallel performance, parallel algorithms, and applications of parallel computing. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Computer-Human Interaction
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Comprehensive study of the Computer-Human Interaction (CHI) area; includes history and importance of CHI; CHI design theories; modeling of computer users and interfaces; empirical techniques for task analysis and interface design; styles of interaction and future directions of CHI including hypermedia and computer-supported collaborative work. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or concurrent enrollment; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or concurrent enrollment; or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Distributed Systems
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles and techniques for engineering distributed systems with topics including communication, concurrency, programming paradigms, naming, managing shared state, caching, synchronization, reaching agreement, fault tolerance, security, middleware and distributed applications; design, implement and debug large software systems. Prerequisite: CSCE 313 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 313 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Data Analytics for Cybersecurity
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Theoretical foundations, algorithms and methods of data analytics for cybersecurity; study of data analytics including cluster analysis, supervised machine learning, anomaly detection, and visualization applied to cyber attacks, anomaly detection, vulnerability analysis, strategic manipulation, propaganda and other topics. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 ; grade of C or better in ECEN 303 , STAT 211 , STAT 301, STAT 302 , or STAT 303 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 ; grade of C or better in ECEN 303 , STAT 211 , STAT 301, STAT 302 , or STAT 303 .

subject: CSCE
title: Quantum Algorithms
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction to the design and analysis of quantum algorithms; basic principles of the quantum circuit model; gives a gentle introduction to basic quantum algorithms; reviews recent results in quantum information processing. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Computer Graphics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles of interactive computer graphics; 2-D and 3-D rendering pipelines, including geometric object and view transformations, projections, hidden surface removal, and rasterization; lighting models for local and global illumination; hierarchical models of 3-D objects; systems and libraries supporting display and user interaction. Prerequisite: CSCE 221 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 221 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Scientific Programming
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction to numerical algorithms fundamental to scientific and engineering applications of computers; elementary discussion of error; algorithms, efficiency; polynomial approximations, quadrature and systems of algebraic and differential equations. Prerequisites: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; MATH 304 or MATH 308 or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; MATH 304 or MATH 308 or concurrent enrollment.

subject: CSCE
title: /VIST 487 Game Development
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Aesthetic and technical aspects of computer game development, including game mechanics, story development, content creation and game programming; includes game design, interface design, 3D modeling and animation, graphics algorithms, shader programming and artificial intelligence; group project includes the design and development of a game from start to finish. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 386 or CSCE 441 , or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: VIST 487/CSCE 443 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in VIST 386 or CSCE 441 , or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Structures of Interactive Information
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. A systems approach to the programming, design, authoring and theory of hypermedia; object-oriented visual and interactive programming; visual design, including color, space, text and layering; the reference as a metadisciplinary structure; collecting and sampling; ontologies, maps and navigation as means of structuring information; create dynamic hypermedia that is expressive and interpretive. Prerequisite: CSCE 315 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 315 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Computers and New Media
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Potential and realized impact of computers in the design of new media; relationship between authors and readers of interactive material; influence of media design on the content expressed. Prerequisite: CSCE 221 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 221 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: /VIST 477 Virtual Reality
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Theory and practice of virtual reality; interactive 3D virtual environments; input/output devices, 3D interaction techniques, augmented reality, role of realism in VR, navigation techniques, design guidelines and evaluation methods. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in VIST 272 , CSCE 221 , or CSCE 441 . Cross Listing: VIST 477/CSCE 446 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in VIST 272 , CSCE 221 , or CSCE 441 .

subject: CSCE
title: /VIST 476 Data Visualization
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Visual representation and design of data and information; 3D visualization, infographics, data narratives, principles of visual data encoding and interaction techniques. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in VIST 272 , or CSCE 221 , or CSCE 441 . Cross Listing: VIST 476/CSCE 447 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in VIST 272 , or CSCE 221 , or CSCE 441 .

subject: CSCE
title: Computational Photography
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Cameras and the image formation process; basic image and video processing tools like sampling, filtering and pyramids; several image-based algorithms, including panorama creation, lightfields, image retargeting, high dynamic range imaging and texture synthesis. Prerequisite: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; MATH 304 or MATH 311 .
prereq_text: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; MATH 304 or MATH 311 .

subject: CSCE
title: Applied Cryptography
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. A comprehensive overview of the theory and practice of securing systems through cryptography. Topics include foundational security design principles, attacker models, classical ciphers and secure randomness; modern symmetric-key (stream and block) and asymmetric/public-key ciphers; cryptographic primitives including hash functions, digital signatures, message authentication codes and key exchange. Applications are explored, along with emerging trends. Hands-on projects provide practical experience with cryptographic tools. Prerequisite: CSCE 221 .
prereq_text: CSCE 221 .

subject: CSCE
title: Computer Animation
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Investigation of computational problems in computer animation; study of the mathematical and algorithmic foundations behind various techniques used for computer animation for real-time and offline use. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; grade of C or better in or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 441 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; grade of C or better in or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 441 .

subject: CSCE
title: Software Reverse Engineering
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Overview of the compilation mechanism to generate executable files and raw binary codes from source codes; executable file formats for an operating system to run the binary code; disassembly algorithms and control graph analysis; static and dynamic analyses; case studies on code obfuscation, codebreaking, malware analysis. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 313 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 313 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Robotics and Spatial Intelligence
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Algorithms for executing spatial tasks; path planning and obstacle aance in two- and three-dimensional robots--configuration space, potential field, free-space decomposition methods; stable grasping and manipulation; dealing with uncertainty; knowledge representation for planning--geometric and symbolic models of the environment; task-level programming; learning. Prerequisite: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; MATH 304 or MATH 311 .
prereq_text: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; MATH 304 or MATH 311 .

subject: CSCE
title: Microcomputer Systems
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 1 Lab Hour. Microcomputers as components of systems; VLSI processor and coprocessor architectures, addressing and instruction sets; I/O interfaces and supervisory control; VLSI architectures for signal processing; integrating special purpose processors into a system. Prerequisite: CSCE 313 .
prereq_text: CSCE 313 .

subject: CSCE
title: Computer Networks
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Basic hardware/software and architectural components for computer communications; delay, loss, throughput and topology of packet networks; application/transport-layer protocols, network-layer routing, data-link switching; security; socket programming, kernel APIs and multi-threading; case studies of existing networks, protocols and architectures. Prerequisite: CSCE 313 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 313 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Wireless and Mobile Systems
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction to wireless and mobile systems; wireless communication fundamentals; wireless medium access control design; transmission scheduling, network and transport protocols over wireless design, simulation and evaluation; wireless capacity; telecommunication systems; vehicular, adhoc, and sensor network systems; wireless security; mobile applications. Prerequisites: CSCE 313 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CSCE 313 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Computer and Network Security
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Fundamental concepts and principles of computer security, operating system and network security, secret key and public key cryptographic algorithms, hash functions, authentication, firewalls and intrusion detection systems, IPSec and VPN, wireless and web security. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 , and CSCE 313 ; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 , and CSCE 313 ; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: /ECEN 469 Advanced Computer Architecture
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Advanced computer architectures including memory designs, pipeline techniques and parallel structures such as out-of-order cores and multiprocessors. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ECEN 350/CSCE 350 or CSCE 350/ECEN 350 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: ECEN 469/CSCE 469 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 350/CSCE 350 or CSCE 350/ECEN 350 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: CSCE
title: Information Storage and Retrieval
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Representation of, storage of and access to very large multimedia document collections; fundamental data structures and algorithms of current information storage and retrieval systems and relates various techniques to design and evaluation of complete retrieval systems. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.

subject: CSCE
title: Natural Language Processing
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. NLP fundamentals including word semantics, language models, discourse and pragmatics; introduction to various applications including information extraction, sentiment analysis, question and answering, text summarization and machine translation. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 331 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 331 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

subject: CSCE
title: /CYBR 403 Cybersecurity Risk
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Risks in cybersecurity; avoidance, acceptance, mitigation, or transference strategies; developing reliable cybersecurity risk assessments to include analysis, categorization, and evaluation; cybersecurity risk audit frameworks. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CYBR 201/CSCE 201 , CSCE 201/CYBR 201 , or CSCE 221 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: CYBR 403/CSCE 477 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CYBR 201/CSCE 201 , CSCE 201/CYBR 201 , or CSCE 221 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: CSCE
title: Seminar
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Investigation and report by students on topics of current interest in computer science. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: CSCE
title: Senior Capstone Design
description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 6 Lab Hours. Development of system integration skills for solving real-world problems in computer science; significant team software project that uses integration of advanced concepts across computer science specializations; projects require design, implementation, documentation and demonstration, as well as design methodology, management process and teamwork. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CSCE 411 , and CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 411 , and CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 ; senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CSCE
title: Computer Systems Design
description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 6 Lab Hours. Engineering design; working as a design-team member, conceptual design methodology, design evaluations, total project planning and management techniques, design optimization, systems manufacturing costs considerations; emphasis placed upon students' activities as design professionals. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 , and CSCE 462 or ECEN 449 , and ECEN 325 ; senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 , and CSCE 462 or ECEN 449 , and ECEN 325 ; senior classification.

subject: CSCE
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 0 to 6. 0 to 6 Other Hours. Permits work on special project in computer science; project must be approved by the department. Prerequisite: Senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CSCE
title: Special Topics in...
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Special topics in computer science that are new or unique that are not covered in existing courses.

subject: CSCE
title: Research
description: Credits 0 to 4. 0 to 4 Other Hours. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in computer science. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

subject: CTFB
title: Coaching Skills
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Study, development, and demonstration of coaching skills; application of pedagogical strategies into learning environment; progressive field-based coaching experience in a secondary school setting. title: /KINE 321 Coaching of Volleyball

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CTSE 215/KINE 215 or KINE 215/CTSE 215 .

title: /KINE 324 Career Development in Coaching and Youth Development

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CTSE 215/KINE 215 or KINE 215/CTSE 215 .

title: /KINE 370 Basic Biology of Performance for Coaches

title: Current Issues in Coaching and Teaching

subject: CULN
title: /NUTR 305 Culinary Health

title: Culinary Health Practicum

prereq_text: CULN 305/NUTR 305 ; enrollment in culinary health certificate program; junior or senior classification.

subject: CVEN
title: Introduction to the Civil Engineering Profession
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 2 Lab Hours. Introduction to the study and practice of civil engineering; specialized subdisciplines of civil engineering; professionalism and professional registration; engineering ethics; exercises in engineering technical communications. prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ENGL 103 or ENGL 104 ; admitted to major degree sequence in civil engineering.

subject: CVEN
title: Engineering Mechanics: Statics
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253, or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 and ENGR 216/PHYS 216 or PHYS 216/ENGR 216 ; admitted to major degree sequence in civil engineering.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253, or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 and ENGR 216/PHYS 216 or PHYS 216/ENGR 216 ; admitted to major degree sequence in civil engineering.

subject: CVEN
title: Introduction to Graphics and Visualization Applications in Civil Engineering Design
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. title: Special Topics in...

title: Research

subject: CVEN
title: /EVEN 301 Environmental Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Water quality; material balances; chemical, physical and biological processes; water quality modeling; water and wastewater treatment; air quality; solid and hazardous waste management; global/national/local environmental challenges, issues and sustainability. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 107 or CHEM 120 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 302 and MATH 308 , or concurrent enrollment. Cross Listing: EVEN 301/CVEN 301 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CHEM 107 or CHEM 120 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 302 and MATH 308 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: CVEN
title: Computer Applications in Engineering and Construction
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Application of computers to solution of civil engineering problems using various numerical methods; structured computer programming; mathematical modeling and error analysis; solution of algebraic and differential equations; numerical differentiation and integration; curve-fitting; root-finding. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102 and PHYS 206 ; grade of C or better in MATH 308 or concurrent enrollment; admitted to major degree sequence in civil or environmental engineering.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102 and PHYS 206 ; grade of C or better in MATH 308 or concurrent enrollment; admitted to major degree sequence in civil or environmental engineering.

subject: CVEN
title: Civil Engineering Measurement
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Introduction to geodetic positions, datums, map projections; theory of civil engineering measurements and errors applied to horizontal and vertical control, curves, earthwork and mapping using state-of-the-art technology for data capture; processing and presentation of result. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MATH 151 ; admitted to major degree sequence in civil engineering.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 151 ; admitted to major degree sequence in civil engineering.

subject: CVEN
title: /EVEN 304 Environmental Engineering Lab
description: Credit 1. 3 Lab Hours. Environmental measurements on physical, chemical, biological and biotechnological parameters of water. Prerequisites: CVEN 301/EVEN 301 or EVEN 301/CVEN 301 , or concurrent enrollment; CVEN 311/EVEN 311 or concurrent enrollment; or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: EVEN 304/CVEN 304 .
prereq_text: CVEN 301/EVEN 301 or EVEN 301/CVEN 301 , or concurrent enrollment; CVEN 311/EVEN 311 or concurrent enrollment; or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
title: Mechanics of Materials
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Applications of stress/deformation relationships to structural members subjected to axial, torsional and bending loading for both determinate and indeterminate members. Applications include thin-walled pressure vessels, shear and moment diagrams in beams, beam design, deflection of members and members subjected to combined loadings. Stability of columns. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 221 , MEEN 221 , MEEN 225 , or AREN 221 ; also taught at Qatar campus.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 221 , MEEN 221 , MEEN 225 , or AREN 221 ; also taught at Qatar campus.

subject: CVEN
title: Materials Engineering for Civil Engineers
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Scientific concepts of civil engineering materials; relationship between macroscopic material properties and response and microscopic properties; physical, mechanical, surface, fracture, and rheological properties of civil engineering materials including metals, composites, and polymers. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 107 and CVEN 221 ; grade of C or better in PHYS 207 , and ENGR 217/PHYS 217 or PHYS 217/ENGR 217 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 305 and MATH 308 , or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CHEM 107 and CVEN 221 ; grade of C or better in PHYS 207 , and ENGR 217/PHYS 217 or PHYS 217/ENGR 217 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 305 and MATH 308 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: CVEN
title: Transportation Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Fundamental principles and methods in planning, design, and operation of transportation systems; driver and vehicle performance capabilities; highway geometric and pavement design principles; traffic analysis and transportation planning. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHYS 206 and STAT 211 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PHYS 206 and STAT 211 .

subject: CVEN
title: /EVEN 311 Fluid Dynamics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Fluid properties; statics; kinematics; basic conservation principles of continuity, energy and momentum; similitude and hydraulic models; incompressible flow in pipes; fluid dynamic drag. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253; grade of C or better in CVEN 221 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: EVEN 311/CVEN 311 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253; grade of C or better in CVEN 221 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CVEN
title: Sensor Technology in Civil Engineering
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Fundamentals of sensor technology and its application in civil engineering; investigation of data acquisition systems and sensors used in the civil engineering field; examples and hands-on demonstrations relevant to the natural and built environment. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
title: Sensor Technology for the Built Environment
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Fundamentals of sensor technology including laboratory safety, error analysis, statistical analysis, electric circuits, data acquisition, signal conditioning, signal analysis, strain gages, laser technology, image acquisition and analysis, fiber optic sensors, wireless sensors; its applications in civil engineering; and hands-on demonstrations relevant to the natural and built environment. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
title: Civil Engineering Systems
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Fundamentals of engineering economics; economic analysis and evaluation of engineering projects; application of systems analysis to civil engineering problems; optimization modeling and solution techniques; introduction to sustainability; simulation and statistical methods. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102 ; grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253; grade of C or better in STAT 211 or concurrent enrollment; admitted to major degree sequence in civil or environmental engineering or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102 ; grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253; grade of C or better in STAT 211 or concurrent enrollment; admitted to major degree sequence in civil or environmental engineering or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
title: /EVEN 339 Water Resources Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CVEN 311/EVEN 311 or EVEN 311/CVEN 311 . Cross Listing: EVEN 339/CVEN 339 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 311/EVEN 311 or EVEN 311/CVEN 311 .

title: Materials of Construction
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in CVEN 305 and CVEN 306 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 207 , ENGL 210 , or COMM 205 ; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in CVEN 305 and CVEN 306 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 207 , ENGL 210 , or COMM 205 ; or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
title: Portland Cement Concrete Materials for Civil Engineers
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Physical and chemical characteristics of Portland cement concrete systems; constituent materials; mixture proportioning; fresh concrete characteristics; hardened concrete properties; durability characteristics; and concrete construction methods. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in CVEN 305 and CVEN 306 ; grade C or better CVEN 207 , ENGL 210 , or COMM 205 ; or approval of instructor.

title: Theory of Structures
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Structural engineering--functions of structure, design loads, reactions and force systems; analysis of statically determinate structures including beams, trusses and arches; energy methods of determining deflections of structures; influence lines and criteria for moving loads; analysis of statically indeterminate structures including continuous beams and frames. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 221 and CVEN 305 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 302 or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 221 and CVEN 305 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 302 or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus.

title: Civil Engineering Project Management
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. title: Engineering Mechanics: Dynamics
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Application of first principles to model dynamic particles and rigid body systems with ordinary differential equations; solutions to models using analytical and numerical approaches; interpreting solutions/performance measures; linear vibrations; modeling of civil engineering systems and evaluating dynamic response to natural hazards. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , CVEN 305 and MATH 308 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , CVEN 305 and MATH 308 .

subject: CVEN
title: Introduction to Geotechnical Engineering
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Physical properties of soils, classification systems, soil exploration, permeability, consolidation, compaction, and shear strength; laboratory tests conducted to determine the physical and engineering soil properties needed for application in geotechnical engineering design. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in CVEN 305 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 207 , ENGL 210 , or COMM 205 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 302 or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in CVEN 305 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 207 , ENGL 210 , or COMM 205 .

title: Design Problems in Civil Engineering

title: Applied Civil Engineering Surveying
description: Credits 2. 6 Lab Hours. Application of land surveying principles; topographic surveying, boundary surveying, and construction staking through field exercises using state-of-the-art equipment and data capture/analysis techniques; preparation of topographic and boundary maps with related documents; presentation of results. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 303 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 303 ; junior or senior classification.

title: Construction Management of Field Operations
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Effects of industrialization on construction methods and resultant construction management problems. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CVEN 349 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 349 .

subject: CVEN
title: /EVEN 406 Environmental Protection and Public Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Communicable and noncommunicable diseases; environmental risk assessment; environmental assessments; comprehensive environmental planning; small water and wastewater systems; solid waste management; hazardous spills and waste management; vector control; environmental administration. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CVEN 301/EVEN 301 or EVEN 301/CVEN 301 ; or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: EVEN 406/CVEN 406 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 301/EVEN 301 or EVEN 301/CVEN 301 ; or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
title: /EVEN 412 Fundamentals of Air Quality
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Provide a comprehensive overview of air pollution. Topics covered include: chemistry and physics of atmospheric pollutants; sources, sinks and controls; atmospheric transport, transformation and models; health and environmental impacts; air quality standards, monitoring and management; climate change; indoor air pollution. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 301/EVEN 301 or EVEN 301/CVEN 301 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , or concurrent enrollment. Cross Listing: EVEN 412/CVEN 412 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 301/EVEN 301 or EVEN 301/CVEN 301 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 302 , or concurrent enrollment.

title: /EVEN 413 Natural Environmental Systems

title: Bituminous Materials
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Origin, production, specifications and tests of bituminous materials and mixtures used in flexible pavements including mix design, construction, maintenance and quality assurance processes. prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 307 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 342 or CVEN 343 .

title: Geomatics for Civil Engineering

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 303 or EVEN 339/CVEN 339 ; or approval of instructor.

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 322 ; satisfactory grade in CVEN 399 ; senior classification in civil engineering.

title: Geotechnical Engineering Design
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. A design course covering prediction of settlement, analysis of the stability of slopes, prediction of bearing capacity of shallow and deep foundations and determination of earth pressures acting on retaining structures; a general course in geotechnical engineering design for undergraduates and for graduate students not primarily interested in the geotechnical field, but desiring additional study beyond the introductory undergraduate level. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CVEN 365 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 365 .

title: Case Histories in Geotechnical Engineering
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Examination of geotechnical problems through the use of case studies associated with foundations, waste disposal, slope stability, retaining structures, soil improvement and other civil engineering works. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CVEN 365 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 365 .

subject: CVEN
title: Structural Concrete Design
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Behavior, design and detailing of reinforced concrete structural members according to the ACI Building Code Requirements; design for ultimate limit states (flexure, shear and axial loads) and serviceability requirements; applications include continuous beams and moment frames. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 345 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 342 or CVEN 343 , or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 345 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 342 or CVEN 343 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: CVEN
title: Matrix Methods of Structural Analysis
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Analysis of trusses, beams and frames using matrix structural analysis (direct stiffness method); matrix algebra and solution of linear algebraic equations; derivation of matrix stiffness relationships; coordinate transformations; topics related to use of commercial software for structural analysis; programming matrix methods to solve structures. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 345 and CVEN 363 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 345 and CVEN 363 .

subject: CVEN
title: Structural Steel Design
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Design of structural steel elements found in building structures, including tension members, compression members, beams, beam-columns and base plates; design of bolted and welded simple connections; design of bolted eccentric connections; design of bolted and welded partially and fully restrained connections. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CVEN 345 ; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 345 ; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: CVEN
title: Visualization and Building Information Modeling in Structural Engineering Design
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Graphical communication in the structural engineering design process; introduction to Building Information Modeling (BIM); construction documents and contract drawings in structural engineering applications, data analysis and project visualization. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 250 and CVEN 345 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 250 and CVEN 345 .

title: AutoCAD in Civil Engineering

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 301/EVEN 301 or EVEN 301/CVEN 301 ; grade of C or better in CVEN 339/EVEN 339 or EVEN 339/CVEN 339 .

Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in CVEN 307 .

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 339/EVEN 339 or approval of instructor.

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in DAEN 321 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: DAEN

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Human considerations and constraints for data engineering, including human factors of data visualization; data processing and analysis of human physiological, psychological and performance data; the role of human biases in model development, analysis and interpretation; human factors of interactions with machine learning-based artificial intelligence tools in complex systems such as healthcare, manufacturing and transportation. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: DAEN

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Mathematical optimization algorithms with applications to data analytics; primary topics include convexity, gradient and subgradient methods and their variants, Newton’s and quasi-Newton methods, Frank-Wolfe, duality, derivative-free optimization. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253; grade of C or better in MATH 304 or MATH 323 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253; grade of C or better in MATH 304 or MATH 323 .

Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in DAEN 331 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in DAEN 331 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: DAEN
