prereq_text: INTS and INTA majors; junior or senior classification; prior background in introductory economics recommended.

subject: INTA
title: Cyberpolicy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of the intersection of technology, policy, strategy and national security, focusing on the national security implications of cyberspace and cyber-enabled technologies, including cyber-enabled influence operations, in support of national security interests. It is not a technical course, but will provide the background necessary for students to understand, discuss and analyze relevant issues related to cyberspace and cyber-enabled operations and activities. The course will also introduce and examine the cyberspace aspects of a number of disruptive technologies in a national security context, including artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous weapons systems, biotechnology and others. Prerequisites: INTS and INTA majors; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: INTS and INTA majors; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: /GLST 401 The City and its Global Contexts
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of rural and urban environments affected by global currents in culture, politics, and society; exploration of urbanism as represented by artists, writers, and filmmakers; study of such topics such as urban design. Prerequisites: INTA 211 or GLST 201 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: GLST 401/INTA 401 .
prereq_text: INTA 211 or GLST 201 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: INTA
title: Nations and Nationalisms
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Interdisciplinary approach where nation is understood as modern political entity distinct from country; examination of historical and philosophical origins of idea of nationalism; theories on nationhood, national identity and rise of nationalism; global variety of concrete test cases to highlight actual functions (wars, decolonization, symbolic representations in film, etc.). Prerequisites: International studies major; INTA 211 .
prereq_text: International studies major; INTA 211 .

subject: INTA
title: War and Memory
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of world wars, colonial wars, genocides, and historical crimes from the late nineteenth century until the present; analysis of the changing memory of those traumatic events as evident in historical accounts, commemorations, film, and literature. Prerequisites: International studies major; INTA 211 .
prereq_text: International studies major; INTA 211 .

subject: INTA
title: Technology and Global Change
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Interdisciplinary examination of the transformative impact of new technologies on global social, economic, political and cultural reality; focus on changes in the exercise of power and state sovereignty, labor and economic transactions, war and social activism, subjectivity and social interactions, surveillance and anonymity, internet of things and artificial intelligence. Prerequisite: INTA 211 ; international studies major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: INTA 211 ; international studies major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: Culture, Neoliberalism and Globalism
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of largely North Atlantic cultural forms and meanings that arise in the context of neoliberalism from the late 1970’s to the present; cultural studies and broad-based social analysis to identify and interrogate the many relational contexts where power circulates through cultural objects and meanings. Prerequisites: INTA 211 ; international studies major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: INTA 211 ; international studies major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: /GLST 410 Gender and Globalization
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Concepts of gender from a global perspective; global theories of gender and sexuality across media. Prerequisites: INTA 211 or GLST 201 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: GLST 410/INTA 410 .
prereq_text: INTA 211 or GLST 201 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: INTA
title: International Economic Development
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examines theories of economic growth and development; explains concepts and methods commonly used when evaluating the effectiveness of international development programs. Prerequisites: International Affairs Major and junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs Major and junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: American Foreign Policy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of political, economic, cultural, and military dimensions of the United States’ interactions with the world since the 19th century; focus on how interests of soldiers, business people, missionaries, civilians within the United States and in combat zones impact policy. Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: Economic Statecraft
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction to emerging field of economic statecraft; use of economic tools of national power; overview of important seminal works on economic statecraft; instruction in theoretical and empirical aspects of economic statecraft. Prerequisites: International Affairs major, junior or senior classification, and ECON 202 , ECON 203 , INTA 301 , and INTA 231 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: International Affairs major, junior or senior classification, and ECON 202 , ECON 203 , INTA 301 , and INTA 231 or approval of instructor.

subject: INTA
title: International Organizations
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Theoretical and empirical aspects of the role, potentials, and limitations of major International Organizations (IO) in world politics; study of norms and rules that govern international relations and institutions where those rules are formulated and implemented; survey of IOs in areas of peace operations, human rights, environment and international trade. Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: Women and International Affairs
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Overview of important dimensions of women and international affairs; stratification of human society by sex, women and international political economy, women and national/international security, women and international human rights; examination of international efforts to improve women’s situation worldwide and other international policy initiatives. Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: Intelligence and National Security
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of historical and contemporary Intelligence capabilities as a part of the National Security environment, study of teamwork used by multiple organizations to inform world leaders; understanding of the major intelligence disciplines; instruction in how the intelligence cycle collects, analyses, and informs decisions related to National Security matters. Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: European Politics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Historical examination of the evolution of the European Union and its contemporary politics; overview of formation of the European Union and its integration processes, contemporary European Politics in Western and Eastern Europe and security developments in the European Union. Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: Chinese Politics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Study of Chinese domestic political history; instruction in the origins and development of the contemporary political system of China; overview of the history and foundational experiences of the Chinese Communist Party and its leaders. Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior and senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior and senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: International Politics of the Middle East
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of interactions among states of the region, the region’s non-state actors and outside powers in the post-World War II period; topics include power distributions within the region and globally, effects of transnational ideological and identity movements, domestic political institutions in the region’s states, regional economic systems, outside power policies in the region, war and peace decisions, alliance and alignment patterns, and regional modes of statecraft. Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: Senior Seminar
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Capstone course designed to produce in-depth research projects; based on student's international experience and specific area of expertise acquired in major. Prerequisites: International Studies major; INTA 211 ; 6 hours of INTA 401/GLST 401 , INTA 403 , INTA 405 , INTA 406 , INTA 407, INTA 409 , INTA 410/GLST 410 , INTA 412 , INTA 415 , INTA 418 , INTA 443 , INTA 445 , INTA 452 , INTA 455 , INTA 473 , INTA 476 , INTA 484 , INTA 485 , INTA 489 , INTA 491 , INTA 494 , or INTA 497 ; senior classification; INTA 300 .
prereq_text: International Studies major; INTA 211 ; 6 hours of INTA 401/GLST 401 , INTA 403 , INTA 405 , INTA 406 , INTA 407, INTA 409 , INTA 410/GLST 410 , INTA 412 , INTA 415 , INTA 418 , INTA 443 , INTA 445 , INTA 452 , INTA 455 , INTA 473 , INTA 476 , INTA 484 , INTA 485 , INTA 489 , INTA 491 , INTA 494 , or INTA 497 ; senior classification; INTA 300 .

subject: INTA
title: Directed Internship
description: Credits 0 to 3. 0 to 3 Other Hours. Directed internship in a private firm, government or non-profit agency outside the United States; provide on-the-job experience appropriate to the student's program of work and career objectives. To be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Maximum of 3 credit hours may count towards degree. Prerequisites: INTA 211 ; approval of internship coordinator.
prereq_text: INTA 211 ; approval of internship coordinator.

subject: INTA
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 0 to 3. 0 to 3 Other Hours. Research problems and readings for students majoring in international studies; directed independent study of an international issue related to student's area of interest. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: INTA
title: Russia and the Former Soviet Union
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Investigation of how history, institutions, and political culture in Russia influences choices that elites and ordinary people make about politics; overview of Tsarist Russian imperialism, Soviet experiment in modernization and multinational governance, collapse of Soviet Union and creation of 15 independent states; examination of processes of political change and governance in post-communist Russia, and factors that influence processes. Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: Special Topics in...
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Selected topics in an identified area of international affairs. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; INTS and INTA majors.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; INTS and INTA majors.

subject: INTA
title: Research
description: Credits 0 to 3. 0 to 3 Other Hours. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in international studies. Prerequisites: INTA 211 ; junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: INTA 211 ; junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

subject: INTA
title: Inter-American Affairs - U.S. Interventions in Latin America and Beyond
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Study of the dynamics of contemporary Inter-American political relations; introduction of policy and security issues relevant to the Americas (US, Canada, Caribbean, and Latin America). Prerequisites: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: International Affairs major; junior or senior classification.

subject: INTA
title: Independent Honors Study
description: Credits 3. 3 Other Hours. Directed independent studies designed to produce a senior honors thesis; based on international experience and interdisciplinary expertise acquired in major. Prerequisites: INTA major; honors candidate; completed international experience.
prereq_text: INTA major; honors candidate; completed international experience.

subject: ISEN
title: Deterministic Optimization Modeling and Design
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Development and application of fundamental deterministic optimization models; emphasis on formulating real-world problems as linear, integer, and network flow models; computer optimization software will be used to solve the linear and integer models. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 152 and ENGR 102 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 152 and ENGR 102 .

subject: ISEN
title: Informatics for Industrial Engineers
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Structured programming concepts for implementing mathematical and statistical models in industrial engineering problems; emphasis on introductory production and service system problems and computer-based approaches to solve the problems; engineering applications of probability and statistics concepts. Prerequisites: CSCE 206 , CSCE 111 , CSCE 120 , CSCE 121 , or CSCE 110 or equivalent; concurrent enrollment in STAT 211 .
prereq_text: CSCE 206 , CSCE 111 , CSCE 120 , CSCE 121 , or CSCE 110 or equivalent; concurrent enrollment in STAT 211 .

subject: ISEN
title: Essentials of Modern Manufacturing Methods for Engineering Design
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. . Fundamental basis from materials and manufacturing methods selection in engineering design; basic elements and theory of a range of materials manufacturing methods, with specific emphasis on recent developments in the field including rapid prototyping 3D, computer control of machines - tools, automation robotics micro-fabrication and metrology. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ENGR 217/PHYS 217 or PHYS 217/ENGR 217 , or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ENGR 217/PHYS 217 or PHYS 217/ENGR 217 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: ISEN
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Problems of limited scope in industrial engineering approved on an individual basis intended to promote independent study. Prerequisite: Approval of department head.
prereq_text: Approval of department head.

subject: ISEN
title: Special Topics in...
description: Credits 1 to 5. 1 to 5 Other Hours. Selected topics in an identified area of Industrial Engineering. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Approval of instructor.

subject: ISEN
title: Research
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in industrial and systems engineering. May be taken four times for credit. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.

subject: ISEN
title: Economic Analysis of Engineering Projects
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Principles of economic equivalence; time value of money; analysis of single and multiple investments; comparison of alternatives; capital recovery and after-tax analysis of economic projects. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 152 or MATH 172 ; also taught at Qatar campus.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 152 or MATH 172 ; also taught at Qatar campus.

subject: ISEN
title: Uncertainty Modeling for Industrial Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Models and methods based on probability and statistics for industrial engineering applications; random variables, expectation, distribution fitting, reliability of systems, central limit theorem and interval estimates in the context of production and service systems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 230 or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in STAT 211 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 230 or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in STAT 211 .

subject: ISEN
title: Introduction to Data Analytics and Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Basic concepts in data engineering, including data acquisition, data management and models for learning with associated algorithms; iterative algorithms; tree-based and regression-based classification; graphs and graph-based methods; clustering; neural networks basics and their training; data structures for storing and processing data; introduction to databases. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 110 , CSCE 111 , CSCE 120 , CSCE 121 , or CSCE 206 ; grade of C or better in STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CSCE 110 , CSCE 111 , CSCE 120 , CSCE 121 , or CSCE 206 ; grade of C or better in STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Operations Research I
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Development and application of fundamental deterministic optimization models and solution methods; focus on quantitative modeling and formulation of linear, integer, and network flow problems; use of computer optimization software to model and solve real-life problems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 304 or MATH 323 ; grade of C or better in ISEN 210 , or approval of department.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 304 or MATH 323 ; grade of C or better in ISEN 210 , or approval of department.

subject: ISEN
title: Human Systems Interaction
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles of human factors and ergonomics; emphasis on design to support human capabilities, limitations, and interaction tendencies in sociotechnical work systems; topics include human information processing, physiological and biomechanical functioning, and implications for design of the workplace and jobs; case studies in manufacturing, medicine, aerospace, ground transportation, and computer interaction. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MEEN 221 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MEEN 221 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Operations Research II
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Probabilistic methods for industrial and service systems; stochastic processes used in industrial engineering, including Poisson processes and discrete and continuous-time Markov chains; applications to production operations, inventory control, revenue management, quality control, reliability, digital simulation and finance. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 304 or MATH 323 ; grade of C or better in ISEN 310 , STAT 212 , or ECEN 303 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 304 or MATH 323 ; grade of C or better in ISEN 310 , STAT 212 , or ECEN 303 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Quality Engineering
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Strategic approach to implementing quality, process and business improvement methods using data analysis tools; total quality management and six sigma approaches to define, measure, analyze, improve and control processes; principles of lean engineering; control charts; process capability analysis; basic metrology, applied statistics, lean principles and process capability. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 310 and ISEN 230 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 310 and ISEN 230 .

subject: ISEN
title: System Simulation
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Systems simulation structure, logic and methodologies; development of simulation models; data handling methods; analysis of simulation data; verification and validation; system simulation languages, models and analysis; applications to industrial situations. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 230 and ISEN 310 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 230 and ISEN 310 .

subject: ISEN
title: Lean Thinking and Lean Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophical, managerial, and operational principles of lean thinking within the context, tools, and practices of lean engineering; focuses on principles and practices of lean engineering that are applicable across industry types; includes design of lean systems, lean cell design, modeling of lean manufacturing systems and operation of manufacturing cells; queuing network theory for the analysis of lean systems. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Production Systems Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles, models, and techniques for planning and analysis of production and distribution systems; application of linear, integer, and nonlinear optimization models and solution methods for aggregate planning, supply chain planning, push (MRP) and pull (JIT) material flow management, inventory control under deterministic and stochastic demands, operations scheduling, and production scheduling. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 230 and ISEN 320 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 230 and ISEN 320 .

subject: ISEN
title: Professional Development
description: Credits 0. 0 Other Hours. Participation in an approved high-impact learning practice; reflection on professional outcomes from engineering body of knowledge; documentation and self-assessment of learning experience at mid-curriculum point. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 and ISEN 230 ; senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 and ISEN 230 ; senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Facilities Design and Material Handling
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles of facilities location, layout, and material handling systems and to practice designing facilities; modeling, design, and analysis techniques; methodologies in facilities location, layout, and material handling; integration of ergonomics analysis techniques and their implications on design, layout, safety and quality. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 and ISEN 320 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 and ISEN 320 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Advanced Engineering Economy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles of economic equivalence; borrowing, lending, and investing; establishing minimum attractive rate of return; replacement analysis; capital budgeting; uncertainty analysis; decision trees. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 or ISEN 302 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 or ISEN 302 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Engineering Management Techniques
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Techniques relating to managing engineering activities; engineer's transition into management; engineering managerial functions; motivation of individual and group behavior; productivity assessment/improvement; managing the quality function and communications. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ISEN 350 ; senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 350 ; senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Advanced Data Analytics for Industry
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Data mining; linear discriminant analysis (LDA), principal component analysis (PCA) and other methods; classification, clustering, and mining, information extraction; dealing with uncertainty, Bayesian inference; neural models, regression and feature selection. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 310 and ISEN 350 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 310 and ISEN 350 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Total Quality Engineering
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Principles of total quality engineering; total quality management philosophy, engineering approaches for designing quality into products and processes; off-line experimentation methods for the robust design; emphasis on teamwork and continuous quality improvement. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in STAT 211 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Design and Analysis of Industrial Systems with Simulation
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. In-depth study into the design-modeling and subsequent analysis of contemporary production/service systems; production/service systems are modeled using a modern simulation software; emphasis is placed on the critical analysis of alternative flow designs of modeled systems using flow and economic parameters to assess system improvement. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 and ISEN 355 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 and ISEN 355 .

subject: ISEN
title: /DAEN 427 Decision and Risk Analysis
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Overview of the state of the art in descriptive and prescriptive theories of decision making under uncertainty with emphasis on the ways in which human decisions depart from normative models of rationality; analytical foundations stemming from several disciplines, economics, psychology, management science; application in engineering systems will be considered. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ISEN 310 , DAEN 321 , or STAT 212 . Cross Listing: DAEN 427/ISEN 427 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 310 , DAEN 321 , or STAT 212 .

subject: ISEN
title: /AERO 436 Human Factors Engineering for Aerospace Designs
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Physiological and psychophysiological issues encountered in aviation and space environments and their effect on human cognitive and physical performance; survey methods for human workload and performance evaluations; apply human-systems design principles to an aerospace design project. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: AERO 436/ISEN 432 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Biomechanics of Work
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Mechanical behavior of the human musculoskeletal system and component tissues during physical activity; fundamental biomechanical concepts, principles, tools and methods for the measurement of human physical attributes, evaluation of human mechanical capabilities and modeling of human musculoskeletal system; application of concepts to improve performance or prevent injuries during daily activities. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ISEN 330 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 330 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Human Error and Resilient System Design
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Human error from a sociotechnical systems perspective; role of error in complex system failures; human behavioral modes and system design factors; analytical methods for defining the roles and impact of errors in large-scale system accidents; real-world case studies. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 330 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 330 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Systems Thinking
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Systems thinking process, systems of systems and the fundamental considerations associated with the engineering of large-scale systems, or systems engineering including systems modeling, design and the system development process. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 304 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 304 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: System Reliability Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Methods of system modeling and analysis to predict and enhance the reliability, maintainability, and availability of complex engineered systems including component and systems reliability models, system life prediction, and data collection and analysis of failure and repair distributions. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in STAT 211 or equivalent; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in STAT 211 or equivalent; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Organizational Systems
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Role of people and organizations in the design and development of complex engineered systems; providing engineers with the skills needed to effectively manage large-scale system development programs. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 330 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 330 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Manufacturing Operations
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Analytical principles of manufacturing systems design, analysis and control; emphasis placed on stochastic analysis; role of variability and impact on cycle time; push versus pull production strategies including Kanban and constant WIP control; probability, queuing theory, Little’s Law, heavy traffic approximations, and queuing networks. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 340 and MATH 304 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 340 and MATH 304 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Capstone Senior Design
description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 6 Lab Hours. Engineering design including identification of a problem; development, analysis and evaluation of alternative solutions; and recommendations for and, where possible, development of systems improvement tools; application of experience and training to provide a product or solution that helps company clients; balancing client needs with academic requirements. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 , ISEN 302 , ISEN 330 , ISEN 340 , ISEN 350 , ISEN 355 and ISEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ISEN 210 , ISEN 302 , ISEN 330 , ISEN 340 , ISEN 350 , ISEN 355 and ISEN 370 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: ISEN
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 1 to 6. 1 to 6 Other Hours. Permits work on special project in industrial engineering; project must be approved by department head. May be taken for credit up to 6 hours. Prerequisites: Senior classification in industrial engineering.
prereq_text: Senior classification in industrial engineering.

title: Special Topics in...
description: Credits 1 to 5. 1 to 5 Lecture Hours. 0 to 5 Lab Hours. In-depth study of areas of current student interest and recent advances; normally used for first time offering of new courses. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Approval of instructor.

subject: ISEN
title: Research
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in industrial and systems engineering. May be taken for credit up to 6 hours. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

subject: ISTM
title: Business Information Systems Concepts
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction to the use of computers in data and document management and as a problem-solving tool for business; fundamental concepts of information technology and theory; opportunities to use existing application software to solve various business information systems oriented problems. May not be used to satisfy degree requirements for majors in business. Prerequisite: For students other than business and agribusiness majors.
prereq_text: For students other than business and agribusiness majors.

subject: ISTM
title: Fundamentals of Information Systems
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (BCIS 1305 and 1405) Fundamentals of Information Systems. Introduction to information systems concepts; study of information systems in the functional areas of business; overview of hardware, software and popular operating systems; study of problem solving tools; human factors. Prerequisite: Business and Maritime Business Administration majors; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Business and Maritime Business Administration majors; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ISTM
title: Business Programming Logic and Design
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Development of structured and object-oriented program logic and design in solving business programming problems; writing, documenting, debugging and testing computer code; emphasis on good coding techniques and logical thinking. Prerequisite: ISTM 210 or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: ISTM 210 or concurrent enrollment.

subject: ISTM
title: Professional Development Information Systems Seminar
description: Credit 1. 1 Other Hour. Exposure to professional issues, contemporary information systems topics, potential MIS careers and employers. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisite: Admission to Mays Business School; intend to major in management information systems.
prereq_text: Admission to Mays Business School; intend to major in management information systems.

subject: ISTM
title: Network Communications and Infrastructure
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Concepts, technologies and applications of on-line and network-based systems; analysis and design of data communications; requirements in an information system environment; impact on business organizations; installation, configuration and management of virtual servers. Prerequisite: ISTM 250 ; ACCT 230 and BUSN 203 , or concurrent enrollment; admission to upper division in Mays Business School, or approval of instructor if major is outside of Mays Business School.
prereq_text: ISTM 250 ; ACCT 230 and BUSN 203 , or concurrent enrollment; admission to upper division in Mays Business School, or approval of instructor if major is outside of Mays Business School.

subject: ISTM
title: Foundations of Data Analytics for Non-MIS Majors
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Use and application of data modeling, Structured Query Language (SQL), Database Management Systems (DBMS) and data visualization in the solution of business problems. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: ISTM 313 or ISTM 315 . Prerequisites: Admission to upper division in Mays Business School.
prereq_text: Admission to upper division in Mays Business School.

subject: ISTM
title: Database Programming
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Use and application of Structured Query Language (SQL); Database Management Systems (DBMS) in the solution of business problems; database programming. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: ISTM 313 or ISTM 315 . Prerequisites: ISTM 310 ; ISTM 320 ; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: ISTM 310 ; ISTM 320 ; or approval of instructor.

subject: ISTM
title: Business Systems Analysis and Design

subject: JOUR
title: American Mass Media
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (COMM 1307) American Mass Media. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the development and role of mass media in the United States across print, broadcast and digital platforms. Surveys ways journalism, entertainment, advertising and/or social media industries have evolved alongside major legal, economic and technological changes. Examines how media shape public understanding of news, culture and community life. Course content may reference current events or contested media topics for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds media literacy essential for participation in contemporary information environments. Supports workforce preparation for fields involving communication, marketing, journalism, public relations, policy and content creation. Strengthens ability to interpret media systems and evaluate messages. Provides academic grounding for further study in media, communication and related social sciences, while promoting informed engagement with public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers ways media messages are not neutral transmissions of facts or entertainment, but are reflections of institutional structures, economic incentives and cultural values. Clarifies differences between news, opinion, analysis, persuasion and/or misinformation, enabling critical comparison. Considers responsible media as involving critical interpretation, evidence assessment and awareness of perspective. Applies media literacy concepts to support informed citizenry through an understanding of First Amendment protections. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media history and industry development; journalism and press freedom; advertising and entertainment business models; media law and ethics; corporate ownership and consolidation; social media platforms and audience participation; representation in film, television and news; and the role of media in elections, crisis coverage or cultural debate. Course materials may include real-world examples that involve political and/or social controversy, examined for purposes of understanding the role of media in the United States and around the globe.

subject: JOUR
title: Mass Media Information
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores methods for locating, verifying and organizing information for use in journalism and related media fields. Examines how reporters, researchers and content creators identify credible sources, interpret data and manage competing forms of evidence. Covers procedures for working with public records, interviews, documents and digital databases. Introduces basic interview techniques and requires a range of interviews. Addresses legal and ethical standards guiding information access, attribution and responsible use. May reference real-world news events and/or disputed claims for purposes of evaluating information practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies directly to careers in journalism, public communication, strategic media, research and content production where accuracy and credibility are essential. Builds fluency in information gathering and source evaluation for professional settings such as newsrooms, nonprofit advocacy, policy communication and organizational messaging. Supports academic preparation for advanced coursework in reporting, media law, research methods or data journalism. Strengthens civic readiness by reinforcing principles of evidence-based decision-making in public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how information is not merely “found” but actively selected, framed and interpreted through methodological choices. Highlights differences between rumor, opinion and verifiable fact, while showing how even credible sources may present information with limitations or bias. Considers that responsible information gathering requires transparency in process as much as accuracy in outcome. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include source credibility and verification; interviewing and data collection methods; public records and open-source intelligence; fact-checking and revision protocols; digital search strategies; statistical interpretation and data visualization; legal frameworks governing access and privacy including public records legislation at the federal and state levels; ethical considerations in handling sensitive or incomplete information. May draw on journalism, government documents, nonprofit reports or corporate communications when relevant to understanding differences in information intent and reliability. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 ; freshman or sophomore classification; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 ; freshman or sophomore classification; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.

subject: JOUR
title: Media Writing I
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. (COMM 2311) Media Writing I. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores foundational practices of news and media writing across print, digital and broadcast formats. Covers core principles of reporting, source development, interviewing, story structure, clarity, accuracy and ethics. Emphasizes deadline writing and editorial standards such as Associated Press style. Includes both classroom instruction and lab-based field reporting and/or writing practice. Course content may reference current events or public controversies as real-time reporting contexts, examined for purposes of journalistic analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds competencies essential for careers in journalism, public communication, media production and content strategy, including information gathering, source evaluation, editing and professional writing. Supports preparation for advanced coursework in reporting, multimedia storytelling, strategic communication or public affairs. Provides transferable skills for civic participation by strengthening the ability to assess evidence, verify claims and communicate clearly in public-facing formats. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights the difference between everyday writing and journalistic writing defined by professional standards of fairness, attribution, style and verification. Considers that responsible reporting involves interpretation, fact assessment, and acknowledgment of perspective without slant or speculation. Develops recognition of how word choice, structure and sourcing shape public understanding. Analyzes how news stories serve both individuals and communities. Develops understanding of professional ethics standards. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of news values, interviewing techniques, attribution and quoting, hard news and feature formats, multimedia writing, legal constraints and ethical dilemmas in reporting. Exercises may involve real or hypothetical scenarios involving crime, politics, social issues or public institutions, used solely to develop reporting judgment and writing skills. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 and JOUR 200 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 and JOUR 200 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.

subject: JOUR
title: Television Sports Production
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how televised sports are produced behind the scenes, from planning to live execution. Introduces the roles of producers, directors, announcers, camera operators and technical crews, emphasizing collaboration across production teams. Examines historic developments in sports broadcasting alongside contemporary industry practices, including graphics, replay operations and/or real-time storytelling. Course content may reference high-pressure or emotionally charged broadcast situations for the purpose of professional analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops workforce-ready skills in research, coordination and deadline-driven collaboration through engagement with live event production and sports media workflows. Provides practical experience in broadcast storytelling, technical setup and real-time decision-making. Builds foundations for effective communication under pressure, rapid problem-solving and teamwork, competencies that transfer to careers in media, athletics, production management and other professional or academic settings requiring precision and adaptability. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how sports broadcasting functions as both entertainment and institutional messaging, shaping narratives of competition, identity and community. Examines ways production choices, such as camera angles, commentary, graphics and pacing, frame audience perception. Informs reflection on how spectacle, emotion and/or technology intersect in mediated sport. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of broadcast history and industry structure; producer and director decision-making; live graphics and replay systems; commentary and on-air performance roles; camera work and technical operations; crisis management during live events; ethics of representation in sports storytelling; evolution of streaming, social media integration and fan engagement. Course materials may include footage depicting intense competition, injury or heightened emotion, examined for purposes of professional critique.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 215 Interviewing - Principles and Practice
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of interviewing as a purposeful form of interpersonal communication. Focus on questioning strategies, listening and interaction between the interviewer and interviewee. Examines informative, persuasive, survey and/or employment interview contexts. Develops skills as both the interviewer and the interviewee. Emphasizes how structure, audience, goals and setting shape communication choices. Addresses the logical and psychological bases of interviewing. Class applications may involve exposure to perspectives and experiences across social, cultural and professional backgrounds. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds transferable skills essential to journalism, media, public communication and organizational practice. Involves questioning, listening, adaptation to audience and purpose and interaction across varied goals. Applies to situations that require navigating unfamiliar or sensitive territory with professionalism. Develops skill in effectively navigating differences in belief, identity, experience and disagreement within interview contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how interviews function as purposeful conversations, showing how credibility, preparation and strategy shape outcomes. Encourages awareness of the interview as a structured exchange rather than spontaneous talk. Broadens understanding of how perspective and authority influence communication across roles and settings for both interviewer and interviewee. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of questioning techniques, listening practices, rapport-building, credibility assessment and ethical responsibility; examination of informative, persuasive, survey, research and/or employment interviews; consideration of how audience, purpose and context govern interview structure and performance. Course work may involve engagement with people from varied backgrounds and experiences. Interview practice may include topics connected to identity, culture, ethics, work and/or participants’ personal lives. Exposure to differing viewpoints and/or lived realities reflects the range of issues encountered in professional and public communication. May include resume writing skills in preparation for career interviews. Cross Listing: COMM 215/JOUR 215 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 230 Communication Technology Skills
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines principles and practices of communication technology in the digital domain. Surveys the history and standards of television, radio, video gaming, streaming media, e-publishing and/or social networking industries and markets. Focuses on production skills such as composing, recording and editing digital content, as well as media literacy across platforms, including the ability to evaluate social, cultural and/or ethical implications of communication technologies. Emphasizes media-centric strategic foresight to postulate regarding the future of the communication and technological landscape. Class applications may also draw on popular culture and/or current events, connecting course concepts to contemporary media environments. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds technical competence and media literacy skills applicable across professional, academic and civic contexts. Develops the skills necessary to create digital media content, adapt communication strategies to emerging technologies, tell stories across multiple media platforms and evaluate the impact of communication technologies on audiences and industries. Strengthens preparation for careers in journalism, media production, marketing, communication design, public relations and related fields where technological fluency and critical analysis are essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds understanding of how communication technologies shape interaction, identity and/or culture beyond their technical functions. Highlights how tools such as streaming platforms, social media and/or virtual environments influence professional practice, everyday communication and public dialogue. Clarifies both opportunities and challenges presented by digital media, including questions of access, ethics and/or social impact. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of the development and application of communication technologies across industries; exploration of audio, video, web and interactive media tools; analysis of digital platforms and markets; consideration of issues such as media convergence, intellectual property, ethics and sociocultural impact. Course work may incorporate case studies from popular culture and/or current events to connect course concepts with real-world practices. The course may include discourses and perspectives that are unfamiliar or controversial, reflecting the diversity of discourses relating to digital technologies and practices. Prerequisites: Enrollment in communication or telecommunication media studies majors, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor. Cross Listing: COMM 230/JOUR 230 .
prereq_text: Enrollment in communication or telecommunication media studies majors, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 248 Podcasting and Audio Storytelling
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores basic audio storytelling techniques required for podcast production within journalism and digital content creation, including principles of podcast development, scripting, interviewing, voice performance, audio recording and editing. May include instructions in microphone selection, sound environments and use of editing software. Covers branding elements such as titles, descriptions, cover art, music and metadata. Introduces strategies for publishing, promotion and audience growth across distribution platforms. Course content may include legal and ethical considerations related to privacy, attribution, licensing or defamation. Course content may reference real-world events or personal narratives for purposes of analysis and production rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops production skills applicable to careers in journalism, strategic communication and digital content creation. Promotes skills in narrative design, research organization, technical proficiency and navigating teamwork in creative industry contexts. Supports academic preparation in media writing, audio reporting and multimedia storytelling. Enhances civic communication skills by training attention to voice, perspective and accountability in public messaging. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights differences between casual conversation and structured audio storytelling designed for listeners’ attention. Clarifies how tone, pacing, editing and sound design influence interpretation and credibility. Encourages recognition of ethical responsibility when representing others’ voices or lived experiences in recorded form. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of podcast formats and genres; interview preparation and questioning techniques; narrative scripting; ambient sound and music beds; recording equipment and vocal delivery; editing workflows and mixing practices; platform distribution and analytics; audience design and engagement. Course material may draw on real-world audio examples involving sensitive or emotional content, used for purposes of critical listening and professional development. Cross Listing: COMM 248/JOUR 248 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 250 New Media and the Independent Voice
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of new and independent media in shaping cultural, political and social life. Surveys forms such as blogs, podcasts, video, digital storytelling and social media platforms. Considers how independent voices create, challenge and reshape narratives in communities and public discourse. Attention to the relationship between personal voice, creativity and professional practice, as well as to issues of credibility, trust, ethics and representation. Explores how traditional and independent media engage with topics including activism, identity, politics and/or popular culture, highlighting both opportunities and challenges for communication in digital environments as they are constantly evolving. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds media literacy and production skills relevant to journalism, communication, marketing and/or creative industries. Develops competence in analyzing the credibility, reach and influence of independent media. Strengthens preparation for roles requiring digital fluency, critical thinking and the ability to adapt messages across platforms. Provides tools for both professional communication and civic engagement in a media environment shaped by independent voices. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how independent media can be both a space of empowerment and a site of contestation. Highlights how digital platforms amplify personal, cultural and political voices, while also raising ethical and practical challenges. Highlights how identity, power and representation shape media production and reception. Develops understanding of the opportunities and limits of independent communication in contemporary society. Explores the opportunities and challenges presented by changes in the media landscape. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of blogs, podcasts, video and social media platforms; exploration of digital storytelling and creative expression; consideration of ethics, representation and credibility in independent media; analysis of activism, politics and identity as expressed through digital platforms; evaluation of how independent voices influence communities, industries and public life. Course applications may draw on popular culture, current events and emerging issues. Discussions may also engage with controversial or contested topics, reflecting the role of independent media in addressing subjects that shape public dialogue. Cross Listing: COMM 250/JOUR 250 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 255 Media Literacy in the Digital Age
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores mass media as a form of communication across cultural, political and creative contexts. Examines how news media, podcasts, social media, video, television and advertising are used to inform, persuade, critique and/or tell stories. Analyzes source, audience, message design and the relationship between medium and purpose. Examines how information, misinformation and disinformation spreads, developing skills and techniques for assessing credibility and verifying sources. Includes engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may arise through topics connected to politics, culture, ethics and/or lived experience. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices relevant to careers in media industries, strategic communication, journalism, political communication, public outreach, community outreach and digital content production. Involves skills relevant to designing messages, engaging audiences and producing or analyzing digital media across professional platforms. Prepares for advanced academic study in communication, media studies, journalism and related fields where digital fluency and critical media analysis are expected. Promotes awareness of how traditional media and independent media practices can contribute to civic discourse, cultural participation and emerging communication markets. Encourages media literacy in both communication careers and everyday life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how new media platforms differ from legacy communication systems in structure, purpose and power. Highlights the role of individual voice, audience interaction and platform design in shaping meaning and influence. Encourages recognition that public communication through digital media may challenge assumptions about authority, expertise and representation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis or creation of blogs, podcasts, social media campaigns, digital storytelling or multimedia commentary; exploration of how mass media engage politics, identity, culture and public issues; study of persuasion, narrative, audience engagement and message strategy in digital contexts. Assignments may involve analysis, production or both, depending on the instructor’s approach. Course materials may involve perspectives or content reflecting varied experiences, beliefs and interpretations encountered in contemporary media environments. Cross Listing: COMM 255/JOUR 255 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 275 Introduction to Social Media
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores social media as a communication environment shaped by technology, audience, participation and platform design. Surveys major platforms, concepts and theories used to understand how individuals, organizations and communities create, share and interpret digital content. Examines how social media intersects with journalism, marketing, activism, entertainment and/or everyday communication. Considers how digital communication practices reflect and influence public discourse, society and culture. Engagement with real-world examples may involve topics connected to politics, religion, identity, ethics and/or lived experiences. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices connected to media industries, strategic messaging, journalism, advertising, nonprofit work, politics and other forms of public communication. Involves skills relevant to content creation, audience analysis, audience engagement, platform analysis and communication strategy. Connects to professional and academic paths in media, communication, journalism, marketing, public affairs and digital culture. Supports academic preparation to analyze ways social media shapes institutional messaging, cultural participation, community formation and civic dialogue. Develops applied skill in using social media strategically within entrepreneurial, organizational or community campaign contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication via social media platforms differs from legacy media in participation, access and influence. Explores communication theories and strategies underpinning social media communication. Highlights tensions involving credibility, persuasion, privacy, visibility and/or identity in digital environments. Builds understanding of how platforms shape perception, behavior and communication norms in ways that are not always immediately visible. Supports informed assessment of one’s own media usage patterns and communication practices as case material for analysis. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication theories, platform histories and digital ecosystems; analysis of messaging strategies and audience behavior; consideration of digital identity, participation and online communities; exploration of ethics, credibility, privacy, representation and influence in online environments; examination of how platforms shape visibility, participation and public discourse; study of consent, branding, advocacy, journalism and influencer practices; comparison of interactive and traditional media. Course materials may reflect varied perspectives and examples from professional, cross-cultural and/or global contexts. Cross Listing: COMM 275/JOUR 275 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 280 Careers in Communication and Journalism
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores fields and pathways in journalism, media and communication-related professions. Considers how professional interests, strengths and personality align with opportunities in media, public communication, journalism, strategic communication, digital platforms and related industries. Addresses foundational practices in networking, resume-writing, application material preparation, informational interviewing and digital presence. Includes exposure to campus resources and career planning tools. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of workforce expectations and industry pathways across communication-related professions. Introduces practical strategies for pursuing careers in media, advocacy, corporate communication, public affairs or related sectors. Assists in translation of classroom knowledge in securing internships, applied experience and long-term professional development opportunities. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication careers vary in purpose, setting and expectation. Highlights differences between common assumptions about media or communication work and the range of roles that exist across industries. Builds awareness of how skills, identity, professionalism and context shape access to and participation in communication fields. Provides support to students transferring into CMJR, promoting academic success and facilitating engagement with campus resources and communities. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include identification of career interests and strengths; exploration of communication professions and industries; development of application materials; digital portfolios and networking strategies; informational interviewing; engagement with professional resources and advising. Course activities may reference academic planning, campus involvement, workplace preparation and/or communications-specific career development. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Cross Listing: COMM 280/JOUR 280 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 307 Communication Law and Policy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the legal and ethical foundations of communication in journalism, media and public life. Considers First Amendment principles, constitutional protections and limits on free speech and free press. Surveys key areas of communication law, including libel, privacy, copyright, obscenity, advertising, broadcast regulation and/or digital communication. Considers ethical standards and professional responsibilities that shape communication practices across diverse contexts. Directs attention to the tensions between individual expression, institutional regulation and public accountability. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in understanding how legal frameworks and ethical codes guide communication decisions in professional, academic and/or civic life. Builds skills for identifying risks, evaluating responsibilities and applying standards to journalism, media and/or organizational settings. Provides preparation for careers requiring knowledge of communication law, professional ethics and public accountability. Strengthens civic awareness by highlighting the role of free expression in democracy and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday assumptions about “free speech” and “freedom of the press” differ from their legal and professional realities. Encourages awareness of the limits, protections and obligations that accompany communication rights. Expands understanding of how legal rules intersect with ethical reasoning, professional standards and social expectations. Promotes careful reflection on how controversies over speech, press and media practice reveal broader tensions in democratic societies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of First Amendment foundations and constitutional principles; libel, privacy and copyright; obscenity, advertising and broadcast regulation; law and policy for digital and social media; ethical theories and professional codes; accountability, fairness, diversity and harm in communication practice. Course discussion may involve contemporary cases and controversial issues, addressed for purposes of legal and ethical analysis within an environment of respectful dialogue. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor; COMM-307 also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: COMM 307/JOUR 301 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor; COMM-307 also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: JOUR
title: The Mass Media and Politics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication practices construct, circulate and contest political ideas and authority. Examines both how media influence political attitudes, participation and policy outcomes, and how political identity and conflict are shaped symbolically through news, entertainment, digital platforms and public rhetoric. Approaches may draw from social scientific models of media effects or rhetorical and critical analysis of political discourse. Emphasizes case-based evaluation of messages, sources and strategies across institutional, journalistic and citizen communication. Course content may include material involving political disagreement, conflict or graphic representation, examined for purposes of analysis rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops literacy in how political messages are constructed, distributed and interpreted across media systems. Applies to careers in journalism, political communication, public affairs, advocacy, research, law and civic or governmental work. Supports informed participation in democratic life by strengthening abilities to evaluate claims, recognize framing and distinguish between reporting, persuasion and manipulation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how politics is communicated not only through speeches or news outlets, but also through satire, visuals, entertainment formats, algorithmic feeds and policy messaging. Demonstrates how political messaging often blends information, symbolism and emotion to shape interpretation. Highlights the ways messages are interpreted differently depending on audience history, identity and media environment. Clarifies how communication shapes what counts as “fact,” “controversy” or “consensus” in public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of political news coverage, campaign strategy, advertising, agenda-setting, framing, propaganda models, political entertainment, social media activism and theories of representation. Consideration of media regulation, government communication practices, the influence of media on policymaking and the production of ideology. Course material may draw on historical and contemporary cases from local, national or international contexts, including disputed elections and outcomes, political controversies and crises, disinformation and surveillance, and contested social movements. Prerequisites: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 302 and POLS 302 .
prereq_text: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification.

subject: JOUR
title: Media Writing II
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Builds on foundational practices of news and media writing by shifting from structured exercises to more independent, publication-oriented work. Deepens proficiency in interviewing, sourcing, verification and AP style while introducing longer-form formats such as features, profiles, explanatory reporting and/or issue-driven narratives. Applies legal and ethical frameworks through scenario-based decision-making rather than rule recall. Reinforces core reporting habits of verification, accuracy and clarity, while advancing professional editorial readiness. May draw on current events or public controversies, addressed through journalistic standards of accuracy, attribution and fairness. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides practical experience valued in newsrooms, digital media, public affairs, nonprofit communications and content development roles requiring rapid research and fact-based writing. Strengthens transferable skills in information gathering, synthesis and public accountability, useful in academic and civic contexts where claims and sources must be critically evaluated. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how journalistic authority is earned through transparency, corroboration and structural discipline rather than voice alone. Builds awareness of framing choices — what to include, exclude or emphasize — and how these decisions influence audience interpretation. Examines reporting not only as information transfer but as ongoing negotiation between accuracy, access, ethics and presentation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include advanced interviewing techniques; background research and source vetting; feature and profile writing; beat development; editorial rewriting and collaborative critique; application of media law to reporting dilemmas; corrections and accountability practices; integration of photographs, headlines or multimedia assets based on publication constraints. May involve field reporting on campus or community issues, conducted within ethical and professional guidelines. Prerequisites: JOUR 203 , enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.
prereq_text: JOUR 203 , enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.

subject: JOUR
title: Editing for the Mass Media
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles and practices of editing across print, broadcast and digital media, focusing on journalistic style and structure. Covers sentence-level refinement, fact-checking, clarity and consistency review, correction of grammatical and structural errors and adaptation of content for varied platforms and audiences. Emphasizes editorial judgment in tightening text without distorting voice or meaning. Includes headline and subhead writing, style guide application, peer-editing and awareness of how legal and ethical standards apply to editing decisions rather than reporting alone. Builds on media writing coursework by shifting focus from content creation to evaluation, revision and publication-readiness. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds advanced competencies central to newsroom, publishing, marketing and content strategy roles, including copyediting, information verification, editorial collaboration and style precision. Reinforces habits essential to academic and professional writing in fields where clarity, accuracy and/or credibility are required. Supports civic literacy by strengthening the ability to assess how wording, structure and omission influence public interpretation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how editing is not merely correction but interpretation, requiring awareness of audience, tone and implication. Considers how editorial choices shape storytelling, accessibility and fairness as much as writing choices do. Builds recognition of how cultural context, legal obligation and ethical norms factor into seemingly small changes. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include editing for grammar, structure and flow; fact-checking and error detection; AP style and style guide adaptation; headline and SEO writing; tone and audience calibration; legal and ethical considerations in revision; collaborative workflows between writers and editors; and analysis of published examples from news, nonprofit and commercial media. Exercises may draw from real or simulated stories involving sensitive or controversial subject matter, introduced for building skills at accurate and responsible editing practice. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 203 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in JOUR 203 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director; junior or senior classification.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 303 Communication and Data Visualization
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores data as a form of communication and examines how information is interpreted, visualized and presented for different audiences and purposes. Emphasizes data storytelling as both an analytical and narrative practice, focusing on how visual choices shape understanding. Considers visualization designs that use data to inform, explain, persuade and/or support decision-making, using tools such as Excel and R. Addresses principles of visual perception, evidence-based messaging and interpretation of qualitative data and quantitative analyses, including descriptive and inferential statistics. Considers how visual choices, context and audience shape meaning in visual communication. Coursework may involve analysis, critique and/or development of data-driven messages in digital or visual formats. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds data visualization skills relevant to journalism, strategic messaging, marketing, public affairs, organizational communication, media production, research presentation and political advocacy. Builds capacity to interpret data, build visual explanations and representations and present insights in accessible formats. Supports effectiveness in academic and professional contexts where evidence, visualization and communication intersect. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how data gain meaning through interpretation, framing and visual design. Highlights the difference between raw information and communicative impact. Encourages attention to credibility, context and the persuasive or explanatory use of visualized evidence. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and critique of data visualizations; analysis of how charts, maps, dashboards, infographics or interactive visuals communicate meaning; consideration of audience adaptation, ethics, representation or narrative framing; exploration of digital storytelling strategies in data communication, including how sequencing, emphasis and interactivity guide interpretation; consideration of persuasive and informative uses of data in media, public communication, organizational settings or digital platforms. Course content may involve real-world issues or case studies that reflect diverse perspectives or public debate. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 303/JOUR 305 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 304 Digital Communication Analytics and Metrics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. . COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of digital communication, data and the use of analytics to generate insight, evaluate communication strategies and inform decision-making. Examines techniques for extracting and interpreting information from websites, social media platforms and/or digital campaigns. Examines how data are used to assess audience behavior, platform performance, search engine optimization, message reach, engagement and/or return on investment. Considers how digital tactics connect across marketing, digital media platforms and communication research. Draws attention to the role of data in strategic planning. Course concepts are illustrated with examples that may involve digital communication in organizational, commercial, journalistic, political and/or nonprofit contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Promotes workforce preparation for careers in strategic communication, public relations, advertising, journalism, marketing, audience research and digital media. Advances understanding and skills related to interpreting performance metrics, applying measurement models and using analytics to support campaigns, outreach, reporting and/or organizational decision-making. Supports academic and professional work in areas where communication effectiveness, audience insight and data-informed planning intersect. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies the role of analytics in shaping communication strategy, storytelling and/or organizational decision-making. Highlights the difference between data collection and meaningful interpretation. Builds recognition of how digital communication practices intersect with privacy expectations, ethical obligations and the constraints of data tracking and measurement. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of web traffic, audience demographics and user behavior; study of paid, earned and owned media metrics; consideration of measurement models, platform dashboards and optimization tactics; exploration of data-driven decision-making, campaign evaluation, content performance, randomized field experiment and competitive research. Course examples may involve sectors such as journalism, marketing, nonprofit advocacy, strategic communication and/or politics, reflecting the varied uses of digital analytics in public communication. Prerequisites: Grade of B or better in COMM 275/JOUR 275 , COMM 323 , or JOUR 200 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 304/JOUR 306 .
