subject: JOUR
title: Photojournalism I
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores still photography practices in journalistic contexts, focusing on camera operation, composition, ethical standards and field-based image production. Emphasizes photography as a tool for documenting people, places, events and/or everyday life. Assignments simulate real-world photojournalism through location-based shoots, peer critique and portfolio development. Course content may involve exposure to newsworthy situations, including moments of conflict, hardship and/or public emotion, examined for the purpose of understanding practices of visual documentation and evaluating ethical and communicative impacts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competencies essential for careers in journalism, visual media, public relations, marketing and content creation, including technical literacy, deadline management, ethical decision-making and client/audience awareness. Supports preparation for advanced visual storytelling, multimedia reporting and professional communication roles requiring accuracy, clarity and visual credibility. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds understanding of how photographic choices such as framing, timing, proximity and editing can shape meaning as much as subject matter. Considers how journalistic imagery involves artistic judgment, public responsibility and industry codes of ethics. Builds awareness of how images circulate, persuade and/or inform differently across media platforms. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of news, feature, portrait, sports and event photography; composition, lighting and image sequencing; ethics of representation, consent and vulnerable subjects; history of visual journalism and iconic images; storytelling across single images and multi-photo narratives. Coursework may involve documenting diverse communities or public environments, approached with sensitivity to accuracy, fairness and professional standards. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Visual Journalism
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the analysis and creation of visual communication in journalistic and documentary contexts. Examines how photographs, illustrations, layout, color and digital design shape meaning across platforms such as news, magazines, social feeds and long-form multimedia projects. Traces aesthetic, technological and ethical developments in visual journalism while incorporating hands-on work in photography, design and digital illustration. Course content may involve exposure to controversial news imagery, including depictions of conflict, crisis and/or intense public emotion, for the purpose of developing visual judgment, ethical decision-making and critical analysis of journalistic documentation. Course content may also review editorial illustrations connected to opinion stories involving politics and/or cultural topics to develop an understanding of the impact of visual communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competencies needed in media professions where visual literacy, editing and/or content production are central. Supports preparation for careers in journalism, documentary work, publishing, advertising and digital communication by emphasizing visual judgment, technical execution and ethical decision-making. Strengthens academic pathways in media studies and provides transferable skills for civic participation in a visually driven information environment. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how images can inform, persuade and/or mislead depending on composition, context and display. Highlights the interpretive layers behind seemingly objective visuals, including choices of framing, editing, sequencing and captioning. Informs reflections on ways visual representation can intersect with questions of identity, credibility and public memory. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of photojournalism and reportage; layout and design principles; illustration and editorial graphics; data visualization and infographics; historical shifts in visual journalism; ethical and legal questions surrounding image use; and the influence of social media platforms on visual circulation. Creative components may involve curated image essays, design mockups or original photographic assignments completed within professional guidelines. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: /SPAN 319 Bilingual Reporting
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores journalistic reporting in Spanish and bilingual media environments. Covers foundational practices in newsgathering, interviewing, writing and/or audio storytelling conducted in both English and Spanish. Examines how bilingual journalists adapt style, tone and/or sourcing when communicating across cultural and linguistic audiences. Considers the distinct histories, media infrastructures and representational challenges associated with Latino/a and Spanish-language communities in the United States and around the globe. Coursework may include projects based on real-world local, national and/or international cases involving cultural identity, migration and/or public affairs. Spanish proficiency required. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds practical readiness for reporting roles in Spanish-language and bilingual media, as well as careers in public communication, community outreach, translation, podcasting and global media markets. Strengthens transferable communication skills valued in civic, nonprofit and governmental sectors that serve multilingual publics. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in journalism, Latino studies, global media or communication research. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how bilingual journalism involves more than translation; it requires cultural sensitivity, linguistic precision and ethical decision-making regarding representation and voice. Highlights differences in news values, sourcing practices and audience expectations between English-language and Spanish-language media. Informs reflection on how language choice can shift narrative emphasis, credibility and/or accessibility. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of bilingual interviewing; translation for journalistic accuracy; Spanish-language media history and market structures; ethics of reporting on immigration, identity, political conflict and cross-cultural communities; podcast scripting and audio editing; comparative analysis of Spanish and English newswriting conventions; trust-building and sourcing in marginalized or multilingual contexts; cross-national journalistic collaboration. Course content may include discussion of reporting on sensitive topics such as immigration, discrimination and political discord. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors who teach this class may assign different readings and/or course topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; SPAN 302 or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: SPAN 319/JOUR 319 .

subject: JOUR
title: Mobile Journalism
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores multimedia reporting using mobile devices as primary tools for journalistic production. Covers techniques in audio gathering, digital still photography and video documentation, with emphasis on recording, editing, scripting and real-time publishing across multiple digital platforms. Simulates newsroom environments through deadline-based production, critique and revision. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds core competencies required in contemporary newsrooms and digital media industries, including rapid field reporting, technical versatility, editorial collaboration and/or content adaptation across platforms. Supports workforce preparation in journalism, strategic communication, digital content creation, nonprofit storytelling and public information roles. Reinforces transferable skills, including judgment under pressure, visual literacy and evidence-based storytelling, relevant to civic participation and public-facing professions. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights the distinction between casual mobile content creation and journalistic media production grounded in ethics, verification and clarity of purpose. Encourages critical reflection on how choices in framing, sequencing and platform affect audience interpretation. Demonstrates how professional credibility is constructed through transparency, accuracy and responsibility in visual storytelling. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of field recording techniques; audio scripting and narration; photo composition and ethical editing; video sequencing and interview setups; platform-specific publishing strategies; story pitching and editorial feedback; coverage of unfolding public events; ethical judgment and/or professional analysis. Assignments may involve documenting real-world environments — including emotionally charged settings or moments of conflict, controversy, hardship, celebration or vulnerability — approached for the purposes of visual analysis and responsible reporting. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Media Industries
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the structures, economics and regulation of media industries across sectors such as film, television, music, publishing, video games, streaming and/or digital platforms. Examines how content is produced, financed, distributed and governed within commercial, public and hybrid systems. Considers trends in media ownership, labor practices, media convergence, globalization, audience markets and/or media policy. Attention to the roles of technology, culture and/or law in shaping how media industries operate. Course material may engage with real-world issues involving politics, regulation, representation and/or controversy, as relevant to understanding industry practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media production, media law and policy, journalism, strategic communication, entertainment management, marketing, publishing and digital platforms. Informs understanding of how media businesses make decisions, respond to regulatory pressures and adapt to changing technologies and audiences. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, business, law and policy. Useful for those navigating or analyzing industries shaped by ownership structures, market forces and cultural influence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how media industries function beyond consumption and cultural familiarity. Highlights the interplay of economic interests, creative labor, technology and public policy. Encourages recognition of the power dynamics and institutional processes that shape media access, visibility and innovation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of media ownership and consolidation; production, distribution and exhibition systems; financing models and supply-chain relations; regulation and public policy; labor and creative work; technology and convergence; niche and mass markets; globalization and cultural circulation; media ethics and advocacy. Examples may draw on current and historical cases across major and emerging sectors. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 345 and FILM 345 .

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 346 Media, Culture and Identity
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how media and technology represent, reinforce and challenge ideas about identity, power and social differences. Examines theories of communication and culture to understand how media shape and are shaped by beliefs about race, gender, class, sexuality, ability, nationality and/or religion. Considers how communication practices construct and contest meanings of belonging, visibility and participation. Engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may involve topics that are culturally, politically and/or socially sensitive, discussed for the purpose of academic analysis and critical understanding. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides foundations for future professionals in journalism, digital media, strategic communication, public advocacy and related fields to anticipate audience response, avoid misrepresentation and build public trust. Builds transferable skills in media literacy, cultural analysis and ethical communication across professional and civic settings. Supports excellence in leadership and teamwork in diverse workplaces by considering how identity and difference influence communication dynamics. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, cultural studies and related areas concerned with diversity and representation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how cultural identities and media forms are interdependent, showing how meaning, power and visibility are negotiated through communication. Encourages reflection on the social roles of media institutions, creators and audiences in shaping public discourse and cultural imagination. Highlights the importance of dialogue, critical awareness and informed engagement in multicultural and mediated environments. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include representation and ideology in film, television, music and digital platforms; intersectionality and social identity; media and power; race, gender and sexuality in cultural production; class, globalization and inequality; disability and visibility; fandom, subcultures and participatory media; and contemporary debates around bias, equity and inclusion. Course material may include media content addressing real-world controversies or differing viewpoints, as relevant to understanding media, culture and identity. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 346/JOUR 346 .

subject: JOUR
title: Reporting Sports
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the principles and practices of sports reporting across professional, collegiate and community contexts. Covers live event reporting, interviewing, beat reporting, deadline writing and industry-standard formatting such as AP style. Emphasizes ethical judgment in reporting of competition, emotion and/or controversy, while maintaining neutrality, accuracy and professionalism. Simulates newsroom workflows through field reporting, editorial review and revision. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds applied competencies essential to careers in journalism, broadcasting, media relations, sports communication and content production. Reinforces transferable skills such as rapid information synthesis, audience adaptation, collaborative communication and deadline management. Supports broader workforce preparation in fields that require precise coordination, public-facing documentation and/or real-time decision-making. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how sports journalism blends entertainment, data, human interest and public accountability. Highlights the role of the journalist in navigating fandom, institutional access and representation, balancing narrative engagement with accuracy and fairness. Encourages awareness of how reporting choices influence perceptions of competition, identity and/or community. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include field interviewing; live coverage of sporting events; beat development; game recaps and feature storytelling; multimedia integration (audio, photo, mobile journalism); sports ethics and conflict-of-interest management; representation of athletes and teams across gender, race, class or institutional lines. Course material may involve observation or documentation of competitive, emotional and/or contentious sports environments, approached with sensitivity and professional responsibility. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 365 International Communication
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores key concepts, theories and practices in international communication and global journalism. Examines comparative media systems by analyzing how media develops across different political, cultural and economic contexts. Considers how world news circulates: who produces it, how it travels and how it is interpreted by diverse audiences. Examines issues such as freedom of the press, political propaganda, international advertising, public diplomacy and/or the impact of digital technologies. Students engage with theoretical, pragmatic, political and/or ethical perspectives to analyze how power, culture and/or technology shape global information exchange. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with tools for working with global media across cultural differences. Builds skills in evaluating international news, identifying propaganda and disinformation and applying ethical standards across cultures. Prepares students for careers in journalism, public affairs and related fields requiring cross-cultural awareness and media literacy. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Develops understandings of press freedom, news values and global information flows, recognizing that media systems operate within distinct political, cultural and economic contexts; exploring how interconnected stories affecting different countries and regions have developed through globalization and social media. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of comparative media systems; study of world news flows and international reporting; press freedom, censorship and ethics; political propaganda, public diplomacy and soft power; international advertising and global news cultures; impact of digital technologies, social media and generative AI; challenges of disinformation and “fake news” in global communication. Course materials may include discussion of sensitive or controversial topics, presented from multiple perspectives to reflect the diversity of global media. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; COMM-365 also taught at Qatar campus. Cross Listing: COMM 365/JOUR 365 .

subject: JOUR
title: Political Reporting
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops advanced reporting and writing skills through coverage of political actors, campaigns, institutions, policies and/or public debate. Emphasizes journalistic forms such as straight news, analysis, commentary, deadline reporting and/or long-form enterprise work. Coursework may involve interviewing public officials and stakeholders, sourcing public records, verifying factual claims and writing for publication under real-world time constraints. Engages legal and ethical challenges common to political reporting through case-based analysis and professional decision-making. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Prepares students for careers in journalism, strategic communication, public affairs, political campaign messaging and media production requiring accuracy, fairness and accountability in public-facing work. Reinforces transferable skills in source evaluation, poll evaluation, fact assessment, editorial judgment and deadline coordination. Supports media literacy and civic readiness by strengthening the ability to interpret competing claims and document political developments with clarity and restraint. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how journalistic credibility is constructed through sourcing, structure, transparency and consistency with professional standards. Highlights how political information circulates across formats such as news stories, speeches, commentary, newsletters, podcasts and/or social media. Encourages attention to how misinformation, framing or selective emphasis influence interpretation, requiring constant assessment of reliability and relevance. Explores ethical and legal issues regarding public records laws and the First Amendment. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of interviewing, source development, fact-checking, news and feature structure, commentary and analysis writing, polling interpretation, deadline reporting and long-form enterprise work; consideration of media ethics, transparency, fairness and public accountability in coverage of elections, legislation, policy debates and/or political conflict. Course material may involve disputed events, competing narratives or controversial figures engaged for purposes of journalistic evaluation. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Arts and Entertainment Journalism
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores reporting and writing practices specific to arts and entertainment journalism across genres such as film, music, visual arts, live performance, food and/or popular culture. Emphasizes feature writing, criticism and commentary, combining descriptive narrative with analytical evaluation. Includes regular drafting, revision and editorial feedback in workshop-style settings. Course material may reference real-world works or events that evoke strong personal and/or cultural responses; such content is approached through ethical journalistic standards of observation, fairness and critique. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops professional habits in research, interviewing, deadline writing and editorial collaboration relevant to journalism, reviewing, cultural reporting, media production, public relations and arts programming. Supports academic pathways in media criticism, narrative nonfiction and cultural studies. Reinforces transferable skills in analytical writing, public communication and civic engagement through responsible evaluation of cultural expression. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how arts and entertainment coverage blends storytelling with informed judgment, requiring both subject knowledge and ethical standards. Informs consideration of how tone, evidence and perspective shape credibility in evaluative writing. Explores how cultural journalism influences public conversation not by prescribing taste, but by modeling interpretation, context and reflection. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis and practice of feature profiles, reviews, cultural commentary and long-form narrative; genre-specific approaches to writing about art, food, music, theater, fashion, television and film; techniques for descriptive reporting and sensory detail; methods of comparative evaluation; ethics of criticism and representation. Course content may involve engagement with controversial works, sensitive subject matter or emotionally charged performances, addressed for purposes of journalistic analysis. subject: JOUR
title: Business Reporting
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the principles and practices of covering business, finance and the economy for general audiences. Emphasizes how companies, markets, government policy and consumer behavior intersect to shape everyday life. Trains students to locate, interpret and translate information from sources such as Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings, economic datasets, industry reports and executive interviews. Coursework may draw on real-world developments involving corporate strategy, labor trends, inflation, energy, technology or regional economic change. Topics are approached through journalistic standards of accuracy, clarity and public accountability. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce preparation for careers in business journalism, data reporting, financial communications, public information and strategic media roles. Develops transferable skills in document interpretation, interviewing, trend analysis and deadline storytelling that apply across sectors including government, nonprofit, policy and corporate communication. Supports academic advancement in media studies, economics, public policy or analytics by reinforcing evidence-based reasoning and clear explanatory writing. Strengthens civic readiness by improving understanding of how economic decisions are communicated to the public and in turn affected by public response. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how business reporting is not limited to stock prices or balance sheets but involves explaining systems, including how decisions made by corporations, policymakers and markets influence employment, cost of living, infrastructure and opportunity. Informs consideration of the ways interpretation of economic data depends on framing, comparison and context. Considers ways clarity and fairness in economic reporting are essential to public trust. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of corporate filings and financial disclosure; market trends, labor shifts and cost-of-living metrics; economic indicators such as inflation, housing or consumer confidence; industry case studies across sectors such as energy, technology, retail or health care; regulatory and policy developments; and narrative approaches to profiling companies, entrepreneurs or local businesses. Course material may involve coverage of contested issues such as corporate incentives, taxation policy, wage debates and/or market volatility. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: /COMM 458 Global Media
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how globalization and media are intertwined across national, transnational and diasporic circuits. Explores frameworks for understanding globalization through media ownership, migration, representation, content flow, technology, everyday life and/or political influence. Considers how news, entertainment, advertising and/or digital platforms travel across regions and are reshaped by local and transnational values, communities and regulations. Highlights both integration and inequality in global media landscapes. Course content may reference political or cultural controversies, including propaganda, censorship, immigration or conflict reporting, for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of how media industries function in global markets, supporting preparation for careers in journalism, strategic communication, public affairs, media production, policy analysis and international business. Supports adaptability within multicultural and internationally connected workplaces. Develops abilities to assess media influence across national and cultural boundaries, relevant skills in organizations operating in global or multicultural environments. Strengthens academic grounding for advanced study in communication, media studies, international relations or cultural analysis. Supports civic literacy by clarifying how global media shape public opinion, diplomacy and perception between nations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals that media are not neutral carriers of information but products of political, economic, ideological and cultural systems. Highlights how similar content can carry different meanings depending on context, history, ideology and/or regulation. Encourages reflection on how local and/or personal media environments are shaped by assumptions and practices that may differ substantially across national and cultural boundaries, fostering greater awareness of perspective and context. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of transnational media ownership and conglomerates; global circulation of news, entertainment and advertising; audiences and consumers; comparative media systems in democratic, authoritarian and transitional societies; localization and cultural adaptation; media policy, censorship and regulatory control; streaming platforms, social media and telecommunications infrastructure; migration, diaspora, citizenship and identity across borders. Course material may reference real-world cases involving political or cultural controversy, such as extremism, disinformation or state propaganda, for purposes of analysis and critique within an environment of respectful dialogue. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 458/JOUR 458 .

subject: JOUR
title: Sports Entertainment Reporting
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines journalistic storytelling within the evolving sports entertainment landscape. Explores formats ranging from narrative features and long-form commentary to rapid-cycle blogging, podcasts and fan-centered analysis. Emphasizes audience engagement, platform-specific voice and the blending of reporting, opinion and personality in sports media. Simulates newsroom or creator environments through recurring publishing deadlines and performance-based feedback. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds marketable skills for careers in sports journalism, content creation, digital media, public relations or brand communications. Reinforces professional practices such as sourcing, accuracy, editorial decision-making, audience strategy and ethical judgment under time pressure. Supports civic and cultural awareness by examining how sports intersect with identity, economics, politics and public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how sports coverage functions not only as entertainment but also as storytelling that frames community, rivalry, aspiration and controversy. Reveals distinctions between reportage, commentary, satire and hype, clarifying how credibility and influence can be negotiated across formats. Informs reflection on how fandom, access and commercial pressures shape journalistic tone and judgment. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis and production of sports blogs, feature stories, commentary pieces, social media threads, podcasts and/or multimedia packages. Consideration of athlete branding and influencer culture; fan communities and online discourse; ethics in sports reporting; representation and identity in sports narratives; commercialization of collegiate and professional athletics. May reference real-world cases involving controversy, misconduct and/or public debate when relevant to understanding communication choices in sports media. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: JOUR
title: Magazine Feature Writing
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops advanced nonfiction storytelling skills through the study and production of magazine-length features, profiles, trend pieces, service journalism and/or first-person narratives. Emphasizes writing for publication across contemporary formats, including print, digital and/or multimedia environments. Involves pitching, researching, drafting and revising multiple feature-length articles under deadline, simulating professional editorial workflows. Includes analysis of publication style, voice and audience expectations across diverse magazine platforms. May involve coverage of current events or human-interest topics, approached through journalistic standards. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds professional competencies used by staff and independent writers within journalism, content strategy and media production, including interviewing, audience analysis, query development, revision and editorial collaboration. Supports preparation for publication-based careers as well as academic and civic contexts requiring long-form narrative communication, evidence-based reporting and/or clear voice. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how narrative journalism blends factual reporting with structure, scene-setting, characterization and perspective to build engagement while maintaining accuracy and accountability. Illuminates how credibility is earned through transparency, sourcing and stylistic discipline rather than formulaic structure. Encourages reflection on the responsibilities of representing real people and events in written form. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of profile writing, trend stories, service journalism, memoir and first-person features, pitch and query formats, magazine house style and voice, interviewing strategies, source documentation, revision techniques and editorial feedback processes. May involve field reporting, live story pitching and analysis of magazine departments or adopted publications. May draw on real-world reporting scenarios, ranging from lifestyle to public affairs, addressed with attention to fairness, accuracy and professional responsibility. subject: JOUR

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Serves as an exit-level seminar for students completing advanced coursework in journalism. Synthesizes prior training in reporting, writing, editing, media law and ethics by requiring production of publication-quality work alongside critical reflection on journalism as a profession. Combines workshop-based writing development with discussion of contemporary issues facing news media, including questions of credibility, labor, technology and/or public trust. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens readiness for careers in journalism, media production, strategic communication and public information by refining writing portfolios, pitching skills, professional presentation and editorial collaboration. Provides preparation for workplaces that value initiative, ethical decision-making and long-form project management. Supports civic literacy by deepening understanding of journalism’s role in public accountability, information access and democratic culture. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights journalism not only as a set of skills but as an evolving institution shaped by economic pressures, technological change, audience behavior and ethical norms. Encourages recognition of the practical and moral challenges journalists face when balancing accuracy with speed, objectivity with transparency and access with independence. Reinforces that credibility emerges through verification, sourcing, clarity and sustained commitment to public responsibility. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include discussions of media credibility, fact-checking in high-risk environments, newsroom labor and diversity, long-form storytelling, press freedom, branding and career sustainability and journalistic responses to misinformation. May contain real-world reporting cases involving political conflict, legal disputes or sensitive human experiences, examined for purposes of professional analysis. subject: LMAS
title: /COMM 423 Communicating Latinidad
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how ideas about Latino identity and community, referred to collectively as Latinidad, are shaped through communication in public, institutional and/or interpersonal settings. Considers how people of Latin American heritage are represented in media, politics and everyday discourse, as well as how they speak, advocate and organize on their own terms. Addresses how language, history and cultural references are used to signal belonging, draw boundaries and/or negotiate differences. Course content and discussion may engage topics related to nationality, race, gender, migration and/or public controversy for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports career pathways in media, public service, advocacy, education, law, nonprofit work and other community-facing professions by examining communication processes grounded in communities and lived experiences. Develops competencies for workplace effectiveness, civic participation and collaborative problem-solving by building recognition of how communication norms can vary across individuals, cultures and contexts. Supports academic preparation in rhetoric, media studies, U.S. Latino studies and social research. Strengthens cultural insight critical for leadership and collaboration in multilingual or multicultural environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Expands recognition of Latinidad as varied rather than monolithic, shaped by history, region, generation, class, race and political context. Clarifies how categories such as “Hispanic,” “Latino/a” or “Latinx” emerge, shift and are debated over time. Highlights how communication both reflects and challenges social hierarchies, encouraging reflection on how voices are amplified, stereotyped or overlooked across public life. Frames identity as negotiated and relational, not assumed or imposed. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of Latino social movements and protest rhetoric; institutional and governmental discourse about immigration or citizenship; representations of Latinidad in news, entertainment or advertising; analysis of terminology and labeling practices; narratives of space, border, diaspora or belonging; exploration of gender, race, indigeneity, class, sexuality, religion and/or Afro-Latinx identity within Latina/o/x communication. Course material may reference politically or culturally sensitive topics when relevant to understanding communication processes, approached within an environment of scholarly inquiry and respectful dialogue. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 423/LMAS 423 .

description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Lecture Hours. Study of selected topics in an identified area of maritime administration. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of MARA department head.
prereq_text: Approval of MARA department head.

subject: MARA
title: Ocean Transportation
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of theory and practice in the management of transportation logistics, labor, rate-making, role of government, international conventions and treaties; exposure to current trends and developments in shipping. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Marine Insurance
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Marine insurance problems and cases and how they relate directly to a ship's officer; hull, cargo, and personal injury cases are examined from the officers' and insurers' points of view; introduction to Admiralty Law and the court process for seamen's rights and ship owners' privileges; actual hearings and trials are observed to complete the background. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Managerial Maritime Finance
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Continuation of topics introduced in Business Finance ( FINC 341 ) including risk and return, investment valuation, the selection of risky investment projects, capital structure, dividend policy, and methods of raising long-term capital; applications to the maritime industry are made where appropriate. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Maritime and Marine Entrepreneurship Ventures
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. The attributes that enable entrepreneurs to pursue opportunities in maritime business development; formation of teams to experience each step of entrepreneurial process; exposure to real entrepreneurial operations and businesses. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Maritime and Marine Business Plans
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Planning described as a mechanism to guide entrepreneurial intentions and behavior; development of formal written plans that allow investors to anticipate future outcomes; discussion of firms from the perspective of nascent entrepreneurs and potential investors. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Maritime Service Operations
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Classical service operations management and contemporary case-by-case based problem-solving in the maritime service sector. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Maritime Cybersecurity Issues
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Discussion of risks and cyber incidents; exploration of computer systems architecture and the framework of computer security on vessels. Prerequisite: MARA 201 ; junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: MARA 201 ; junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Management Processes
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Management as an academic discipline; goal setting; planning, controlling and decision-making; models for thinking about organizations; organization design; organization change; models for understanding individual behavior; job performance and job satisfaction; interpersonal behavior, motivation and leadership, behavior in work groups; careers in management, ethics and international management; strategic issues in managing human resources; shared responsibilities of line managers and human resource staff for developing and implementing human resource policies and procedures; human resource planning; job design, analysis and evaluation; staffing; compensation; performance appraisal; training and development career management; labor relations. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Personnel Management
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Strategic issues in managing human resources; shared responsibilities of line managers and human resource staff for developing and implementing human resource policies and procedures; human resource planning; job design, analysis and evaluation; staffing; compensation; performance appraisal; training and development career management; labor relations; legal, ethical and international issues. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Brokerage and Chartering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Operational and legal environment of ship brokerage and chartering; responsibilities of owner and charterer under various charter forms; American, British and Canadian acts governing charters and bills of lading; rules and regulations concerning loading and discharging. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Inland Waterways
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Development of inland waterways of the U.S. and federal policies relating to them; port and terminal development, competition with other transportation forms, manpower, rates, environmental concerns and the impact of waterway systems on regional economies. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Law and Policy in Cybersecurity
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of law and policy issues related to cybersecurity for the spectrum of cybersecurity jobs; includes procurement, operations and maintenance, governance and oversight, protection and defense, analysis, intelligence collection and operation and investigation cybersecurity jobs. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; MARA-403 taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: CSCE 402 and CYBR 402 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; MARA-403 taught at Galveston campus.

subject: MARA
title: Port Operations, Administration and Economics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Concepts of the port and methods of intermodal transfer; port functions divided and analyzed along business lines - economics, management, finance, accounting and marketing; cost studies. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Admiralty Law
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Essential principles of admiralty, general maritime, and international law as applicable to the marine industry and ocean shipping; evolution and state of the law concerning maritime liens, ship mortgages, rights of seamen and harbor workers, limitation of liability, bills of lading and cargo carriage, collision liability, general average, marine salvage, charter parties, and international rights and responsibilities of ships and shipping. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Intermodal Transportation
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Historical development, structure, function, and regulation of highway, rail, water, pipeline, and air transportation systems. Application of economic concepts and principles to transportation development and operations. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Labor Law and Policy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Federal and state public policy and laws regulating human resource management including National Labor Relations Act, Railway Labor Act, Fair Labor Standards Act, employment discrimination statutes, statutes regarding public sector unionization, and other relevant legal authorities; various forms of dispute settlement including litigation, mediation, fact finding and arbitration; legal ramification of strategic human resource management decision making. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Global Economy and Enterprise Management
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Economic, political, social and ethical environments of international business including the determinants of trade and investment patterns and the logic of government interventions in both trade and capital markets; structure, strategy and operations of the international firm. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Maritime Supply Chain Management
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction to the concepts involved in supply chain management (SCM); SCM encompasses the functional areas of procurement, operations management, inbound/outbound transportation, customer service, and information technologies; emphasizes how these functional areas are integrated to achieve the firm's overall objectives. Prerequisites: BUSN 203 and SCMT 364 ; junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: BUSN 203 and SCMT 364 ; junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Strategic Management
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Strategic issues facing organizations, including top management decision making and social responsibility; environmental and industry analysis; establishing organizational mission and objectives; corporate, business and functional level strategy formulation; global and multidomestic strategies; strategic implementation and control; integrating operations, finance, marketing and human resource strategies; case analysis. Prerequisites: MARA 363 , MKTG 321 , SCMT 364 , and FINC 341 ; senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: MARA 363 , MKTG 321 , SCMT 364 , and FINC 341 ; senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Environmental Law
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Broad background of basic statutes, regulations and cases dealing with the major issues in international and federal environmental law; focus on pragmatic training in statutory, regulatory and treaty reading and interpretation; analysis of administrative and legislative intent for law. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Business Leadership
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Focus on theory and practice of leadership; familiarize with components, theory and models of leadership; compare/contrast styles; review leadership/followership relationship as a collaborative activity resulting in achieved goals; analyze cultural and global components and ethical issues associated with leadership. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Internship
description: Credits 0 to 4. 0 to 4 Other Hours. Internship in management; staffing, planning, organizing, leading and controlling. Enrollment is limited to those who have managerial responsibilities for the resources used by a business, non-profit or other organization. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Directed study on selected problems in the area of maritime administration not covered in other courses. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; approval of department head.

description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Lecture Hours. Study of selected topics in an identified area of maritime administration. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; approval of department head.

subject: MARA
title: Research
description: Credits 0 to 4. 0 to 4 Other Hours. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in Maritime Administration. May be repeated 2 times for credit. Please see academic advisor in department. Registration in multiple sections of this course is possible within a given semester provided that the per semester credit hour limit is not exceeded. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; approval of department head.

subject: MARB
title: Succeeding in Science
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. An introduction to skills in the field of marine biological sciences including science communication in the form of analyzing and presenting data. Education trajectories (i.e., graduate school) will be explored and professional networking opportunities will be available. Laboratory portion provides hands-on experiences to familiarize students with methods and equipment used in the marine biological science fields.

subject: MARB
title: Evolutionary Biology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Conceptual examination of evolutionary theory; not a survey of specific organismal evolutions; evidence for the abiotic origin; discussion of micro-evolutionary (including drift and natural selection) and macro-evolutionary (including evolutionary trends) mechanisms; application of these concepts to human evolution. Prerequisites: BIOL 111 .
prereq_text: BIOL 111 .

subject: MARB
title: Marine Zoology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. The study of multicellular animal life and the traits, adaptations, and ecology of major metazoan groups, emphasizing patterns of evolutionary change. Includes laboratory dissections and exploration of preserved displays to reinforce lecture material and provide supplemental information to the topics discussed in lecture. Prerequisites: BIOL 111 and MARB 214 .
prereq_text: BIOL 111 and MARB 214 .

subject: MARB
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Special topics and problems in field and/or laboratory work suited to analysis by individuals or small groups concerning aspects of marine biology. Usually requires a report describing techniques and results. Only 3 credit hours may be used in the degree plan curriculum. Prerequisites: 2.25 GPR, Approval of instructor.
prereq_text: 2.25 GPR, Approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Special Topics in Marine Biology
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Lecture Hours. Study of selected topics in an identified area of marine biology. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Genetics
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Fundamental principles of genetics; physical basis of Mendelian inheritance; expression and interaction of genes, linkage, sex linkage, biochemical nature of genetic material, and mutation. Prerequisite: BIOL 111 .
prereq_text: BIOL 111 .

subject: MARB
title: The Sea World Experience
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Exploration of marine organisms, survey topics in vertebrate marine biology and the role that aquatic oriented parks play in education, research and conservation; hands-on experiences by participating in aspects of maintaining aquatic organisms in captivity including animal care and nutrition, physiology, behavior, animal training and water quality; exposure to marine organismal taxonomy, natural history, anatomy and ecology. Prerequisites: BIOL 111 with a grade of C or better; GPA greater than 2.00.
prereq_text: BIOL 111 with a grade of C or better; GPA greater than 2.00.

subject: MARB
title: Biostatistics
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Descriptive statistics, data visualization, probability and probability distribution, parameter estimation, and testing of hypotheses, analysis of variance, correlation and regression, parametric and non-parametric techniques with emphasis on methods applied to biological investigations. Prerequisite: MATH 142 , MATH 147 or MATH 151 .
prereq_text: MATH 142 , MATH 147 or MATH 151 .

subject: MARB
title: Introduction to Cell Biology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. An introduction to the basic concepts of cell biology. We will cover topics in cell physiology, the regulation of gene expression, protein structure and function, the role of mitochondria in health and disease, and other topics of relevance to cell biology. Prerequisites: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; CHEM 227 and CHEM 237 , or CHEM 257 .
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; CHEM 227 and CHEM 237 , or CHEM 257 .

subject: MARB
title: Ichthyology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Freshwater and marine fishes. Subject will be mainly systematic, but evolution, ecology, life history, and economics of more important species will be treated. Prerequisite: BIOL 112 or MARB 215 .
prereq_text: BIOL 112 or MARB 215 .

subject: MARB
title: Natural History of Vertebrates
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Natural history of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals, with emphasis on coastal Texas vertebrates. Prerequisite: BIOL 112 or MARB 215 .
prereq_text: BIOL 112 or MARB 215 .

subject: MARB
title: Fisheries Techniques
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Theory and techniques in fisheries biology and ecology; experience with fisheries equipment and techniques provided in both field and laboratory; practical sampling design, collection and interpretation of data from estuarine, coastal and offshore environments. Prerequisite: MARB 311 .
prereq_text: MARB 311 .

subject: MARB
title: Fish Physiology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Study of the basic physiology of fishes; examination of fish cardiovascular, renal, digestive, locomotor, reproductive, and central and peripheral nervous systems; discussion of physiological adaptations enhancing survival in a water medium. Prerequisite: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Marine Conservation Biology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Lectures and laboratories cover the major principles of conservation biology; a new synthetic field that applies concepts of ecology, systematics and evolution, biogeology, genetics, behavioral sciences, and social sciences to the conservation of marine fisheries resources. Lab exercises include morphometric and genetic variation, GIS, molecular systematics and phylogenetic inference. Prerequisites: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Biology of Marine Mammals
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. A broad-spectrum course on the taxonomy, evolution, morphology, behavior, and ecology of marine mammals, including sirenians, carnivores, baleen and toothed whales and dolphins. Prerequisite: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .

subject: MARB
title: Physiological Ecology of Marine Mammals
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. 0 Lab Hours. Anatomy, taxonomy, phylogeny and physiological adaptations of marine mammals. Prerequisite: MARB 215 , BIOL 112 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 215 , BIOL 112 or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Cetacean Behavior and Behavioral Ecology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Up to date descriptions of Cetacean behavior and ecology. Prerequisite: MARB 215 , BIOL 112 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 215 , BIOL 112 or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Marine Parasitology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Fundamentals of parasitology, with emphasis on marine applications; survey of major parasites of marine animals and the diseases they cause, especially in ecologically and commercially-important host species. Prerequisite: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Life in Extreme Environments
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. This course will study the key metabolic and physiological innovations of extremophile organisms; topics include the molecular biology, biochemistry and physiology of organisms living in extreme environments. This course will provide a comprehensive understanding of the biochemical and physiological adaptations of extremophile organisms. Key concepts covered will include: the types of extreme environments, extremophile metabolism and physiology, along with an overview of how changing environmental conditions impact the adaptive capabilities of threatened species. Prerequisites: MARB 315 ; CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 315 ; CHEM 228 or CHEM 258 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Marine Botany
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Morphology, systematics, ecology, and biochemistry of representative algae, fungi and submarine grasses. Prerequisites: BIOL 111 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: BIOL 111 ; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Animal Behavior
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of ethological concepts; discussion of the development, genetics, physiology and evolution of animal behavior patterns involved in reproduction, territoriality, aggression, communication, population dispersion, sociality and sociobiology of invertebrates and vertebrates. Prerequisite: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .

subject: MARB
title: Elasmobranch Ecology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Investigation of the ecological processes that shape the life histories and behaviors of sharks, skates and rays, including an introduction to methods used to study elasmobranchs and their applications to conservation and management. Prerequisite: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .

subject: MARB
title: Toxicology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Toxicology is the study of how environmental or human-made chemicals can cause adverse health effects in exposed organisms, such as wildlife and humans. This course aims to provide a general introduction and understanding of toxicology, in relation to both environmental and human health. Fundamental toxicological concepts covered will include: the history of toxicology, common contaminants, disposition and metabolism of toxic substances, reproductive and genetic toxicology and an overview of toxicological testing methods. Prerequisites: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; CHEM 227 and CHEM 228 , or CHEM 257 and CHEM 258 .
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; CHEM 227 and CHEM 228 , or CHEM 257 and CHEM 258 .

subject: MARB
title: Comparative Animal Physiology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Principles of animal physiology are examined using invertebrate and vertebrate model systems; includes osmoregulation in marine versus freshwater versus terrestrial organisms, excretion, fluid circulation, nervous system structure and function, muscle activity, sensory neurobiology and endocrine mediation. Prerequisites: BIOL 112 or MARB 215 ; CHEM 227 and CHEM 237 , or CHEM 257 ; MARB 310 .
prereq_text: BIOL 112 or MARB 215 ; CHEM 227 and CHEM 237 , or CHEM 257 ; MARB 310 .

subject: MARB
title: Community Ecology in the Tropics
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Field-based exploration of the connections between producers and consumers in tropical marine ecosystems, including coral reefs, seagrass meadows, and mangrove forests; immersive understanding of symbiotic relationships that shape ecological communities, including mutualism, predation, and competition, with an emphasis on nearshore ecosystems in the tropics. Prerequisites: MARB 215 ; swim test completion; concurrent enrollment in MARB 422 .
prereq_text: MARB 215 ; swim test completion; concurrent enrollment in MARB 422 .

subject: MARB
title: Tropical Marine Botany
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. A field-based course exploring the connections between primary producers and organisms that utilize the marine environment; observation, identification, and counting of organisms in tropical marine environments including phytoplankton in coastal waters, coral reefs, seagrass meadows, and mangrove forests. Prerequisites: MARB 215 ; concurrent enrollment in MARB 421 ; completion of swim test.
prereq_text: MARB 215 ; concurrent enrollment in MARB 421 ; completion of swim test.

subject: MARB
title: Mariculture
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Study of factors determining the success of efforts to cultivate estuarine and marine species of economic importance. Mariculture practices used worldwide in the production of algae, mollusks, crustaceans, and fishes will be discussed. Prerequisites: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Estuarine Ecology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Processes that occur within an estuary including the role that estuarine habitats provide for marine organisms; includes examination of estuarine circulation, geomorphology, chemical cycling and biological production; how human impact and pollution affect estuarine systems. Prerequisites: MARS 102 ; MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARS 102 ; MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Marine Ecology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Relationship between various marine environments and their inhabitants; intra- and interspecific relationships between organisms; structure and function among marine communities; laboratory emphasis on study of living material and natural habitats in the Gulf of Mexico. Prerequisites: MARB 315 or MARB 435 ; senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 315 or MARB 435 ; senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Aquatic Animal Nutrition
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Chemistry, digestion, absorption and intermediary metabolism of nutrient classes with special emphasis on their relationship to warmwater fish nutrition. Determination of nutrient requirements, feed evaluation, feed processing, ration formulation and feeding practices. Prerequisites: CHEM 227 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: CHEM 227 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Coastal Plant Ecology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Study of the identification, distribution, production, and ecological importance of estuarine, coastal marsh, and dune vascular plants; the interaction of plants with their abiotic and biotic environments; and techniques of vegetation management and evaluation. Prerequisite: BIOL 111 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: BIOL 111 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Applied Bioinformatics
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Fundamental concepts and methods in bioinformatics using sequence analysis and practical applications; includes biological databases, sequence and structure alignments, structural bioinformatics, gene prediction and genome analysis; emphasis on understanding and application of these concepts. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: MARB
title: Marine Invertebrate Zoology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. General biology of marine invertebrate animals; morphology, evolution, and systematics; studies of local fauna in laboratory. Prerequisite: BIOL 112 or MARB 215 .
prereq_text: BIOL 112 or MARB 215 .

subject: MARB
title: Pathology of Marine Animals
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examination of changes or loss of physiological function as related to common diseases, viral, bacterial, parasitic, or injury; mechanisms of disease in cells, tissues and organ systems of marine vertebrates; emphasis on marine mammals; fishes and marine reptiles and birds; clinical manifestations, diagnostics and treatments. Prerequisite: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .

subject: MARB
title: Coastal Ornithology
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Field and laboratory studies on the identification, classification, distribution and ecology of birds with special emphasis on birds of the Texas Gulf Coast; topics include anatomy, physiology, behavior and migration; field trips required. Prerequisites: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 .

subject: MARB
title: Coral Reef Biology
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Coral reef biology and ecology, environmental impacts that affect reefs and current and potential reef restoration solutions that may mitigate the current decline in the health of coral reef organisms, biodiversity and ecological functions. Prerequisites: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; grade of C or better in MARB 420 or MARB 435 ; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: MARB 215 or BIOL 112 ; grade of C or better in MARB 420 or MARB 435 ; or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Marine Fisheries Management
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Basic knowledge from marine ichthyology, biology of fishes and biological oceanography related to applied aspects of marine fisheries sciences; emphasis placed on management techniques applicable to tidal-influenced inland water, estuaries, and oceans. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: MARB
title: Fisheries Population Dynamics
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Principles and concepts of population dynamics related to fish; methods of estimating abundance, mortality, recruitment and sustainable harvest levels; introduction to models for population analysis with emphasis on stock assessments and quantitative fisheries; basic computer programming to explore population behavior and interactions. Prerequisites: MARB 303 ; MARB 311 , MARB 315 or MARB 435 .
prereq_text: MARB 303 ; MARB 311 , MARB 315 or MARB 435 .

subject: MARB
title: Internship
description: Credits 0 to 9. 0 to 9 Other Hours. Supervised study in a research or teaching laboratory remote from Texas A&M University at Galveston. Student involvement is to consist of real-life learning or marine biological research, teaching, management or a combination of these. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Special topics and problems in field and/or laboratory work suited to analysis by individuals or small groups concerning aspects of marine biology. Usually requires a report describing techniques and results. Only 3 credit hours may be used in the degree plan curriculum. Prerequisites: 2.25 GPR. Curriculum sophomore, junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: 2.25 GPR. Curriculum sophomore, junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
