Emphasis is placed on developing analytical skills through the examination of research design, data interpretation and methodological rigor across varied organizational contexts. Topics will vary across instructors and have included but are not limited to job stress, occupational health, diversity in organizations, job attitudes, motivation, organizational behavior and leadership. subject: PETE
title: Introduction to Petroleum Engineering
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Overview and history of the petroleum industry and petroleum engineering; nature of oil and gas reservoirs, exploration and drilling, formation evaluation, well completions and production, surface facilities, reservoir mechanics, improved oil recovery; impact of ethical, societal, environmental considerations; career development resources, including professional society. description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. . prereq_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 and MEEN 221 .

subject: PETE
title: Formation Evaluation
description: Credits 4. 3 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Well-log interpretation for formation evaluation of hydrocarbon-bearing reservoirs; basic rock physics principles; theory of tool operation; analysis of open hole logs and core measurements to estimate hydrocarbon reserves and petrophysical properties of the formation such as porosity, net pay thickness, water/hydrocarbon saturation, permeability and saturation-dependent capillary pressure; formation evaluation of clay-free and shaly-sand formations as well as basic introduction to formation evaluation of organic-shale formations. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 305 , PETE 219 , PETE 301 , PETE 310 and GEOL 404 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 305 , PETE 219 , PETE 301 , PETE 310 and GEOL 404 .

subject: PETE
title: Fundamentals of Reservoir Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Determination of reserves; material balance methods; aquifer models; fractional flow and frontal advance; displacement, pattern and vertical sweep efficiencies in waterfloods; enhanced oil recovery processes; design of optimal recovery processes; introduction and performance analysis of unconventional reservoirs. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 305 , PETE 219 , PETE 301 , PETE 310 and GEOL 404 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 305 , PETE 219 , PETE 301 , PETE 310 and GEOL 404 .

subject: PETE
title: Well Testing
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Analysis of well performance under varied reservoir conditions including evaluation of unsteady, pseudo-steady and steady state flow; well testing methods used to determine well and reservoir parameters; applications to conventional and unconventional wells producing gas and/or liquids; fundamentals of preparing and operating well test equipment to monitor, measure and gather samples for evaluating well performance. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 305 , PETE 219 , PETE 301 , PETE 310 and GEOL 404 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 305 , PETE 219 , PETE 301 , PETE 310 and GEOL 404 .

subject: PETE
title: Petroleum Production Systems
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 3 Lab Hours. Petroleum operation and oil field equipment including onshore and offshore production systems; wellbore inflow and outflow and backpressure analysis; downhole completion and sand control equipment; artificial lift equipment and design; stimulation, workover/completion nomenclature; flow assurance; produced fluids, fluid separation and metering, safety systems, pressure boosting and monitoring. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PETE 301 , PETE 310 and PETE 314 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 301 , PETE 310 and PETE 314 .

subject: PETE
title: Technical Presentations I
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Preparation of a written technical paper proposal on a subject related to petroleum technology and an oral presentation of the proposal in a formal technical conference format. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in COMM 203 , COMM 205 , COMM 243 , or ENGL 210 , or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in COMM 203 , COMM 205 , COMM 243 , or ENGL 210 , or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification.

subject: PETE
title: Petroleum Technical Presentation I
description: Credit 1. 3 Lab Hours. Preparation of a written technical paper on a subject related to petroleum technology. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ENGL 210 ; junior or senior classification, petroleum engineering majors only or approval of department head; Qatar campus.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in ENGL 210 ; junior or senior classification, petroleum engineering majors only or approval of department head; Qatar campus.

subject: PETE
title: Junior Student Paper Contest
description: Credits 0. No Credit. Presentation of a technical proposal on a subject related to petroleum technology judged by petroleum professionals at the junior level departmental student paper contest. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PETE 336 or concurrent enrollment, or grade of C or better in PETE 335 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 336 or concurrent enrollment, or grade of C or better in PETE 335 .

subject: PETE
title: Petroleum Project Evaluation
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Economic analysis and investment decision methods in petroleum and mineral extraction industries; depletion, petroleum taxation regulations, and projects of the type found in the industry; mineral project evaluation case studies. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PETE 301 and PETE 310 , or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 301 and PETE 310 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: PETE
title: Drilling Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Design and evaluation of well drilling systems; identification and solution of drilling problems; wellbore hydraulics, well control, casing design; well cementing directional drilling, offshore drilling. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CVEN 305 , PETE 225 , and PETE 314 ; grade of C or better in PETE 321 and PETE 325 , or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in CVEN 305 , PETE 225 , and PETE 314 ; grade of C or better in PETE 321 and PETE 325 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: PETE
title: Reservoir Simulation
description: Credits 2. 1 Lecture Hour. 3 Lab Hours. Solution of production and reservoir engineering problems using state-of-the-art commercial reservoir simulation software, using data commonly available in industry; emphasis on reservoir description, reservoir model design and calibration, production forecasting and optimization, economic analysis and decision making under uncertainty. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PETE 310 , PETE 321 , PETE 323 , PETE 324 , and PETE 353 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 310 , PETE 321 , PETE 323 , PETE 324 , and PETE 353 .

subject: PETE
title: Integrated Asset Development
description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 6 Lab Hours. Capstone design encompassing previously acquired skills; project teams formed to solve practical petroleum engineering problems using current tools; technical content of the projects may include any combination of drilling and completion, formation evaluation, inflow/outflow design and analysis, and application of reservoir engineering principles. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PETE 355 , PETE 401 , PETE 404 , and PETE 410 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 355 , PETE 401 , PETE 404 , and PETE 410 .

subject: PETE
title: Integrated Reservoir Modeling
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Geophysical, geological, petrophysical and engineering data with geostatistical methods to create reservoir descriptions for dynamic reservoir modeling (simulation); geostatistical concepts such as variogram modeling, kriging and sequential Gaussian simulation; combines several techniques to quantify uncertainty in a realistic dynamic reservoir simulation. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PETE 401 , or concurrent enrollment.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 401 , or concurrent enrollment.

subject: PETE
title: High Performance Drilling Design and Operational Practices
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Preparation in achieving differentiating drilling performance in the most complex wells; includes training in the underlying physics of each type of performance limiter and real time and engineering practices to address the limitation; performance management workflows and change models required to effectively change the way organizations conduct work essential in achieving higher performance. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PETE 355 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 355 .

subject: PETE
title: Probabilistic Reserves Evaluation
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Oil and gas reserves definitions and reporting regulations; probabilistic reserves estimation methods; unconventional resources characterization; reserves valuation techniques. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PETE 353 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 353 or approval of instructor.

subject: PETE
title: Production Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Fundamental production engineering design, evaluation and optimization for oil and gas producing well; well deliverability; formation damage and skin analysis; well completion selection; technologies that improve oil and gas well performance including artificial lift and well stimulation. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PETE 321 , PETE 323 , PETE 324 and PETE 325 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 321 , PETE 323 , PETE 324 and PETE 325 .

subject: PETE
title: Surface Production Facilities
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Overview of separation and treatment of production fluid; fundamentals of gas-liquid separation; design and performance analysis of two- and three-phase separators; oil desalting, sweetening and stabilization; water treatment; overview of gas separation, dehydration and sweetening. Prerequisite: Senior classification or approval of instructor; Qatar campus.
prereq_text: Senior classification or approval of instructor; Qatar campus.

subject: PETE
title: Natural Gas Engineering
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Flow of natural gas in reservoirs and wellbores and gathering systems; deliverability testing; production surveillance and monitoring; production forecasting; flow measurement; and compressor sizing. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PETE 323 , PETE 324 , and PETE 325 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 323 , PETE 324 , and PETE 325 .

subject: PETE
title: Solving Common Production Engineering Problems
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Application of petroleum engineering tools, methods and techniques to solve real problems that petroleum engineers encounter in producing individual wells; focus primarily on problems associated with single-phase gas wells and uses Microsoft Excel to solve many of these problems. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PETE 410 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 410 .

subject: PETE
title: Deterministic Reserves Evaluation
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Oil and gas reserves definitions and reporting regulations; deterministic estimation methods; unconventional resources characterization; reserves valuation techniques. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PETE 353 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 353 or approval of instructor.

subject: PETE
title: Petroleum Data Analytics and Machine Learning
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Working knowledge about data analytics suitable for petroleum engineers and geoscientists; emphasis on implementing data-driven methods on various types of subsurface data; assembly of data-driven workflows and application of them on various types of subsurface data generated during petroleum engineering and geoscience operations and work on case studies that integrate various domains of petroleum engineering and geoscience; emphasis on the use of supervised learning, classification and regression, unsupervised learning, transformations, clustering, and feature extraction, and neural networks using open-source Python computational platforms; facilitation of understanding the basics of machine learning, data science and data analysis and their applications to petroleum engineering and geoscience. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PETE 219 and PETE 301 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 219 and PETE 301 or approval of instructor.

subject: PETE
title: Unconventional Reservoir Methods and Analysis
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Unconventional reservoirs and the latest practices of reservoir characterization, horizontal drilling and completion optimization methodologies, reservoir engineering and production. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PETE 323 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 323 .

description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Preparation of a written technical paper on a subject related to petroleum technology and an oral presentation of the paper in a formal technical conference format. Prerequisites: PETE 337 .

title: Senior Student Paper Contest

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 435 or PETE 436 .

subject: PETE
title: Petroleum Entrepreneurship
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of the various aspects of entrepreneurship with a focus on petroleum asset valuation and prospect analysis in the energy sector; exposure to all aspects of the journey including business idea generation, raising early stage capital, staffing the enterprise, developing the business plan and selling the concept to investors. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PETE 353 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PETE 353 .

subject: PETE
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 1 to 5. 1 to 5 Other Hours. Special problems in various phases of petroleum engineering assigned to individual students or to groups. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of department head.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification and approval of department head.

title: Special Topics in...
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Selected topics in an identified field of petroleum engineering. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Approval of instructor.

subject: PETE
title: Research
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Other Hours. Research conducted under the direction of a faculty member in petroleum engineering. May be taken two times for credit. Registration in multiple sections of this course is possible within a given semester. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Contemporary Moral Issues
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (PHIL 2306) Contemporary Moral Issues. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students evaluate the claims, presuppositions and reasoning of various positions, including one’s own, on contemporary social problems and analyze those problems using ethical and social theories. Students examine how ideas, values and other aspects of culture (including power and authority) shape and are shaped by human experience and institutions. Students practice respectful and thoughtful engagement on contentious matters, such as abortion, euthanasia, capital punishment, the relationship between ethics and religion, violence and war, animal ethics, sexual morality, gender issues, health care ethics, equality and discrimination, biotechnology and bioengineering, economic injustice, climate ethics and global hunger and poverty, among others; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: The Human Experience
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction to classic transformative texts in the history of the arts, sciences, and humanities; interdisciplinary methods and approaches within the humanities; key ethical and moral debates across the human experience. Cross Listing: ARSC 202 and HIST 202 .

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Education
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Basic social ideas and concepts of human nature in Western civilization; their implications for theories of education.

subject: PHIL
title: Introduction to Logic
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (PHIL 2303) Introduction to Logic. Introduction to formal methods of deductive and inductive logic including, but not limited to, truth-tables, formal deduction and probability theory; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Introduction to Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (PHIL 1301) Introduction to Philosophy. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students are introduced to perennial and central topics in philosophy such as the good life and happiness, the problem of death, the existence of God, the nature of reality, the relationship of mind and body, the scope and limits of knowledge, the foundations of ethical life and moral judgment, the individual and the community, and the place of the human being in the cosmos. Students critically consider how ideas, values and other aspects of culture shape human experience. Students develop a deeper understanding of their individual responsibilities and become more effective in engaging in a variety of cultural contexts. Instructors may organize the course either by central figures in the history of philosophy or by topic; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Ethics in a Digital Age
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students explore the interplay between ethical and social theories, principles, and values, and the interconnected digital world, on concerns related to topics such as artificial intelligence, social media, intellectual property, privacy, surveillance, cybercrime and cyberwarfare, internet governance, computing professionalism and cyber policy and law. Students reflect on whether and how traditional moral conceptions (e.g., on the good life, personal and civic responsibility and virtues) have been transformed. Students examine how ideas, values and other aspects of culture (including power and authority) shape and are shaped by human experience and institutions. Students practice respectful, thoughtful and self-aware engagement to prepare them to navigate a variety of cultural environments; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Directed Studies
description: Credits 0 to 4. 0 to 4 Other Hours. Directed studies in specific problem areas of philosophy. Prerequisite: Approval of department head.
prereq_text: Approval of department head.

description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Lecture Hours. Selected topics in an identified area of philosophy. May be repeated for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Research
description: Credits 0 to 3. 0 to 3 Other Hours. Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in the department of philosophy and humanities. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of department head.
prereq_text: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of department head.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Natural Science
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students investigate scientific methods and achievements. Students examine the nature and types of explanation, discovery, confirmation, models and theories. Discussions may touch on questions such as: How sound are our reasons to think that accepted theories are better than rejected theories? What is required for something to be explained scientifically? How do we demarcate science from pseudoscience? For example, what is the status of Creation Science? Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Social Science
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students investigate the nature and objectivity of the social sciences, their paradigms and patterns of explanation. Students explore questions such as: Are there explanatory laws in the social sciences? Should social explanations always include information about individuals or can social facts by themselves be explanatory? What does the reproducibility crisis in the social sciences tell us? Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Environmental Ethics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Moral basis of duties to preserve or protect plants, animals and environmental systems; foundations of environmental law and policy; the idea of nature in philosophy; critique of social and economic analyses of environmental values. Prerequisite: Sophomore classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Sophomore classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Military Ethics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Major ethical issues in modern military practice: ethics of leadership, just war theory, killing of the innocent and the moral status of the rules of war.

subject: PHIL
title: Climate Ethics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Ethical and value questions related to climate change and climate policy; moral responsibility for and theoretical approaches to climate change; climate justice; ethical analysis of mitigation, adaptation and geoengineering policies. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Mind
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Relation of mind to body, nature of thought and knowing, the free will problem, death and immortality. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Art
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students read texts that examine fundamental questions about the creation of art, the nature of beauty and aesthetic experience. Possible themes for exploration include the relationship of art to morality, the role of art in society and the impetus for artistic production. Classes may treat these themes through contemporary writings, through an historical approach that engages thinkers in the history of philosophy or by examining specific art forms. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: /RELS 331 Philosophy of Religion
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophical problems of Western religion such as the existence of God, the problem of evil, types of theism, rational, empirical and mystical approaches to God. Cross Listing: RELS 331/PHIL 331 .

subject: PHIL
title: Social and Political Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenge students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students investigate key questions, concepts and debates in social and political thought, including those that were particularly influential on the founding generation of the United States. Sources include canonical primary texts but may also encompass more contemporary or critical responses to the canon. Emphasis is on fundamental problems in political life and may include: the source of political authority, the just distribution of the burdens and benefits of social life, the limits of state authority, the essence of political community, citizenship or responsibilities of civic life. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Law
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students survey debates regarding foundational philosophical issues about the law. While the specific issues covered may vary from semester to semester, paradigmatic topics include: what makes a law a law, the relation of law to morality, the appropriate aim of criminal punishment, the basis of criminal responsibility, methods for interpreting the U.S. Constitution, the scope or limits of a specific constitutional right, the obligation to obey the law and civil disobedience, critiques of liberalism and the aim of tort law. Students examine major jurisprudential theories — such as natural law, positivism, realism and critical and phenomenological approaches — to understand how legal systems define justice, obligation and authority. Readings include both historical and contemporary jurisprudence as well as case law. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Advanced Topics in Philosophy of Law
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students pursue focused and in-depth study of a specific topic in philosophy of law. The topic changes semester to semester. Recent versions focused on: the meaning and scope of First Amendment rights, the legal protection of privacy, the history of differing conceptions of the rule of law, modern theories of legal positivism and realism and the study of legal ontology, which investigates the ways in which laws and legal institutions exist relative to other social objects. Readings are drawn from historical and/or contemporary jurisprudence as well as case law. Students design and execute independent research projects connected to the theme of the seminar. Contact the department for information about the theme for an upcoming semester. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Symbolic Logic I
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Students explore the metatheory (formal languages, model theory and proof theory) of several basic systems of mathematical logic, including at least classical propositional logic and first-order logic with the theory of identity. Prerequisite: PHIL 240 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: PHIL 240 or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Symbolic Logic II
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Students explore advanced topics in logical theory. Instructors choose from topics such as: modal logic, higher-order logic, set theory, the theory of computability, Gödel's incompleteness theorems and non-classical logic. Prerequisite: PHIL 240 , PHIL 341 or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: PHIL 240 , PHIL 341 or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Theory of Knowledge
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Major topics in epistemology such as the problem of induction, perception theory, memory and the problem of other minds. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: /AFST 352 Africana Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Students understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view and may consider perspectives from a range of cultures. Students examine the philosophical contributions born of and germane to the experience of the African diaspora, which includes but is not limited to those who identify as African, Afro-Caribbean or African-American. Emphasis, themes and readings vary depending on the instructor; possible themes may include various conceptions of modern notions of freedom, equality, humanity and reason, taken up in the historical context of institutional slavery and the colonization of the Global South. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: AFST 352/PHIL 352 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Metaphysics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Topics concerning the fundamental nature of reality such as what exists, the mental and the physical, universals and individuals, space and time, God. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Literature
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students analyze multifaceted relationships between philosophy and literature. Class may include philosophical analysis of major recurrent themes in world literature as well as examination of what is philosophical about literature itself. Students may read works by philosophers in addition to novelists and essayists.

subject: PHIL
title: /FILM 376 Philosophy, Film and Evil
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students examine the concept of evil through the medium of film, exploring how cinema reflects, interprets and interrogates philosophical understandings of morality, suffering and human nature. Students engage with major philosophical approaches to evil, such as classical theodicies and free will defenses and modern accounts of cruelty, moral psychology and systemic violence, while analyzing cinematic depictions that illuminate these themes. Students investigate how film both represents and questions moral experience. Lectures, discussions, screenings and writing projects combine to cultivate philosophical insight through visual storytelling in cinema. Students practice respectful, thoughtful and self-aware discourse on contentious issues and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they are able to competently navigate a variety of cultural environments. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: FILM 376/PHIL 376 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Ethical Theory
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Values and conduct such as moral relativism, self-interest, utilitarianism, rules, nature of valuation, ethical language and argumentation. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHIL
title: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Ethical, social, and epistemic aspects of the development of artificial intelligence (AI); foundational normative principles and their application; consequences of AI; responsible use and regulation. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy and Technology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophical investigation of the creation and use of technology; the relations between technology, science and engineering; and how technology influences human existence, ethics and society. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Latin American Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Advanced philosophical investigation into the tradition of Latin American philosophy and its key approaches, ideas, cultural production and politics; major figures from the colonial period to the present; philosophical themes related to areas such as legacies of colonialism, identity, ethics, culture, politics, knowledge and meta-philosophy. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Gender
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students pursue advanced philosophical investigation into key approaches and themes of feminist thought. Students engage in philosophical and critical evaluation of the role of gender and sex in the formation of intellectual and cultural history, social norms and identity. May be taken two times for credit as content varies. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Classical Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Major philosophers from 600 BCE to the end of the third century CE such as the Pre-Socratics, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Hellenistic, and Roman philosophy. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Medieval Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Major philosophers from the fourth century through the 14th century, emphasizing writers such as Augustine, Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Hildegard of Bingen, and William of Ockham. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Seventeenth-Century Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Significant seventeenth-century texts in metaphysics, epistemology, moral psychology, and political philosophy; authors such as Cavendish, Descartes, Hobbes, Spinoza, Leibniz, and Locke. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Eighteenth-Century Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Significant eighteenth-century texts from philosophers such as Berkeley, Cockburn, Hume, Kant, and Rousseau. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Nineteenth-Century Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Significant nineteenth-century texts from philosophers such as Bettina, Bradley, Dubois, Hegel, Husserl, Kierkegaard, Marx, Mill, and Nietzsche. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: American Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. The thought of philosophers such as Peirce, James, Royce, Santayana, Mead, Dewey and Whitehead. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: History of Early Analytic Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Major philosophers in contemporary Anglo-American thought such as Moore, Russell, Wittgenstein, Ayer, Quine, Austin, Ryle, and Barcan Marcus. Prerequisites: PHIL 240 .
prereq_text: PHIL 240 .

subject: PHIL
title: Phenomenology
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Phenomenology from its nineteenth-century origins to the present; authors such as Brentano, Husserl, Scheler, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, Levinas, Henry, Marion, and Irigaray. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Existentialism
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Existentialism from its nineteenth-century origins to the present; philosophers such as Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Buber, Rosenzweig, Sartre, de Beauvoir, and Camus. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Current Continental Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students focus on major philosophers and philosophical approaches from the 20th and 21st century in reference to primary texts associated with areas such as: phenomenology; hermeneutics; critical theory; structuralism, deconstruction and poststructuralism; feminist theory; postmodernism; and related areas. Students explore themes such as understanding and interpretation, language and meaning, ideology critique, power and issues of social justice. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Comparative Philosophy
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Use of comparative methods, ranging from comparison and contrast of methods, problem framing, and argumentation, to cross-cultural problem-solving employing resources drawn from different traditions, to examine philosophical topics such as reality, knowledge, and morality. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Philosophy of Language
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. The nature of language; the various uses of language and their philosophical import; the nature of meaning, truth, reference and issues surrounding formal representations of natural languages. Prerequisites: PHIL 240 and junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: PHIL 240 and junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Probability and Decision
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Philosophy of probability, including such topics as competing interpretations of probability, confirmation theory and the relation between probability and degrees of belief; decision theory, including such topics as utility and expected utility, causal decision theory vs. evidential decision theory and game theory. Prerequisites: 3 hours of core MATH and 3 hours of PHIL.
prereq_text: 3 hours of core MATH and 3 hours of PHIL.

subject: PHIL
title: Social Choice
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. An exploration of social choice theory and different approaches to decision-making in groups, including applications to voting and democratic theory. Possible topics include interpersonal utility comparison, Arrow's impossibility theorem, Condorcet’s jury theorem, strategic voting, gerrymandering and political polarization. Prerequisite: 3 hours of core MATH and 3 hours of PHIL.
prereq_text: 3 hours of core MATH and 3 hours of PHIL.

subject: PHIL
title: Animal Welfare, Ethics and Law
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Key conceptions of animal welfare; approaches to animal ethics; analysis of important ideas in animal law; consideration of animal contexts such as agricultural, experimental, wild, companion and zoo animals. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
title: Medical Ethics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Critical analysis of major ethical issues in medicine including truthtelling, confidentiality, paternalism, genetics, abortion, infanticide, euthanasia and social justice in health care.

subject: PHIL
title: Ethics and Engineering
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students explore ethical and social theories, principles and engineering codes of ethics and their application to ethical challenges faced by engineers. Students engage with issues, such as satisfying responsibilities to an employer, client, fellow employees, one’s profession and the public; managing project pressures, risks, liability, regulations and environmental concerns. Students practice resolving challenges that arise from varying norms found in international and cross-cultural initiatives, especially on gifts, bribes and extortion. Students critically consider the ways engineers and engineering change the human experience, cultures and the environment. Students practice respectful and thoughtful dialogue on contemporary issues, become aware of their own perspectives and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they can competently navigate a variety of cultural environments. Coursework focuses on independent ethical analysis of real and hypothetical cases and on the techniques that can be used to evaluate them. Prerequisite: Junior classification.
prereq_text: Junior classification.

subject: PHIL
title: Professional Internship
description: Credits 0 to 6. 0 to 6 Other Hours. Practical experience in an institutional or organizational setting appropriate to analysis and understanding of issues in some area of applied philosophy. May be taken five times for credit. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor and department head.

subject: PHIL
title: Directed Studies

title: Research

subject: PHIL
title: Independent Honors Studies
description: Credits 1 to 3. 1 to 3 Other Hours. Directed independent studies in specific philosophical problems. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification either as Honors students or with overall GPR of 3.25; letter of approval from head of student's major department.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification either as Honors students or with overall GPR of 3.25; letter of approval from head of student's major department.

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health First Year Experience I
description: Credits 0-1. 0-1 Lecture Hours. The purpose of this course is to create a welcoming and affirming environment for new public health students. Through the course, students will develop self-efficacy, self-awareness and a sense of purpose while learning strategies for success both inside and outside the classroom. Topics include academic success skills and campus resources, wellness, Aggie traditions and core values, active engagement in and beyond the classroom, and social integration within the School of Public Health community. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisites: First-year and first-time-in-college public health student.
prereq_text: First-year and first-time-in-college public health student.

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health First Year Experience II
description: Credits 0-1. 0-1 Lecture Hours. The purpose of this course is to build on the foundation established in PHLT 101 by deepening students’ understanding of personal, academic and professional growth within public health. Students will continue developing self-efficacy, self-awareness and a sense of purpose while exploring topics such as leadership, communication, professionalism, career readiness and community engagement. Emphasis will be placed on applying academic success strategies, strengthening connections within the School of Public Health and preparing for continued success in upper-level coursework and future public health experiences. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisites: PHLT 101 .
prereq_text: PHLT 101 .

subject: PHLT
title: Healthy Lifestyles
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. (PHED 1304) Healthy Lifestyles. Health issues relevant to students; included are mental health, use and abuse of drugs, human sexuality, communicable diseases, environmental and consumer health.

subject: PHLT
title: First Generation Scholars I
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. First year experience; coverage of a range of topics for success inside and outside of the college classroom such as, self-efficacy, self-awareness, sense of purpose, active engagement in and out the classroom and social integration. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor; freshman classification; PHLT majors.
prereq_text: Approval of instructor; freshman classification; PHLT majors.

subject: PHLT
title: First Generation Scholars II
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. subject: PHLT
title: Broad Street Learning Community I
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Introduction to the program, development of critical thinking skills and international perspectives; introductory for the Public Health Studies Broad Street Honors Learning Community. Prerequisites: Admission to Broad Street Society Honors Learning Community; public health major.
prereq_text: Admission to Broad Street Society Honors Learning Community; public health major.

subject: PHLT
title: Special Topics In...
description: Credits 1 to 4. 1 to 4 Lecture Hours. 0 to 4 Lab Hours. Selected topics in an identified area of public health. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisite: PHLT major or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: PHLT major or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health Concepts
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Familiarization with public health including aspects such as different disciplines within the profession; local, national and international agencies that have interest in public health and public health code of ethics.

subject: PHLT
title: Foundations of Public Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. History, philosophy, development and careers of public health; core values, ethics, concepts, functions and essential services of public health; population health and health improvement. Prerequisites: Public health major or minor, junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major or minor, junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Social Context of Population Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of social determinants of population health and the socio-cultural roots of health improvement; socio-economic, behavioral and other factors that impact human health and contribute to health improvement and health disparities. Prerequisites: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: Biological Basis of Public Health Diseases & Disorders
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Biological Basis of Public Health Diseases & Disorders. Overview of the underlying science of human health and disease, considering biological mechanisms in the individual and in populations; topics include a broad set of categories of adverse health events: infectious and chronic diseases, exposure to pathogens and toxins, nutritional deficiencies, child and maternal health, biological bases of mental and behavioral health and addiction; examination of the interactions between biologic and sociocultural factors and the biology of epidemics; foundational understanding of opportunities to promote and protect health across the life course; application of disease knowledge in community and allied health professions. Prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: Epidemiology in Public Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles of epidemiology, a systematic approach to collecting and evaluating information on distributions of health outcomes in populations; history of epidemiology, descriptive epidemiology, epidemiologic methods, association and causation, evidence-based public health and applications. Prerequisites: Public Health major or minor; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Public Health major or minor; junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health in the Global Context
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Frameworks for understanding public health on a global scale; description of current and emerging global health priorities, such as emerging infectious diseases and chronic diseases; health systems reforms; cultural competence, human rights and ethics in global health; science and technological innovation for global health; global institutions and partnerships. Prerequisite: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Population Health Promotion
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of the application of social determinants of health to population health promotion; identification of socio-economic, behavioral, cultural, societal and political factors that influence population health promotion; utilization of a socio-ecological approach in health promotion to address major health-related needs and concerns of populations; use public health planning models, theories and methods for effective health promotion. Prerequisite: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health Writing
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Strategies to become more familiar with types of writing required as public health students or public health professionals; strengthens and increases general writing skills; establishes a foundation for continued development in writing. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Narrative Approach to Public Health
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Familiarization with the writing style required for public health; instruction in writing styles and narrative techniques to increase and strengthen writing abilities in public health disciplines such as environmental and occupational health, health promotion and community health sciences, health policy and management, epidemiology and biostatistics. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Health Care and Public Health System
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Two distinct systems – health care system: an individual and medical services model and the public health system: population level disease prevention and health education. Prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health Data Management and Assessment I
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Familiarization with using the CDC software Epi-Info for managing, analyzing and assessing population health data; focus on using Epi-Info to produce descriptive data reports including tables and graphs. Prerequisite: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health Data Management and Assessment II
description: Credits 2. 2 Lecture Hours. Continuation of PHLT 314 ; familiarization with using the CDC software Epi-Info for managing, analyzing and assessing population health data; focus on using Epi-Info to generate inferential statistics such as confidence intervals and p-values. Prerequisite: Public health major; grade of C or better in PHLT 314 .
prereq_text: Public health major; grade of C or better in PHLT 314 .

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health Data Management and Assessment
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Familiarization with descriptive and analytical statistics and biostatistical methods with using Microsoft Excel for managing, analyzing and assessing population health data; focus on using Microsoft Excel as a biostatistical tool to produce descriptive and analytical data reports including tables, graphs and biostatistical analysis results; to analyze and assess public health data for decision making. Prerequisites: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: Concepts in Health Education
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Preparation as peer health educators and campus community leaders; experiential learning; includes various health topics, program development, presentation and public speaking, communication, and group facilitation. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHLT 303 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in PHLT 303 .

subject: PHLT
title: The Environment and Public Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Public health core knowledge address factors that pose risks and hazards in homes and workplaces; methods for defining environmental contamination; identifying contaminants, pathogens and toxins; assessing risks and causality; ameliorating hazards. Prerequisites: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: Occupational Safety and Health I
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Regulations and topics of relevance to occupational health professionals; includes legislation and regulations, workers’ compensation, accident investigation, industrial hygiene, ergonomics and fire prevention with an emphasis on the health professionals’ role. Prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Accident Investigation
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles of accident investigation and how accidents happen in the workplace; integrates procedural, systematic, corrective and formative applications for the occupational health professional. Prerequisite: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Health Disparities and Diversity in Society
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of in-depth racial, ethnic, and cultural dimensions that underlie health and health disparities; emphasis on culture, social economic status and governmental policies as they influence the adaptation of health practices. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: /HLTH 342 Human Sexuality
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Many aspects of human sexuality; physiology and function of human reproductive system, factors involved in learning sex roles, biological and emotional motivations associated with the sexual aspects of life and their relationship to marriage and family planning. subject: PHLT
title: /HLTH 353 Drugs and Society
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Use and abuse of drugs in today's society; physiological, sociological and psychological factors involved. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in HLTH 210 or PHLT 302 . Cross Listing: HLTH 353/PHLT 353 .
prereq_text: Grade of C or better in HLTH 210 or PHLT 302 .

subject: PHLT
title: /HLTH 354 Medical Terminology for the Health Professions
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Designed for students interested in pursuing a career in a health, medical, scientific or other helping profession; develop medical word power skills combined with related health and disease knowledge. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: HLTH 354/PHLT 354 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: Women's Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. A broad range of health issues that are either unique to women or of special importance to women; information for the health consumer; preparation as an advocate of healthy lifestyles; awareness of the role health plays in the life of all women. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: HLTH 334 and WGST 334 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: /HLTH 333 Spirituality and Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of the relationship between spirituality, religion, health, health education and spiritual health; identification of techniques to measure spiritual health/wellness and enlighten healthcare professionals to the role spiritual health plays in healing; identification of spirituality topics important to health care professionals. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; School of Public Health majors. Cross Listing: HLTH 333/PHLT 363 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; School of Public Health majors.

subject: PHLT
title: Broad Street Learning Community II
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. International perspectives on public health and healthcare, comparative historical, political and cultural effects on public health; second course in the Broad Street Learning Community sequence. Prerequisites: Grade of B or better in PHLT 270 .
prereq_text: Grade of B or better in PHLT 270 .

subject: PHLT
title: /HLTH 403 Consumer Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Selection, evaluation and understanding of health information, medical services, advertising of products and sociocultural factors in consumer health protection. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: HLTH 403/PHLT 403 .
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification.

subject: PHLT
title: /HLTH 405 Rural Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Issues facing rural health care; emphasis on understanding the geographical characteristics of rural communities and their affect on health care delivery. prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; School of Public Health major.

subject: PHLT

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Prerequisites: PHLT 310 ; public health major.
prereq_text: PHLT 310 ; public health major.

title: Project Management in Public Health

title: Emergency Management in Public Health

Principles and practices of emergency management at the local, state, national and international levels; explores stages of emergency management such as preparedness, response and recovery; includes population health and the basic processes, approaches and interventions; emergency management systems in the United States; actors in emergency management. Prerequisites: Public health major; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

subject: PHLT
title: Public Health Leadership and Ethics

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in HLTH 222 and HLTH 331 , or a grade of C or better in PHLT 441 .

title: /MKTG 443 The Business of Healthcare
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Prerequisites: Business and Public Health majors; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor. Cross Listing: MKTG 443/PHLT 426 .

subject: PHLT
title: Human Factors and Ergonomic Health and Safety
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Principles of ergonomics including principles of anatomy, physiology, instrument design, and work environments; emphasis on ergonomic design, implementing ergonomic programs. Prerequisites: Public health major or minor; junior or senior classification.

title: /HLTH 440 Contemporary Issues for Community Health Interns

prereq_text: Grade of C or better in HLTH 222 , HLTH 231, HLTH 240 , HLTH 331 , BIOL 320 , and COMM 203 ; grade of C or better in ENGL 103 or ENGL 104 ; admission into internship program.

subject: PHLT
title: Strategies for Population Health Improvement

May be taken for credit up to six hours. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.

description: Credit 1. 1 Other Hour. Discussions of the transition from the college environment to professional school and/or career environments, including professional development. prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; grade of C or better in public health coursework; instructor approval; Public Health major.

title: Freshman Physics Orientation
description: Credit 1. 1 Lecture Hour. Critical thinking skills and problem solving in physics: time management and teaming skills. Prerequisite: Physics majors; non-majors requires approval of instructor.

Student-led organizations and informal physics programs in the department. Development of career skills. Prerequisites: First-semester transfer and change-of-major students.
prereq_text: First-semester transfer and change-of-major students.

subject: PHYS
title: Contemporary Issues in Science - Cosmos, Earth and Humanity
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. This team-taught, interdisciplinary course builds scientific literacy by examining contemporary issues — current questions, discoveries and challenges at the intersection of science and society. Topics may include the Big Bang, evolution, genetics, human reproduction and health, vaccines, drugs, artificial intelligence, cryptography and cybersecurity. Students will learn to evaluate scientific claims and critically analyze how science is presented in the news, on television and on social media. Cross Listing: ARSC 104 and BIOL 104 .

subject: PHYS
title: /ASTR 109 Big Bang and Black Holes
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Designed to give an intuitive understanding of the Big Bang and Black Holes, without mathematics, and de-mystify them for the non-scientist. Cross Listing: ASTR 109/PHYS 109 .

Prerequisite: Basic math skills; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Basic math skills; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: PHYS
title: Soft Matter Physics for Non-physicists
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. Modern physics in action with hands-on physics experience in simple experiments for non-physics majors; introduction to thermodynamics and soft matter physics; heat, temperature, thermodynamic efficiency, phase transitions, mechanical properties of soft matter, heat transfer mechanisms; physical measurements.

subject: PHYS

subject: POLS
title: The Mass Media and Politics
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication practices construct, circulate and contest political ideas and authority. Examines both how media influence political attitudes, participation and policy outcomes, and how political identity and conflict are shaped symbolically through news, entertainment, digital platforms and public rhetoric. Approaches may draw from social scientific models of media effects or rhetorical and critical analysis of political discourse. Emphasizes case-based evaluation of messages, sources and strategies across institutional, journalistic and citizen communication. Course content may include material involving political disagreement, conflict or graphic representation, examined for purposes of analysis rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops literacy in how political messages are constructed, distributed and interpreted across media systems. Applies to careers in journalism, political communication, public affairs, advocacy, research, law and civic or governmental work. Supports informed participation in democratic life by strengthening abilities to evaluate claims, recognize framing and distinguish between reporting, persuasion and manipulation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how politics is communicated not only through speeches or news outlets, but also through satire, visuals, entertainment formats, algorithmic feeds and policy messaging. Demonstrates how political messaging often blends information, symbolism and emotion to shape interpretation. Highlights the ways messages are interpreted differently depending on audience history, identity and media environment. Clarifies how communication shapes what counts as “fact,” “controversy” or “consensus” in public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of political news coverage, campaign strategy, advertising, agenda-setting, framing, propaganda models, political entertainment, social media activism and theories of representation. Consideration of media regulation, government communication practices, the influence of media on policymaking and the production of ideology. Course material may draw on historical and contemporary cases from local, national or international contexts, including disputed elections and outcomes, political controversies and crises, disinformation and surveillance, and contested social movements. Prerequisites: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 302 and JOUR 302 .

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. This course provides abstract theoretical and real-world practical approaches to leadership, the study of leadership and its application in the public service sector and/or other settings where leadership is required. This course studies leadership models, styles and practices highlighting the paradigm shift from the industrial age to the information age. This course focuses on the characteristics of leaders important to effective leadership outcomes, cross-cultural skills essential for effective leadership in international and culturally diverse settings, self-assessment and the development of a personal leadership vision, and the strategic skills necessary for providing vision and strategic direction of the organization. This course challenges students to reflect on personal experiences, seek out information on how to become more effective leaders and construct a leadership journey map for ongoing growth and development beyond the classroom. This course is broken into four blocks of instruction: leadership traits and principles, applied leadership, leadership ethics and leadership development. subject: PSAA
title: Public and Nonprofit Budgeting
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. This course provides an in-depth examination of the theories and practices of budgeting for public and nonprofit organizations, emphasizing the role of budget as a planning and management tool for the strategic allocation of scarce resources. In this course, students will have the opportunity to gain a comprehensive understanding of budget formats and budget processes, encompassing preparation, approval and execution, as well as revenue structures, capital budgeting, debt management across federal, state and local governments and the nonprofit sector. Through the analysis of real-world case studies and hands-on exercises utilizing Excel and practitioner-oriented workbooks, students will develop the technical skills necessary to manage organizational resources effectively. The course emphasizes technical proficiency in revenue forecasting, calculating budget variance and interpreting complex budgeting information to ensure the responsible stewardship of public resources. By the end of the semester, students will be equipped to navigate budgetary challenges, communicate findings through concise reporting and make informed decisions that advance organizational goals and public interests. The course provides an in-depth exploration of the core principles and the fundamentals of effectively leading people, teams and organizations by applying essential organizational behavior and leadership theories. The course provides a broad foundation in organizational analysis, including organizational culture, group behavior, communication and change management while specifically examining their practical applications in public and nonprofit organizations. In this course, students will explore different leadership styles and management approaches to decision-making processes that align with public service values, integrity and ethics. Skill development is a central focus, covering competencies such as motivation, coaching, teamwork, empowerment and conflict resolution. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, the course’s case studies and classroom discussions focus specifically on the public and nonprofit organizations, requiring students to propose administrative and policy solutions for complex management problems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PSAA 210 and PSAA 340/POLS 340 ; junior or senior classification.

subject: PVFA
title: Introduction to Arts in Health
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. This course introduces the interdisciplinary field of arts in health, tracing its development from ancient healing rituals to contemporary programs in hospitals, community centers, and public health initiatives. Students will examine philosophical foundations and cross-cultural histories of healing — music, movement, storytelling, visual symbolism and performance — as well as the methodological and epistemological shifts that have brought the arts into dialogue with modern healthcare. Drawing on perspectives from performance studies, anthropology, philosophy and the health sciences, the course explores how creative practices have been used to restore balance, foster resilience and generate meaning across time and cultures, and how these practices inform today’s evidence-based models and professional standards. Through lectures, case studies, guest speakers and participatory activities, students will engage with both the enduring questions of art’s relationship to well-being and the current best practices, ethical considerations and research methods shaping the field. As the entry point for advanced courses in Arts in Health programming, interactive design and practicum experiences, this course provides students with the critical vocabulary, historical perspective and conceptual frameworks needed to engage creatively and responsibly in the design and delivery of arts-based health initiatives.

subject: RELS
title: /COMM 257 Communication, Religion and the Arts
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of art and religion as forms of communication, with attention to how visual and artistic expression conveys meaning across cultures and traditions. Surveys artistic and media practices in religious and secular contexts, considering how aesthetics mediate religious experience and shape public understanding. Examines the role of art in supporting, questioning and/or challenging religious and social perspectives. Focus on interpretation and critique and dialogue of artifacts across diverse traditions, including attention to issues of pluralism, inequality, power, class and/or representation. Includes engagement with perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in interpreting and discussing art and religion across diverse cultural and historical contexts. Builds skills for engaging respectfully with differences in belief, practice and/or worldview. Strengthens intercultural awareness, critical thinking and creative communication skills, which can be applied to dialogue across divisions in civic, professional and interpersonal settings. Enhances understanding of how art and media shape public awareness of religion and contributes to broader conversations about meaning, identity and social conflict. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how the study of art and religion in communication differs from devotional or confessional approaches. Expands understanding of religion as a cultural and communicative practice shaped by history, power and interpretation. Highlights how art functions not only to express belief but also to question, challenge or reframe religious ideas. Introduces perspectives that encourage critical analysis of how religion and art intersect with broader cultural, social and/or political contexts. Emphasizes reflection on pluralism and contested meanings, deepening awareness of how religion and art shape, and are shaped by, the wider human experience. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication, art and religion as interrelated cultural practices; exploration of how visual and artistic forms convey meaning within Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, secular humanism and other traditions; consideration of iconoclasm, pluralism and the role of art in shaping or challenging belief and practices; attention to aesthetics, power, inequality and representation in religious and secular contexts. Course materials may also engage with the profane or the obscene when relevant to understanding how religion, art and communication define, resist and/or reframe cultural boundaries. Content may include perspectives that are unfamiliar, contested or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ways art and religion intersect in public life. Cross Listing: COMM 257/RELS 257 .

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces students to the archaeology and material culture of the Land of the Bible from the Epi-Paleolithic period through the first century A.D. The course examines the peoples, cities and societies of biblical times through material remains, integrating artifacts, iconography and texts to develop a holistic understanding of the ancient Near East. Students explore archaeological discoveries in relation to biblical narratives, including early agricultural communities, Canaanite city-states, Egyptian influence and Iron Age polities. The course also emphasizes the interpretation of archaeological evidence, historical context and the relationship of seafaring and trade to cultural development in the ancient biblical world. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in biblical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Epi-Paleolithic period; Neolithic period; first agriculturists; Chalcolithic period; Early Bronze Age; Early Bronze IV; Middle Bronze Age I-II; Late Bronze Age; Egyptian influence in Canaan; maritime trade and seafaring; Iron Age I; Sea Peoples; Philistines; United Monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon); Divided Monarchy; Persian period; archaeology of biblical texts; material culture; urbanism; Canaanite city-states; fortifications; religious architecture; iconography; ceramics; metallurgy; inscriptions; settlement patterns; excavation techniques; interpretation of artifacts; relationship between archaeology and biblical narrative; cultural geography and human-environment interaction. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: ANTH 317/RELS 317 .

title: /ANTH 403 Anthropology of Religion
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Develops skills to critically assess research findings, analyze differing viewpoints and perspectives and formulate hypothetical research agendas. Engages potentially charged topics in diverse settings, challenging students to explore their own assumptions and biases regarding their personal worldview. Fosters greater understanding of self-awareness and personal responsibility in society through exploration of the diversity of religious behaviors. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers theoretical approaches to the study of religion; analyzes religious features including symbolism, myth and ritual; studies religious specialists, magic, divination and witchcraft; explores altered states of consciousness; evaluates beliefs regarding gods, spirits, souls, ghosts and death; assesses religious change and searches for new meaning; examines religious violence and fundamentalism; and investigates vernacular religion, secularism, atheism and irreligion. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus. subject: RELS
title: /ANTH 438 Ancient Egypt II - Egypt in Decline
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from the end of the New Kingdom through the Graeco-Roman period, focusing on the years 1185–30 BCE. Examines the decline of pharaonic power, the rise of foreign influences and the resilience of Egyptian society under Libyan, Nubian, Persian and Ptolemaic rule. Reviews the interplay between political, social and cultural dynamics, exploring Egyptian adaptations to Hellenistic dominance, while tracing continuity and change in art, religion, literature and urban development. Through lectures, readings and analyses of primary and secondary sources, students gain a humanistic understanding of Egyptian civilization during its final dynastic phases and develop skills in interpreting archaeological, textual and iconographic evidence. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues pertaining to ancient Egypt. TOPICS AND THEMES. Decline of pharaonic authority; fragmentation of the Egyptian state; Libyan, Nubian and Persian interventions; internal political strife and social change; resilience of Egyptian cultural identity; Ptolemaic dynasty and Hellenistic influence; Cleopatra VII and the last Ptolemies; Alexandria as a cultural and economic center; Greco-Egyptian art, religion and literature; continuity and transformation of Egyptian traditions; interactions between foreign rulers and Egyptian elites; archaeological and textual methods for reconstructing late Egyptian history; humanistic approaches to interpreting material culture; synthesis of historical, artistic and archaeological evidence. Prerequisites: Completion of ANTH 436/RELS 436 or RELS 436/ANTH 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: ANTH 438/RELS 438 .
