subject: SPMT
title: Diversity in Sport Organizations
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examine an encompassing perspective of diversity within North American and international sport organizations. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: SPMT
title: International Sport Business
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Sport has evolved into a global industry, with organizations increasingly expanding into international markets to access new consumers, revenue streams and development opportunities. Given this shift, current and aspiring sport industry professionals must understand various aspects of international sport business, such as economic and legal environments, governance structures, cultural differences, communication styles, management practices and the strategic challenges associated with operating in the global marketplace. Case studies, lectures, scenarios and both individual and collaborative research projects introduce students to a range of international sports organizations (e.g., FIFA, IOC). Explore potential opportunities and issues, with a particular emphasis on examining distinctions between the U.S. sport industry and sport markets worldwide. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prereq_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: SPMT
title: Sport Governance
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Governance and policy development in sport management; managerial activities related to governance, strategic management, ethics in sport, governance and policy development in specific sport contexts. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. subject: SPMT
title: Predictive Analytics in Sport
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Overview of predictive analytics utilizing linear regression-based modeling approaches to analyze sport-related data; learning the iterative process of model building through trial and error and by working on hands-on problems and a team-based project; collection and analysis of sport-related data using predictive analytics, whether the dependent variable is continuous (i.e., attendance or revenue) or binary (i.e., a win or a loss) in nature, or whether group membership is being predicted; selection of appropriate model given the data to be analyzed or research question to be answered, the selection of appropriate independent variables based on knowledge of the sport industry, theory, or the scientific literature, interpretation of coefficients and measures of model fit, and ability to communicate advanced statistical information to a lay audience. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in STAT 201 , STAT 301, STAT 302 , or STAT 303 .

title: Urban Analytical Methods I
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Study of various analytical techniques used in urban and regional decision making; quantitative approaches to analyze and manipulate data; utilization of statistical packages for data, analysis and communication to enhance urban planning modeling. Prerequisite: URPN majors only or approval of instructor.
prereq_text: URPN majors only or approval of instructor.

subject: URPN
title: Digital Communication I
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Applications of computer graphics, rendering, and visualization software in urban design, landscape architecture, and environmental analysis; introduction to basic concepts and principles of graphic composition; rendering, visualization, and linkages to landscape-referenced data. Prerequisite: Landscape Architecture and Urban Planning majors only or approval of instructor.

subject: URPN
title: Communication, Engagement and Ethics for Planners
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Exploration of community and stakeholder engagement in the development of urban and regional plans; theory and practice of communication and its relationship with urban planning process; study of effective listening, managing conflict and engaging in difficult conversations; evaluation of how verbal, written, graphical and non-verbal communications contribute to conveying planning concepts and values transparently, clearly and effectively to a variety of planning audiences and contexts; analyzes barriers that reduce participation in planning processes and evaluates methods for achieving broad and representative participation; exploration of planning ethics and related ethics in public-decision-making. title: Urban Analytical Methods II
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. subject: URPN
title: Land Development I

subject: URPN

subject: URPN
title: Artificial Intelligence for Urban Design
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. In the digital age, AI technologies are revolutionizing landscape architecture and urban planning, providing innovative solutions for complex design and planning challenges. This course offers a comprehensive introduction to the application of AI tools in these fields. Students will explore practical applications such as writing design statements, conducting research, creating and modifying images and generating high-quality renderings. The course integrates key aspects of landscape architecture design, such as site analysis, conceptual design and detailed planning, as well as urban planning processes including land-use planning, infrastructure management and smart city solutions. Through a practical, "learning by doing" approach, students will develop visual and textual communication skills essential for translating design concepts into various digital formats. They will gain hands-on experience with AI tools to enhance their ability to perform site analysis, generate design alternatives, optimize designs for sustainability and user experience, and simulate urban growth. Additionally, the course emphasizes ethical considerations, ensuring students understand the social impacts of AI and learn to use AI responsibly to create equitable and inclusive designs. Prerequisites: Landscape Architecture and Urban Planning majors or approval of instructor.

subject: URPN
title: Issues in Environmental Quality

subject: VIST
title: Foundations of Digital Filmmaking
description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 5 Lab Hours. This course introduces students to the essential creative, technical and analytical foundations of digital filmmaking. Emphasizing the integration of production craft and cinematic literacy, students engage in hands-on exercises in camera operation, lighting, sound recording and non-linear editing while critically analyzing how these techniques shape meaning, emotion and rhythm. Through the study of film form, aesthetics and visual storytelling, students develop the ability to translate abstract narrative ideas into concrete audiovisual expressions. The course positions filmmaking as both a practical craft and an interpretive art, an iterative process of seeing, composing, recording and refining, linking the expressive choices made on set and in post-production to the analytical understanding of cinematic form. By the end of the term, students will have completed a short digital project demonstrating technical fluency, aesthetic awareness and reflective critical insight. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 106 or VIST 283 .

subject: VIST
title: Digital Storytelling - Narrative Design Across Media
description: Credits 3. 2 Lecture Hours. 2 Lab Hours. This course introduces students to the creative, analytical and technical techniques required to translate rich narrative ideas into innovative digital experiences across multiple media forms. Building from script analysis and visual storytelling fundamentals, students will explore how story structure, character and thematic intent transform when reimagined for screen, immersive and interactive contexts. The course spans linear and nonlinear modes of narrative, from short-form cinematic sequences and documentary hybrids to site-specific installations, augmented reality environments and online participatory works. Through both individual and collaborative exercises, students learn to adapt written and conceptual materials into digital storytelling prototypes that integrate visual, spatial and experiential design. Students will also examine the cultural and industrial frameworks surrounding intermedia and transmedia production, including intellectual property development, adaptation ethics and cross-platform authorship. By semester’s end, participants will have created a portfolio-ready project demonstrating their ability to translate complex textual or thematic material into a compelling, media-specific form of digital storytelling. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 305 or VIST 372 , or approval of instructor.

subject: VIST
title: Cinema Editing and Post-Production
description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 5 Lab Hours. This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the art, theory and technical practice of film editing and the post-production pipeline. Anchored in a non-linear editing system the fundamental principles taught are applicable across all professional, leading, editing platforms. Students explore the history and theory of film montage, continuity editing and stylistic techniques across fiction and non-fiction cinema. Technical training covers the complete editorial workflow, from media management, assembly, rough and fine cuts, to post-processing stages that include sound design fundamentals, professional color correction and grading, and final delivery for multiple distribution formats. The primary goal is to teach students to think like editors, understanding post-production as both a technical discipline and a vital phase of cinematic storytelling where rhythm, structure and affect are refined into expressive coherence. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 200 .

description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 5 Lab Hours. This course explores the principles and practices of cinematography and lighting in the context of contemporary virtual production. Students engage with both the practical craft of image, making and the critical analysis of cinematic form, investigating how light, lens and movement operate as expressive, technical and interpretive tools. Through film analysis, design exercises and virtual simulation with a 3D real-time game and simulation development system, the course bridges the traditions of studio cinematography with emerging digital workflows. Students learn how to construct, evaluate and refine cinematic imagery, translating aesthetic and narrative intention into visual and spatial composition. The course emphasizes cinematography as a language of thought and emotion, uniting analytical insight with creative experimentation in both physical and virtual environments. description: Credits 3. 1 Lecture Hour. 5 Lab Hours. This course serves as the culminating experience for the virtual production focus area, integrating prior coursework in digital storytelling, virtual cinematography, lighting and post-production. Structured as a simulated professional production environment, students work in small teams to conceive, pitch, plan and execute a short narrative film utilizing the university’s LED volume stage (or equivalent virtual production technology). The course emphasizes advanced project management, iterative content development (ICVFX/Unreal Engine asset creation), collaborative pre-visualization and the rigorous schedule of a physical virtual production shoot. The semester functions as a single, continuous production cycle culminating in post-production finishing and professional delivery, resulting in a portfolio-ready short film that demonstrates technical fluency, creative leadership and team-based collaboration. description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Students need to be able to describe potential impact of specific diseases to wildlife population, if it is zoonotic and/or can be transmitted to/from domestic animals. subject: WGST
title: Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course explores the core concepts of the interdisciplinary field of women’s and gender studies, focusing on various perspectives, scholarship, theories and histories of sex, gender and sexuality; examines theories of intersectionality, analyzing the interplay among race/racism, class/classism, sex/sexism, disability/ableism, nation/nationalism, religion/religious bias among other factors in gendered experiences and systems; surveys feminist, queer, anti-racist, decolonial and/or global scholarship that examines how social institutions and control mechanisms enact power, privilege and bias; engages controversial material and historical and/or contemporary case studies that challenge and/or support conventional understandings of gender, sex, sexuality, identity and power as necessary to achieve course learning outcomes and proficiency in disciplinary concepts and ideas. TOPICS. Course may include and is not limited to discussions and descriptions of violence, sexual assault, homophobia, transphobia, femicide, genocide, familial/domestic abuse, forced sterilization and workplace harassment; investigations of political controversies centered on reproductive and gender healthcare, gender identity, policing and/or immigration; analysis of popular culture and creative expression, including but not limited to: performance, literature, drag, music, visual culture; examinations of primary texts from historical and/or contemporary social movements and activists across the United States and around the globe; investigations of contemporary and historical labor relations and globalization; analyses and descriptions of anatomy, physiology and psychology. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives.

subject: WGST
title: /SOCI 215 Introduction to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Studies
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an interdisciplinary survey of the histories and theories regarding lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer (LGBTQ+) identities and communities. The course focuses on current scholarship addressing the social construction of sex, sexuality and gender; institutional ways in which homophobia, biphobia and transphobia are systematically deployed; histories and examples of LGBTQ+ activism; evolution of desire and subjectivity; and the contributions of queer scholarship in understanding society. TOPICS. Course may include but is not limited to discussions and readings that address queer approaches to institutions; intersections of sexual and gender identity with race, class, ability/disability and/or nationality; digital activism; gender violence; controversies related to LGBTQ+ issues and politics, among others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives. Cross Listing: SOCI 215/WGST 205 .

subject: WGST
title: /SOCI 207 Introduction to Gender and Society
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Explore the historical, cultural, social, economic and political dimensions of gender; define and distinguish gender roles and norms and identify sociological theories important to the study of gender; examine ideas and expectations about gender including historical and contemporary norms; understanding of scholarship on this topic increases intercultural competence and effective cross-cultural communication for participation in civic contexts and public life. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The specific topics and readings assigned may vary depending on the instructor’s areas of focus and research expertise. Cross Listing: SOCI 207/WGST 207 .

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. Examine human sexuality through biological, psychological, social, relational and cultural lenses. Explore topics including love, attraction, sexual health, sexual victimization, diversity and sexuality as a commodity. Apply the bio-psycho-social-cultural model to understand how various factors shape sexual experiences and attitudes. Develop skills to assess sexual health, promote well-being and articulate what healthy sexuality means. Prerequisite: PBSI 107 . Cross Listing: PBSI 210/WGST 210 .

Use empirical and theoretical research to investigate the roles of gender across social institutions such as family, state, law, marriage, nation and others. Students will learn to apply gender theories and empirical research to analyze current social issues and debates, both locally and globally. By the end of the course, students will be able to evaluate how gender shapes outcomes and how research explains change. In line with the American Sociological Association, sociology is the study of social life, social change and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations and societies and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities; from deviance to organized crime; from religious traditions to state institutions; and from the divisions of race, gender and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. subject: WGST
title: /COMM 407 Gender, Race and Media
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how gender, race, sexuality, ethnicity and related identities are produced, represented, negotiated, contested, consumed and/or performed in relation to media. Explores contributions of historically marginalized groups to media production, alongside analysis of how these groups have been portrayed as characters, audiences, communities and/or target markets. Focuses on media as a site of competing commercial, cultural, political, satirical and/or resistance narratives, rather than as a single, unified voice. Emphasizes critical interpretation of media texts and systems, while allowing space for multiple viewpoints and interpretations. Course material may include historical and contemporary examples that reflect both progress and controversy, analyzed for their cultural and communicative significance. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages issues central to media literacy, political economy, representation and audience awareness in contemporary communication industries. Builds recognition of the ways portrayals of gender and race shape perception, credibility and/or trust in journalism, entertainment, advertising, representatives, community and public communication. Supports careers in communication, media industries, public relations, education, nonprofit work and leadership roles where navigating diverse audiences is essential. Supports informed decision-making in professional and civic contexts by highlighting how media representations influence identity, inclusion and public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies that studying media portrayals of gender and race is not limited to celebration or criticism but involves examining how representation functions within broader cultural, social, economic, political and/or institutional systems. Illustrates how media are grounded in economies of production, representation and consumption across platforms, products and pipelines. Considers ways media might be empowering, stereotypical, commercial and/or transformative, depending on context, audience and community. Promotes awareness that interpretations of media content may differ across social, cultural and/or generational perspectives and that disagreement over meaning is part of scholarly analysis rather than a flaw in the material. Normalizes engagement with sensitive or contested topics as a means of understanding how media both reflect and shape public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media across film, television, news, advertising, music and digital platforms through production, representation and consumption; analysis of gender, race, ethnicity and intersectional identities in historical and contemporary contexts; consideration of media production practices, audience reception and the economic and institutional forces shaping representation; examination of stereotypes, invisibility, empowerment narratives and commercialized identity; discussion of how media both reinforce and challenge social norms related to power, privilege and belonging. Course material may include content that reflects real-world disparities or conflicting viewpoints. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 407/WGST 407 .

subject: WGST
title: /COMM 411 Representations of Motherhood
description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of motherhood as a cultural, social and communicative construct rather than a singular biological or personal identity. Examines how ideas about motherhood are created, reinforced or challenged through literature, film, popular media, digital media, political rhetoric, public policy, advertising, news, medical institutions and/or everyday discourse across different time periods and cultural contexts. Considers both idealized and marginalized portrayals, attending to such matters as gender, race, class, sexuality, ability and nation. Course material may include historical texts, contemporary examples, commentary and/or fictional representations. Content may include portrayals that are celebratory, critical or controversial, examined for purposes of interpretation. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds critical literacy for analyzing how cultural expectations shape perceptions of family, caregiving and social roles. Promotes awareness of how media narratives, cultural practices and public discourse influence policies, workplace norms, interpersonal expectations and public debates surrounding parenting, labor and care work. Supports workforce preparation in fields such as media, healthcare, public health, social work, policy development, education and public communication where sensitivity to diverse family structures and practices is essential. Enhances academic readiness for further study in rhetoric, gender studies, media studies and/or cultural studies. Encourages reflection on how public narratives about motherhood have evolved over time, affect social inclusion, policy decisions and public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how ideas about motherhood vary across cultures, eras, socio-economic groups and/or ideological perspectives, challenging assumptions of universality. Encourages recognition of both biological and socially constructed dimensions of maternal identity. Clarifies the difference between personal belief and cultural representation, prompting reflection on how individuals internalize or resist public narratives about care, responsibility and motherhood and how it may modify behavior. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of motherhood in literature, film, television, music, news, advertising, music and digital media; historical shifts in maternal ideals; feminist and anti-feminist discourses; motherhood and labor; political uses of maternal identity; race, class and marginalized motherhoods; disability and motherhood; reproductive technology and infertility narratives; representation of motherhood in children's literature and films, childfree identities and resistance to maternal norms. Course material may involve emotional and sensitive content such as depictions of grief, trauma, marginalization or public controversy as relevant to understanding how motherhood is framed in culture. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 411/WGST 411 .

description: Credits 3. 3 Lecture Hours. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of how gender shapes and is shaped by communication across interpersonal, organizational and public contexts. Examines how people express, interpret and negotiate gender in everyday interaction, media environments and/or institutional settings. Explores both stability and change in gendered expectations, roles and identities. Course content and discussions may touch on differing perspectives or points of disagreement for purposes of understanding communication dynamics surrounding gender. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports career pathways in media, public service, advocacy, education, law, nonprofit work and other community-facing professions by examining communication as grounded in diverse communities and lived experiences. Enhances preparation for careers involving interpersonal interaction, public communication, education, health, social work, policy development, human relations, consulting, advocacy or management. Builds recognition of how communication norms vary across individuals, cultures and contexts, which is an essential competency for workplace effectiveness, civic participation and collaborative problem-solving. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Explores how communication research addresses biological sex alongside cultural understandings of gender identity and gender roles and how each may influence interaction across different contexts. Highlights that everyday assumptions about gender and communication can vary across individuals, cultures and/or historical periods. Encourages examination of multiple scholarly perspectives on how gender-related patterns emerge, are perceived or are reinforced through communication, without prescribing a single interpretive lens. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of gendered language, voice and nonverbal expression; feminist and critical perspectives on communication and gender; communication across friendship, romantic, family and workplace relationships; leadership, authority and collaboration in professional settings; media portrayals of femininity, masculinity and gender diversity; intersections of gender with race, sexuality, class, nationality, religion and/or ability; communication surrounding health, body image, caregiving or identity disclosure; historical and cross-cultural perspectives on gender roles and expectations; analysis of humor, conflict, persuasion or storytelling through a gendered lens. Course material may reference real-world cases involving disagreement or controversy as relevant to understanding communication dynamics. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 420/WGST 420 .
